migration: Mostly resident in the Lowveld, but its movements are poorly understood: southern African birds are described as more nomadic than migratory, and numbers seem to build up in north-eastern South Africa in winter. Breeds August to February, mainly September to November.
size: 26-30 cm: about the size of a dove, female a little bigger than the male.
keys: Small pale grey hawk with fine rufous-orange barring on whitish underparts
Red eye in the adult male (more orange-yellow in the female), yellow cere and legs
Plain grey rump (no white) and an almost plain grey tail at rest
Juvenile brown above, with brown streaks and drop-shaped spots on the breast

confuse.how: Has an obvious white rump, a dark eye and a red cere and legs; grey breast in the adult, and some birds are all black.
Smaller and darker above, with a yellow eye, a narrow white rump band and two white spots on the upper tail.
Bigger and much darker slate or brown above, with a yellow eye and coarser barring; a forest and riverine bird.

voice: A sharp, high two-note call, the first note higher and the second longer, repeated noisily when breeding; Fork-tailed Drongos often imitate it.
behaviour: Hunts from cover in a leafy tree and drops onto lizards, its main prey, also taking small birds and insects. Moves through the bush in short flights from tree to tree with a few flaps and a glide; small birds scatter and babblers or drongos mob it.
memo: The lizard hawk: small, pale grey, red-eyed, no white rump.

migration: Resident and sedentary, though young birds disperse after breeding. Uncommon and easily overlooked in tall riverine woodland. Lays September to December, peaking in October.
size: 23-27 cm: the smallest African hawk, about the size of a dove; the female is a little larger than the male.
keys: Tiny hawk, dark slate-grey above, white below finely barred rufous
Narrow white band across the rump and two white spots in the middle of the upper tail
Yellow eye, yellow cere and yellow legs
Juvenile brown above with drop-shaped spots below, brown eye

confuse.how: Paler grey above with no white rump or white tail spots, and red or deep orange eyes.
Also has a white rump, but is larger, with a plain grey throat and breast and red cere and legs.
Much bigger, with a grey or greenish cere and no white rump; the male's tail has only small spots.

voice: Usually silent away from the nest; near it a high series of “kik-kik-kik” or “kew-kew-kew” notes, the male higher-pitched.
behaviour: Hunts from a perch hidden in dense foliage, making a short, fast dash to snatch small birds such as sunbirds, waxbills and weavers in flight, mostly early and late in the day. Very aggressive near its nest, chasing off larger raptors.
memo: A dove-sized hawk with a white rump and two white tail spots: the bushveld's pocket ambusher.

migration: Resident and largely sedentary; juveniles leave the parents' territory once independent. In the Lowveld it lives mainly in riverine forest and dense woodland. Lays from July to December, peaking September to November, which is when display flights are most frequent.
size: 35-40 cm, the female about a third larger than the male: roughly the size of a pigeon, but long-tailed and broad-winged.
keys: Dark slate-grey upperparts (male) or dark brown (female)
White underparts finely barred rufous-brown, more rufous in the male
Yellow eye, yellow legs, dull greenish-yellow cere
Juvenile brown above, white below with bold brown drop-shaped spots, brown eye

confuse.how: Smaller and paler, with plain pale-grey upperparts, a deep red eye in adults and faint pinkish barring below; a bird of open savanna rather than riverine forest.
Much smaller (about 25 cm), with a white rump band and two white spots on the upper tail.
Red cere and legs, plain grey throat and breast, and a white rump.

voice: A sharp, dry “krit” click, like two stones knocked together, repeated every 2-3 seconds, mostly in display flight in the first half-hour after dawn.
behaviour: An ambush hunter that sits hidden in dense foliage and dashes out after birds, rodents and lizards. Early in the morning it circles very high over the canopy, so high that often only its regular clicking call betrays it.
memo: A click falling from the dawn sky: the goshawk is on patrol.

migration: Resident wherever there is permanent shallow water with floating plants. It is nomadic: when a pan or dam dries up the birds leave, and they quickly colonise new temporary wetlands after the rains. Breeds all year, mainly November to March.
size: 23-31 cm (female larger than male): a body between a blackbird and a moorhen, perched on very long legs and huge toes.
keys: Rich chestnut body and wings, black flight feathers
White face, throat and upper breast fading into a golden chest; black line through the eye and black hindneck
Pale blue bill and frontal shield on the forehead
Extremely long grey toes; juvenile has white underparts, a white eyebrow and no blue shield

confuse.how: All black with a yellow-green bill and bright red legs; skulks at the reed edge rather than walking openly over the lilies.
Dark grey-black, with a red frontal shield and yellow bill tip; usually swims, with white flashes under the tail.

voice: Noisy: sharp, rasping “krrrek” notes, short repeated “kreep” series and barking calls, given on the ground and in flight.
behaviour: The “lily-trotter” walks over water lilies on its enormous toes, flipping leaves to pick off insects. Roles are reversed: the female mates with several males, and each male alone incubates and raises the chicks, carrying them tucked under his wings with only their long legs dangling out.
memo: The lily-trotter: chestnut, blue forehead, and a single dad carrying the kids under his wings.

migration: Sedentary resident, fairly common in broad-leaved bushveld woodland; pairs or family groups stay in their territory year-round. Breeds August to January, peaking September to November.
size: 15-17 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow, but slimmer and more upright.
keys: Plain, dull mouse-brown upperparts with no streaks or bold marks
Paler, buffy-grey underparts, slightly darker on the breast
Sits upright on a low open perch, plain face with a dark eye
Juvenile heavily spotted and streaked with buff and dark brown

confuse.how: Summer visitor with a streaked crown and fine streaks on the breast; sits higher and sallies into the air rather than dropping to the ground.
Blue-grey rather than brown, with a white eye-ring and a dark line through the eye.

voice: Rather quiet: soft chirps and a subdued, warbling song, with harsh scolding notes when alarmed.
behaviour: Watches from a low perch and drops onto insects on the ground, like a small shrike. Sometimes joins mixed bird parties. Young can stay with their parents for a very long time, in one case over a year and a half.
memo: The mouse-coloured flycatcher: plain brown, perched low, dropping to the ground.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, and the commonest waterfowl in southern Africa. Ringed birds wander 70-800 km, so numbers at dams and pans change with the water levels. Lays eggs in any month, with a peak from May to December.
size: 63-73 cm: a big goose-like duck, much larger than a Mallard, standing tall on long legs.
keys: Pale buff-grey goose with a dark chestnut patch around the eye
Chestnut patch in the middle of the lower breast and a thin brown collar
Bright pink bill and long pink legs
In flight, big white forewing panels against black flight feathers. Sexes alike (male larger); juvenile duller, without the eye and breast patches

confuse.how: Much bigger and mostly glossy black with white on the face and belly, red bill and bare red face, no chestnut eye patch.
Black-and-white, with a speckled white head and neck and a black bill (with a large knob in breeding males), no buff plumage or pink legs.

voice: Noisy and quarrelsome: the female gives loud, raucous honks, while the male makes a hoarse, breathy hissing given in rapid bursts, likened to a steam engine.
behaviour: Pairs are fiercely territorial and chase intruders in noisy aerial fights. Most nests are on the ground near water, but it often takes over old nests of Hamerkop, crows or raptors, or tree holes, sometimes high up: the day-old goslings simply jump down to the ground.
memo: The pink-legged goose with a black eye, honking at every pan.

migration: In northeastern South Africa it is resident while breeding but wanders nomadically outside the breeding season, so it turns up irregularly. Egg-laying can happen all year but peaks from December to April. Described as fairly common in the northern half of Kruger, scarcer further south.
size: 11-12 cm: a little smaller than a House Sparrow, with a thick, pale conical bill.
keys: Male: a bright red band across the white throat, as if its throat had been cut
Sandy-brown plumage finely barred and scaled black all over, with a chestnut patch on the belly in the male
Thick, pale grey-pink bill and pink legs
Female lacks the red band and is paler below with bolder bars; juveniles like duller adults

confuse.how: Non-breeding birds are streaked, not barred, and have a bright red bill instead of a pale one.
The female is plain grey-brown below with a streaked back, without the fine black barring of the Cut-throat.

voice: Chirpy, sparrow-like or parrot-like calls; nesting pairs give a loud “keee-air” and a faint “eee-eee-eee” in flight.
behaviour: Usually in pairs or small flocks feeding on the ground on seeds and termites, often mixed with queleas and weavers, and it needs to drink. It rarely builds a nest from scratch: the pair stuffs a grass ball lined with feathers inside an old weaver or buffalo-weaver nest, or a woodpecker hole.
memo: A barred little finch with its throat “slit” in red.

migration: Sedentary resident of Lowveld woodland: one ringed bird was found 9 years later less than 5 km from where it was ringed. Breeds in summer, with eggs laid from about September to February, peaking September to November.
size: 12-15 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow, with a long, thin, pointed bill.
keys: Breeding male: crimson head, breast and mantle, contrasting with clean white belly
Long, slender reddish-orange bill (heavier, conical bills in other weavers)
Female and non-breeding male: yellow head and breast, white belly, grey-brown back, yellow edges to the wing feathers
Juvenile paler, with a grey bill

confuse.how: The breeding male can have a red head, but it has a black mask, a thick conical red bill, a streaked brown back, and lives in flocks.
Females are yellowish all over, including the belly, with a thick conical bill; Red-headed females have a yellow head but a white belly and a slim bill.
Bigger, with a heavy black or horn bill, a spotted black-and-yellow back and yellow underparts.

voice: A rather unsteady song of fast, squeaky, crackling notes; the alarm is a sharp “chi-chi”.
behaviour: Unlike most weavers it eats mainly insects and spiders, often hanging upside down to probe dead leaf clusters and bark, and joins mixed bird parties. The male alone builds an untidy upside-down bottle nest of twigs and leaf midribs (not grass), with a long entrance tube pointing down, often hung on wires, windmills or thatch eaves.
memo: The red-headed weaver with a slim red bill that builds with twigs, not grass.

migration: An intra-African wanderer whose movements follow the rains and the snails they bring. In South Africa it lives mainly in the Lowveld, with a small population of a few hundred in Kruger; numbers vary a lot between years and it is most likely in the wet season, when pans fill. Breeds in colonies in the rainy season, peaking January to March.
size: 80-94 cm: a medium-sized stork, smaller than a White Stork but much bigger than a Hadada Ibis.
keys: Looks all black at a distance, with a green, bronze or purplish gloss up close
Heavy dull-brown bill with a visible gap between the mandibles, which only touch at the tip
Grey-black legs; often wades slowly alone or in loose groups at pan edges
Immature browner and duller, with a straight bill and little or no gap

confuse.how: Glossy black too, but with a bright red bill and legs and a clean white belly.
Smaller, with a white belly and lower back, and a short greenish bill with no gap.
Smaller and browner, with a long thin downcurved bill, and very noisy “ha-ha-ha” calls.

voice: Usually silent when feeding. At colonies and in groups it gives harsh, rasping croaks and honks.
behaviour: A snail specialist: it pins a snail down, cuts through the trapdoor (operculum) with the bill tip and shakes out the body without breaking the shell. Freshwater mussels are harder: it may line them up on the shore and wait for the sun to kill them so they open.
memo: The stork whose bill doesn't close: a black snail-opener.

migration: Resident all year, holding territories in dense riverine thickets and bush clumps. The lowland race oleaginus occurs in the Limpopo and Mozambique lowlands. Breeds September to April, mainly October to December.
size: 15-18 cm: a bit bigger than a House Sparrow, about the size of a Dark-capped Bulbul but slimmer.
keys: Plain, dull olive-green bird, paler and greyer below, with no markings at all
Striking pale, creamy-white eye in the adult (dark grey in the juvenile)
Usually hidden in dense foliage, betrayed by its loud song
Sexes alike

confuse.how: Bright yellow underparts, browner back and a dark eye with white eyelids, in noisy groups.
Brown with a black head and crest and a yellow vent, far more conspicuous and perches in the open.

voice: A loud, piercing whistle “Willie!” (Afrikaans name Gewone Willie), in the breeding season followed by a babbling trill: “Willie! Come out and fight!… scaaared”, the last word drawn-out and nasal.
behaviour: Sings all day and all year, even in the midday heat when other birds are silent, yet stays almost invisible in the thicket. Eats mostly fruit (wild figs, num-nums, mistletoe) and is an important seed disperser; also takes aloe nectar and insects.
memo: “Willie! Come out and fight!” shouts the plain green bird nobody sees.

migration: Resident wherever there is permanent, still or slow-moving water with perches. It moves to other water when a dam or pan dries up or food runs short. Breeds in colonies, mostly from October to December, often mixed with cormorants and herons.
size: About 80 cm, including a very long neck and tail: as long as a Grey Heron but low-slung, like a cormorant.
keys: Long, thin, kinked neck and a straight, dagger-pointed bill with no hook
Male glossy black, with a rufous foreneck and a white stripe down each side of the neck
Long white streaks on the back and a long, fan-shaped tail
Female and juvenile browner and paler; juvenile lacks the white neck stripe

confuse.how: Much smaller, with a short neck, a stubby hooked bill and a red eye; it does not swim with only its neck showing.

voice: Mostly silent; around the nest it gives harsh croaks, clicks and grunts.
behaviour: Swims submerged with only its snake-like neck showing, hence the name “snakebird”. Underwater it spears fish with its pointed bill, then flicks them into the air to swallow them head first. Its plumage is not waterproof, so it often perches with wings spread to dry.
memo: The snakebird: a neck rising from the water, then a bird drying its wings on a stump.

migration: Resident and sedentary all year, staying near its breeding area. Outside the breeding season it joins mixed feeding flocks of small birds moving through the woodland canopy.
size: 8-9 cm and about 6.5 g: one of the smallest birds in Africa, much smaller than a sparrow, about the size of a crombec without a tail.
keys: Tiny and round, with a very short tail and a short, sharp, pointed bill
Plain grey upperparts
Buffy face and forehead; whitish-grey throat and breast
Cinnamon-buff belly and flanks

confuse.how: Larger, with a long, slightly curved bill and a tiny tail. Creeps along branches rather than hanging from leaves.
Green above and yellowish, with an obvious white eye-ring; often in noisier flocks.

voice: High, thin, squeaky contact notes, given constantly as the group moves through the canopy; easy to miss.
behaviour: Works through the foliage in pairs or small family groups, often hanging upside down among leaves and flowers bigger than itself. Its hanging felt nest has a false entrance above the real one. The parents slip in through a hidden flap and close it behind them, sealing it with spider web. In Kruger the nests are said to look like the webs of social spiders.
memo: A grey-and-buff cotton ball with a fake front door.

migration: Resident all year. The south-eastern lowland race (traylori) is thought to be essentially sedentary, unlike the race further north and west, which moves into Zambia and Malawi after breeding. Breeds in summer, laying from October to March, in a grass cup hidden at the base of a grass tuft. In winter it often joins mixed flocks of bushveld birds.
size: 12-14 cm: smaller than a House Sparrow and slimmer. A small, rather short-tailed pipit.
keys: Small brown pipit with streaked brown upperparts and buff underparts
Clear dark-brown streaks on the throat and breast
Paler stripe over the eye and pale chin
On bare, trampled or overgrazed ground littered with dung inside open woodland, and it flies up into a tree when flushed

confuse.how: Bigger, longer-tailed and more upright, in open grassland and burnt areas rather than under trees, and it lands back on the ground when flushed rather than in a tree.

voice: Unobtrusive, but its distinctive scratchy, buzzy call often gives it away before it is seen.
behaviour: Walks quietly on the ground under the trees, picking insects from short grass and leaf litter. When disturbed it does what most pipits don't: it flits up and perches in a tree.
memo: The pipit that hides in trees: small, streaky, and up a branch when you get close.

migration: Mainly resident, but outside the breeding season it can wander nomadically to areas that have just had rain or been burnt. Lays almost all year, with a peak from August to May, males singing in display flight over their territory.
size: 15-17 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow, but slimmer, with long pink legs and an upright stance.
keys: Brown, streaky back; whitish to pale buff underparts with streaks on the breast only, plain belly and flanks
Pale eyebrow and a contrasting dark moustache (malar) stripe
Thin dark bill with a yellowish base to the lower mandible
White outer tail feathers, obvious when it flies off; juvenile has scaly upperparts and a blotched breast

confuse.how: Smaller and shorter-tailed, more heavily streaked below, and lives in open woodland, often flying up into a tree when flushed, whereas African Pipit keeps to open grassy ground.
Bigger and stockier, with a yellow throat and belly ringed by a black necklace (dull buff in juveniles).

voice: A twittering run of repeated notes given in an undulating song flight or from a low perch; the call when flushed is a short, sneezing “tsship”.
behaviour: Runs about on short or burnt grass, stops upright, then dashes on after insects, flicking its tail. Males climb and dip over their territory in a deeply undulating song flight. When a predator nears the young, the parent fakes a broken wing to lead it away.
memo: The upright, streaky “grass sparrow” with white tail sides that likes freshly burnt ground.

migration: Sedentary: pairs keep the same territory for years. It is absent from most of the lowveld and at Pidwa should be looked for in hilly or dense riverine thickets; some birds may drift to lower ground in winter. Breeds mainly October to February, peaking November-December.
size: 11-13 cm: smaller than a sparrow, slender with a long tail.
keys: Narrow black band across the breast, below a white throat
Pale, cream-yellow eye in a grey or green face
Grey-green upperparts, white or pale yellow underparts, white outer tail feathers
Female has a narrower band; juvenile buffier, band sometimes incomplete

confuse.how: Stubbier with a short tail, a black mask through the eye and a white wing stripe; the female has a chestnut chin spot and breast band.
No black breast band; brown above with a pale eyebrow and buff flanks, often cocking its long tail.

voice: Loud, rapid series of repeated notes; pairs often duet, the female's part higher than the male's.
behaviour: Stays mostly hidden in dense foliage, gleaning caterpillars and other insects, often in mixed bird parties. Detected far more by the pair's ringing duet than by sight.
memo: A tiny warbler with a black necktie and pale eyes.

migration: Mostly resident in the Lowveld, though southern African birds are partly migratory and some leave colder areas in winter. Flocks wander widely every day, up to 20 km, to feed. Breeds in colonies from September to May, under bridges, eaves and rock overhangs.
size: 12 cm with a 33 cm wingspan: smaller than a swallow, but stockier.
keys: Square-cut short tail (looks rounded when spread), not forked
Broad white rump that wraps round onto the flanks, visible even from the side
Large white throat patch on an otherwise blackish-brown body
Fluttering flight broken by short glides, often in noisy flocks; sexes alike

confuse.how: Slimmer, with a deeply forked tail (often held closed in a spike) and only a narrow white crescent on the rump.
Very slender, plain grey-brown with no white rump and a long, thin, deeply forked tail; tied to palms.
Also shows a pale rump, but has an orange rump and head, streaked white underparts and long tail streamers.

voice: A shrill, rapid twittering trill, given non-stop by groups screaming around their nests and roosts, especially in the late afternoon.
behaviour: Very gregarious: dozens of nests are glued side by side under bridges or roof overhangs, made of feathers and grass stuck together with saliva, sometimes built on old swallow nests. In the evening the colony swirls round its nest site in noisy 'circus' flights. Swarms gather over termite emergences and bush fires.
memo: The swift with the square tail and the white band round its bottom, screaming under the bridge.

migration: Some South African birds move north for the winter, but the SABAP2 atlas records it over the Lowveld in every month, a little more in spring and summer. It breeds on escarpment cliffs and forages far over the lowlands, often in mixed swift flocks.
size: 16-18 cm: a large, bulky all-dark swift, clearly bigger than a Little Swift and longer-winged than a Barn Swallow.
keys: All blackish-brown with only a small pale chin patch, no white rump
Short, shallowly forked tail and long sickle-shaped wings
From above, the black back contrasts with paler grey-brown inner wing feathers (secondaries)
Powerful level flight broken by short glides

confuse.how: Slimmer, with a narrow white band on the rump and a long, deeply forked tail often held closed like a spike.
Smaller and stubbier, with a square tail and a broad white rump band; nests under bridges and buildings.
Much bigger, brown above with a white belly and throat separated by a brown breast band.

voice: A harsh, double-rasped screaming hiss, given by screaming parties in flight.
behaviour: Spends almost its whole life in the air and can travel around 1,000 km in a day of hunting. Joins big mixed swift flocks that feed on termite alates when they swarm after rain, and nests in colonies in cliff crevices, sometimes with Alpine Swifts.
memo: The dark swift with no white: a black crescent from the mountains screaming over the bush.

migration: Intra-African breeding migrant: arrives from August to October and leaves in April and May for equatorial Africa, its exact wintering grounds not well known. A few birds may stay through the winter.
size: 14-16 cm: about the size of a sparrow, but slender, with long sickle-shaped wings.
keys: All blackish swift with a narrow white crescent on the rump
Deeply forked tail, often held closed in a single point
Small pale throat patch
Slimmer and darker than the Little Swift

confuse.how: Stockier, with a broad square white rump that wraps round onto the flanks and a short square tail, and it twitters noisily in flocks.
Very slender and pale grey-brown, with no white rump and a long thin forked tail; lives around palms.

voice: Rather quiet compared with the Little Swift; sometimes a short twittering trill near the nest.
behaviour: A nest squatter: it rarely builds its own nest but takes over those of Little Swifts and swallows (often the mud tunnels of Lesser Striped Swallows), chasing the owners away, sometimes throwing out their eggs, then lining the nest with feathers glued with saliva. It spends its life in the air and drinks on the wing.
memo: A thin white rump and a forked tail: the swift that moves into a swallow's house without asking.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld: adult pairs hold the same territory for years and seldom leave it, and young birds only wander a few dozen kilometres. It can move locally to where food suddenly becomes plentiful, such as a quelea colony. Breeds in the dry season, laying mainly April to June.
size: 58-75 cm, wingspan 1.6-1.9 m: a medium-sized eagle, smaller than a Martial Eagle, much bigger than a Yellow-billed Kite. Female up to 15% larger.
keys: Scruffy brown eagle, very variable: from pale tawny-buff to dark rufous or almost uniform dark brown, with darker flight feathers and tail
Heavy yellow-based bill whose gape ends below the middle of the eye (not behind it)
Baggy, loose 'trousers' of feathers down to the yellow feet
Adult has a pale yellowish-brown eye; juvenile is pale rufous to almost cream, with a dark eye, and takes 4-5 years to reach adult plumage

confuse.how: Smaller and slimmer, with a small crest on the back of the head and a long, narrow, square-ended tail; a summer visitor only.
Summer visitor with tight, narrow 'stovepipe' leg feathering, a shorter neck and a smaller bill than the Tawny.
The brown juvenile Bateleur has a bigger, rounder head, a small bill, bare-looking legs and a very short tail.

voice: Usually silent; the most common call is a harsh, barking “kwok-kwok”, given mainly by the male in display or during chases after other birds' prey.
behaviour: An opportunist and a pirate: it hunts from a perch, scavenges at carcasses alongside vultures and regularly steals food from other raptors, usually getting the better of Bateleurs. A tawny or two sitting in a tree with vultures often means a carcass nearby.
memo: The scruffy brown pirate in baggy trousers, always first in line at a carcass.

migration: Resident: pairs stay on the same territory year after year. Only young birds disperse, sometimes far, and adults may wander during severe drought. It breeds in the dry winter, laying from April to August with a peak in June-July.
size: 55-68 cm, wingspan 1.3-1.6 m: a bit bigger and much more powerful than a Common Buzzard; the female is larger than the male.
keys: Adult: blackish above, white below with neat black streaks, yellow eye, feathered legs
In flight from below: white underwing with a black trailing edge and a pale whitish 'window' at the base of the primaries
Grey tail with a broad black band at the tip
Juvenile: brown above and plain tawny-rufous below, brown eye; takes about four years to reach adult plumage

confuse.how: Far bigger, with a dark hood and upper breast, a white belly only lightly spotted, and dark underwings without white windows.
Plain dark chest and an unmarked white belly, big rounded owl-like head and bare grey legs; flight feathers barred, with no black tail tip.
Smaller and usually plain brown, with a long square-ended tail held closed in flight and no white wing windows; a summer migrant only.

voice: Usually silent; the pair call to each other with a melodious, fluting “klooee” that can run into “kluu-kluu-kluu”.
behaviour: Pairs often hunt as a team: one flushes guineafowl or francolins and the other strikes. It also likes to watch a waterhole from a hidden perch and dash out low at birds coming to drink.
memo: A black-and-white streaked eagle that hunts in pairs and nests in winter.

migration: Present all year in the Lowveld on rivers, dams and pans, but nomadic: numbers go up and down as water levels change, and birds move on when pans dry out. Some birds in southern Africa are thought to be non-breeding visitors from central Africa. Breeds in colonies in summer (September to March, peaking January-February).
size: 80-104 cm, standing about 1 m tall: almost as big as a Grey Heron, but slimmer, with a very long neck.
keys: Very large, all-white heron with a long neck held in a deep S-shaped kink
Yellow bill; the gape line runs well behind the eye
Long all-black legs and feet
Breeding adult: long lacy plumes on the back, bill darkens and the bare skin in front of the eye turns green

confuse.how: Half the size, with a slim black bill and black legs ending in bright yellow feet.
Much smaller and stockier with a short neck and a short yellow bill; usually feeds in dry grass around game and cattle.
Also big, white and yellow-billed, but has a bare red face, black wings and tail, and a thick, slightly drooping bill.

voice: Usually silent; when disturbed it gives a low, harsh, rolling croak (“kraaah”) as it flies off.
behaviour: A patient hunter: it stands motionless, hunched, or stalks very slowly through shallow water before spearing a fish or frog with a lightning strike. It also stirs the water with a foot to flush prey, and has been seen following hippos to catch animals they disturb.
memo: A tall white statue at the water's edge: yellow dagger, black legs, black feet.

migration: Resident in southern Africa (only northern populations migrate), always near water: rivers, dams and waterholes. It may move locally as water levels change. Breeds in colonies, often with other herons, mainly July to January.
size: 90-100 cm tall, wingspan 155-195 cm: a big heron, much larger than a Western Cattle Egret.
keys: Grey back, whitish neck and underparts, with a black stripe running from the eye to a thin black crest
Yellow to orange-yellow bill and pale legs
In flight: neck pulled in an S, legs trailing, black flight feathers contrasting with grey wing coverts; underwing all grey
Juvenile duller, with a grey (not black) head stripe and a darker bill

confuse.how: Slimmer and darker, with a rufous neck striped black; shy, hiding in reeds.
Much larger (about 140 cm), with a rufous head and neck and a heavy dark bill.
Similar size and shape but all white.

voice: A loud, harsh croak 'fraaank', often given when it takes off.
behaviour: A patient fisher: it stands motionless in the shallows or stalks very slowly, then stabs with lightning speed. It turns fish to swallow them head first, and also takes frogs, small reptiles, rodents and even small birds.
memo: The grey statue at the waterhole, with a black eyebrow and a 'fraaank' when it leaves.

migration: Resident along rivers, dams and large pools, but partly nomadic: birds have been recorded moving 100-290 km, so individuals may come and go as water levels change. Can breed at any time of year, with a peak in the rainy season (about November to March).
size: 135-150 cm long, standing up to 1.5 m tall, wingspan around 2 m: the world's largest heron, far bigger than a Grey Heron.
keys: Enormous size, with a long, heavy dark bill
Rich chestnut head, crest, neck sides and belly; slate-grey back and wings
White throat and foreneck streaked black, black legs, yellow eye
Sexes alike; juvenile paler and more rufous, with a less clean neck pattern

confuse.how: Much smaller and slimmer, with a black crown and bold black lines down the sides of a rufous neck, and yellowish legs.
Grey and white with no chestnut, a white neck and a yellow bill; clearly smaller.

voice: Usually silent, but its call is a very deep, loud, barking “kowoork” that can carry up to 2 km.
behaviour: A patient, solitary hunter: it stands motionless in the shallows for long periods, then spears a large fish (often around 30 cm) with its open bill and carries it ashore to swallow it head first. Because it takes so long to handle its catch, African Fish Eagles often rob it, and Saddle-billed Storks sometimes do too.
memo: A chestnut giant that stands still for an hour, then has its fish stolen by an eagle.

migration: Southern African birds are mostly resident at permanent wetlands, but some wander to temporary pans and dams after the rains. European birds winter in tropical Africa, mostly north of us. Egg-laying can happen in any month, peaking from July to February.
size: 78-90 cm: smaller and much slimmer than a Grey Heron, with a thin, snaky neck.
keys: Rufous neck with a black stripe down each side, black crown
Dark grey back and wings, chestnut breast and blackish belly
Long, thin yellowish bill and yellow eye, giving a reptilian look
Juvenile: dull brown and buff, without the neck stripes

confuse.how: Much bigger (about 140 cm), with a rufous crown, not black, a heavier dark bill and no black stripes along the neck.
Grey and white with a white neck, not rufous. Hunts more in the open.

voice: Usually silent. When flushed it gives a harsh croak, “frank”, higher and thinner than the Grey Heron's.
behaviour: Secretive: it skulks in reedbeds and thick waterside vegetation, and its long toes let it walk on floating plants. It stands still with its neck stretched out or stalks very slowly before stabbing fish and frogs. Most active at dawn and dusk.
memo: The snake-necked heron, striped rufous and black, hiding in the reeds.

migration: The southern African population stays all year on permanent wetlands but wanders to fill new temporary pans and flooded areas after rain, so it is commonest at Lowveld dams in summer. In South Africa it breeds mainly August to March in mixed heron colonies. Eurasian birds winter mostly north of the equator in the Sahel.
size: 42-47 cm: slightly smaller and stockier than a Western Cattle Egret, with a short neck.
keys: Perched: warm buff-brown and streaky, looks like a small brown heron
In flight: suddenly almost all white, as the white wings, rump and tail appear
Breeding adult: long buff and black-streaked plumes on the nape, turquoise-blue bill tipped black, pinkish legs
Non-breeding and juvenile: duller and more streaked on the head and neck, greenish-yellow bill with a dark tip

confuse.how: All white even when perched (buff patches only when breeding), with a yellow bill; feeds in grassland near large mammals.
Dark grey-green back, black cap and dark wings in flight; no white flash when it takes off.
Dark slate-grey above with heavily streaked buff underparts, and dark wings in flight.

voice: Mostly silent. When flushed or in flight, especially at dusk, it gives a harsh, croaking 'karr', likened to a jackdaw.
behaviour: Hunts alone at the edge of reedy dams and pans, creeping slowly with the head held forward, or waiting motionless before striking at frogs, fish and insects. It climbs about in reeds and perches in trees. It is easily overlooked until it flies off, flashing white.
memo: A brown heron that turns white when it takes off.

migration: Mostly resident, though it may move locally in winter after prey such as chameleons and insects. Breeds from September to March, peaking in October to December, after spectacular display flights.
size: About 40 cm, wingspan 85-95 cm: the size of a small buzzard, but slim, with long wings and a long tail.
keys: Grey head and chest; white belly with broad, widely spaced chestnut bars, like a cuckoo
Small crest on the nape, often folded flat
Short black bill, yellow cere and legs; rufous underwing visible in flight
Juvenile: brown above, white below with heavy dark blotches and streaks

confuse.how: Finer, denser rufous barring right up the breast, with no plain grey chest and no crest; flies fast and dashing.
Plain grey chest but a white throat with a single black central stripe, a white rump and one or two white tail bars.
A true cuckoo with a slender yellow bill, a long graduated tail and fine grey (not broad chestnut) barring.

voice: Mostly silent, but before breeding it gives a loud, far-carrying, plaintive whistle, “teee-oooo” or “pee-ooo”.
behaviour: Shy and hard to see: it sits quietly with drooping wings under the canopy, waits a long time, then drops onto chameleons, lizards and large insects such as grasshoppers and mantids. Its flight is slower and weaker than a sparrowhawk's.
memo: A raptor in cuckoo's clothing: grey chest, chestnut bars and a taste for chameleons.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld. The male defends a territory of about 5 ha all year. Lays from late September to early January, peaking in November.
size: 12-13 cm: smaller than a House Sparrow, compact and stocky, with a short tail.
keys: Grey cap, black mask and bright yellow eye; white wing stripe on grey upperparts
Male: white throat and a broad black breast band
Female: chestnut breast band and a round chestnut spot on the white chin, which gives the name
Juvenile like the female, but with a tawny band and chin spot
voice: A clear, descending three-note whistle, "three-blind-mice", from a high perch; the female sometimes joins in a duet, and bill clicks and snaps are often heard.
behaviour: Very active, constantly turning its head as it searches the canopy for insects, which it snaps up with an audible click of the bill. In winter and early spring small groups of up to ten may gather and display, making a whirring wing noise and sometimes fighting.
memo: "Three blind mice" in the thornveld: black band for him, chestnut chin spot for her.

migration: Resident and non-migratory: pairs stay together all year and use the same tree roosts for years. It may wander in response to rain, especially in droughts, and juveniles disperse. In the Lowveld it sticks to rivers, dams and green lawns. Breeds mostly after the rains, peaking September to November.
size: 65-76 cm with the long curved bill: about the size of a small heron, bigger than a domestic hen but on short legs.
keys: Dull grey-brown ibis with a long, down-curved dark bill
Purple-green metallic sheen on the wing coverts in good light
Thin pale (white or buff) stripe across the cheek, below the eye
Red ridge at the base of the upper bill, brighter when breeding; juvenile greyer without gloss

confuse.how: A dark stork, larger and longer-legged, with a straight heavy bill that has a gap in the middle. It is almost silent.

voice: The famous loud, braying “ha-ha-ha-de-dah”, which gives the bird its name. Pairs and groups call raucously as they leave the roost at dawn and return at dusk.
behaviour: South Africa's living alarm clock: groups fly out from their roost trees at first light, calling loudly with jerky wingbeats, and come back noisily in the evening. By day pairs walk slowly over damp ground, probing deep into the soil with the curved bill for worms, beetle larvae, snails and millipedes.
memo: Ha-ha-ha-de-dah! The bird that says its own name at dawn.

migration: Resident in the Lowveld's thornveld, though colonies may wander locally and flocks roam in the dry season. Breeds September to June, peaking December to March in the summer rains.
size: 21-25 cm: about the size of a starling but much heavier; one of the biggest weavers.
keys: All black or very dark brown, with a heavy, bright red conical bill
Male: white flecks on the wing edges, showing as small white patches in flight
Female and juvenile: browner, with whitish-scaled throat and underparts; juvenile bill duller orange-pink
Huge untidy communal nest of thorny twigs in a big tree or on a windmill or pylon

confuse.how: Slimmer and olive-brown with a thin red bill and a yellow eye-ring, and clings to large mammals instead of feeding on the ground.

voice: Noisy at the colony: loud chattering, squawks and wheezy notes, with males calling loudly when defending their nest chambers.
behaviour: Colonies build a massive heap of thorny twigs split into several "lodges", each with grass-lined egg chambers. A dominant male may control several chambers and up to three females. White-backed Vultures and Bateleurs sometimes nest on top of the heap.
memo: Black weaver with a red bill and a thorny tower block.

migration: Resident all year in pairs that probably stay together for life. Breeds mainly from late July to early February, with egg-laying peaking August to December, often in a scrape on the ground, in a tree fork or on a building.
size: About 45 cm, wingspan 100-140 cm: about the size of a crow, but bulky. One of the smallest eagle-owls.
keys: Bright yellow eyes and prominent ear tufts
Grey-brown upperparts with white spots, pale underparts finely barred grey-brown
Pale facial disc edged with a dark rim
Juvenile: finely barred brown and white, greyish-yellow eye

confuse.how: Much bigger and paler grey, with dark eyes and bright pink eyelids.
Smaller, with orange eyes and a white face boldly framed in black.

voice: A soft, musical duet of hoots, the pair's 'hoo-hoo' and 'hoo-hoo-hoo' merging so that it sounds like a single bird.
behaviour: Often seen at dusk or on night drives sitting on roads and road verges, where it catches rodents, insects and other prey, which is why many are killed by cars. By day it roosts in trees or rocks, and if found it is quickly mobbed by small birds.
memo: Yellow eyes and ear tufts: the night-drive owl on the road.

migration: Present all year in southern Africa but nomadic, moving with the rains; young birds can disperse thousands of kilometres. In the Lowveld numbers rise in summer, when birds breed in colonies near water, laying mainly September to December.
size: 46-56 cm: a small, stocky white heron, smaller than Little Egret, about the size of a domestic chicken standing up.
keys: Small, compact white heron with a short thick neck and a 'jowled' chin, the head often hunched into the shoulders
Short, stout yellow bill (not black) and short dark or greenish-yellow legs
Breeding: orange-buff plumes on the crown, breast and back; bill and legs flush red-orange before pairing
Juvenile has a black bill

confuse.how: Slimmer and longer-necked, with a thin black bill, black legs and yellow feet; feeds in water, not around grazers.
Much bigger (about 90 cm), with a very long kinked neck, a long yellow bill and long black legs.
Buffy-brown body at rest; only shows white wings when it flies up, and keeps to the edge of water.

voice: Mostly silent away from the colony; at the colony it gives a throaty “rick-rack” or “roc-roc”.
behaviour: Walks beside buffalo, elephants, rhinos and cattle, catching the grasshoppers they flush, and sometimes rides on their backs; feeding next to a large animal is far more successful than feeding alone. At dusk lines of birds fly in loose groups to shared roosts in trees near water.
memo: The little white heron that lives with the buffalo.

migration: Resident and sedentary all year: each group holds a huge territory of about 100 km². Young birds, mostly females, are the ones that disperse to other groups. Breeds in summer, egg-laying starting with the first heavy rains (September to December, peaking October-November).
size: 90-129 cm, wingspan up to 1.8 m: about the size of a turkey, the largest hornbill.
keys: Big all-black bird walking on the ground, usually in a group
Bare red skin around the eye and a red inflatable throat pouch; female has a violet-blue patch on the throat
Heavy, curved black bill with a small casque (bigger in the male)
White flight feathers show only in flight. Juvenile browner, with dull yellowish facial skin
voice: A deep, booming “oomph, oomph-oomph” repeated in chorus by the group, mostly at dawn, at dusk or before rain. Sounds a bit like a distant lion and carries several kilometres. An old edition of Roberts gives an indigenous reading of the duet: she says “I'm going, I'm going, I'm going home to my relations”, he answers “You can go, you can go, you can go home to your relations!”
behaviour: A group of 2-8 birds walks several kilometres a day hunting on the ground, taking insects, frogs, snakes, tortoises and even hares. Only the dominant pair breeds; the helpers feed the female in a tree-hole nest. She usually lays two eggs, but the second chick almost always starves within a week, and a group may raise one young only every few years.
memo: A black turkey with a red throat that booms at dawn: Africa's endangered walking hornbill.

migration: Resident, but scarce and localised in South Africa (listed as Vulnerable there), at the southern edge of its range. Moves locally with the large herds it feeds on. Breeds September to March, nesting in tree holes lined with hair plucked from its hosts.
size: About 20 cm: the size of a starling, with a thick bill and strong claws.
keys: Thick bill, bright yellow at the base with a red tip
No yellow ring of bare skin around the eye
Pale buff rump contrasting with the brown back in flight
Plain brown upperparts, buff belly; juvenile has a dark brown bill

confuse.how: Much commoner, with a slimmer all-red bill, an obvious yellow eye-ring, and an all-brown back without a pale rump.

voice: A hissing, crackling “krisss, krisss”, given often from the host or in flight.
behaviour: Clings to buffalo, rhino, giraffe and other big mammals, taking ticks but also blood from wounds. It prefers the largest hosts, can gather in big numbers on buffalo herds, dominates the Red-billed Oxpecker when feeding, and even roosts on its hosts at night.
memo: Yellow bill with a red tip, and a buffalo for a home.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, never far from herds of large mammals. Groups move about by day from herd to herd and return to roost or nest at dusk. Breeds October to March, in tree holes lined with hair plucked from its hosts.
size: About 20 cm: a little smaller than a blackbird, slim, with a long stiff tail.
keys: Slim all-red bill, on a plain olive-brown bird with a buffy belly
Red eye ringed by a bright yellow fleshy wattle
Dark rump, same colour as the back
Juvenile: darker, with a dark olive or yellowish bill and no yellow eye wattle; the bill becomes red after about four months

confuse.how: Heavier, broader bill, yellow at the base with a red tip, a pale rump that shows in flight and no yellow wattle round the red eye; prefers buffalo and rhino.

voice: A hissing, crackling “trik-quisss”, and a harsh chatter when a group flies off; it raises the alarm loudly when people or predators approach.
behaviour: Clings to giraffes, zebras, impalas, buffalo and rhinos with its stiff tail as a prop, scissoring through the coat for ticks. One bird can eat nearly 100 engorged ticks a day, but it also pecks at wounds to drink blood and keeps them open. Its alarm calls warn short-sighted rhinos of danger.
memo: Red bill, yellow spectacles: the tick-picker riding the impala.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, in pairs or family groups that may gather in loose flocks of 20-30 outside the breeding season. Lays mainly September to December, and can raise two or three broods a season.
size: 37-44 cm: about the size of a small chicken, standing tall on long legs, with a big round head.
keys: Sandy-brown plumage evenly covered with dark spots, no wing bar on the folded wing
Huge staring yellow eye in a big round head
Short, stout bill, black with a yellow base
Long yellow legs with thick 'knees'; in flight, small white flashes in the dark flight feathers

confuse.how: Streaked rather than spotted, with a grey-and-white wing bar on the folded wing and larger white wing flashes in flight; it stays close to rivers and dams.

voice: Mainly at night: a loud, musical series of piping whistles that rises, then slows and falls away, often several birds answering one another. It also has a sharp alarm call.
behaviour: Nocturnal: by day it crouches motionless under a bush, trusting its camouflage, and it is often seen on roads at night. To protect eggs or chicks, adults spread their wings and cock their tails at intruders, or fake a broken wing to lure the predator away, while the chicks freeze flat on the ground.
memo: Big yellow eyes and a spotted coat: the night-time whistler of the roads.

migration: Resident where there is permanent water, such as the larger rivers and dams; it moves locally as water levels change. Breeds August to January, mostly September to December.
size: 38-41 cm: about the size of a feral pigeon but much taller on long legs, slightly smaller than a Spotted Thick-knee.
keys: Big yellow-green eye, heavy black bill with a yellowish base, long greenish-yellow legs
Grey-brown upperparts finely streaked and vermiculated, not spotted
A pale grey panel along the folded wing, edged with a thin white line
Always near water: riverbanks, sandbars, dam shores

confuse.how: Larger, boldly spotted (not streaked) above, without the grey wing panel, and usually in dry open bush rather than at the water's edge.

voice: A loud, plaintive whistle at dusk and at night: a series of “ti-ti-ti-tee-teee-tooo” notes that slow down and fall in pitch, often in chorus.
behaviour: Spends the day resting quietly in shade near water and feeds at night on insects, crabs and frogs, running a few steps, pausing and jabbing like a plover. It often nests right next to a Nile crocodile's nest: its alarm calls warn the crocodile, which in turn deters predators.
memo: The thick-knee of the riverbank, with a grey wing bar and a crocodile as a neighbour.

migration: Palearctic migrant (the Steppe Buzzard, race vulpinus) that breeds from eastern Europe to Siberia. It leaves in September-October, travels in loose flocks along the Rift Valley and southern African mountain chains such as the Lebombo, and reaches the Lowveld from late October to November, roughly with the first rains. It heads back north from late February, mainly in March; a few birds overwinter.
size: 45-50 cm, wingspan 1.1-1.3 m: about the size of a Pied Crow, but with broad wings and a short fanned tail.
keys: Medium, stocky raptor sitting upright on a pole, dead tree or fence, with bare yellow lower legs
Very variable plumage from pale to dark brown, often rufous, with a paler band across the breast and barred flanks
In flight: dark wrist patch on the underwing, pale flight feathers with a dark trailing edge
Short, rounded tail, often rufous, finely barred with a darker band at the tip

confuse.how: Slimmer, with fully feathered legs, a small crest and a long, narrow, square-ended tail held closed in flight.
Smaller and grey, with a white throat split by a black vertical stripe and a single white band on the black tail.
Yellow bill and a long, forked tail it constantly twists in flight; rarely sits still for long.

voice: Mostly silent in Africa; when it does call, a plaintive, far-carrying “pee-yow” whistle.
behaviour: A patient perch-hunter: it can sit for hours on a telephone pole or dead branch, then glides down to the ground to grab rodents, lizards, termites and grasshoppers. It is the buzzard most often seen in Kruger in summer.
memo: The summer “fingerprint buzzard”: no two look alike, but all sit on poles.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, in north-eastern South Africa. It is generally sedentary but makes local moves after rain, following where water and cover are good. Lays eggs in any month, with a peak after the rains.
size: About 40 cm: a small, hunched heron, clearly smaller and stockier than a Western Cattle Egret, with short legs.
keys: Black cap, often raised into a small crest, and a dark line from the bill to below the eye
Dark slate-grey back and wings with a greenish gloss, pale grey neck and underparts with a white stripe down the throat
Dagger-shaped dark bill, yellow eye and short yellow to orange legs
Juvenile: brown above with pale spots, whitish below with heavy dark streaks

confuse.how: Also small and hunched, but dark slate above with buff underparts boldly streaked dark, and it is a summer visitor that hides in flooded bush.
Buff and sandy brown, not grey, and it shows startling white wings when it takes off.

voice: Usually silent; when flushed it gives a harsh, explosive “skow” or “kyow”, and a grating “skeow” in alarm.
behaviour: Waits crouched and motionless on a branch or root at the water's edge, neck pulled in, then shoots out its bill. It is one of the few birds that fishes with bait: it drops an insect, a feather or a scrap of bread onto the water and catches the fish that rise to it, moving the bait back if it drifts away.
memo: The hunched grey angler under the bank, who fishes with bait.

migration: Sedentary overall, but it wanders widely between patches of riverine forest after fruiting figs and other trees, flying 10-15 km or more across open bush. Around Pidwa it is an occasional visitor, mostly along big rivers with tall fig trees. Breeds September to January.
size: 58-65 cm: much bigger than a Southern Yellow-billed Hornbill, longer than a Pied Crow.
keys: Big, dark bill topped by a large grey casque (reaching almost to the tip in the male; much smaller in the female)
Glossy black head, breast, back and wings contrasting with a clean white belly, rump and vent
Red to purplish bare skin around the eye
In flight: white trailing edge to the wing and white corners to the tail

confuse.how: Smaller, grey-brown with a white stripe above the eye and a thin bill with only a small casque; no glossy black and white.
Smaller, with a bright yellow bill and white-spotted wings; feeds mostly on the ground in savanna.

voice: Loud, drawn-out, nasal wailing “waaah… waaah…”, often described as sounding like a crying baby; flocks call noisily in flight.
behaviour: Lives in pairs or noisy small groups that can spend a whole day in one fruiting fig, then move on the next day. The wingbeats make a loud whooshing sound. At the nest the female is sealed into a tree hole with mud and droppings and fed by the male through a slit.
memo: A wailing baby in the fig tree: the black-and-white trumpeter of the river forest.

migration: Resident all year in broad-leaved and knobthorn woodland. It is far easier to find in spring and summer, when it calls a lot, than in winter, when it is quiet. Breeds September to March, mainly November to February in the Lowveld.
size: 13 cm: smaller than a House Sparrow, slim, with a long tail that is often cocked.
keys: White underparts finely and evenly barred black from the throat to the vent
Plain grey-brown upperparts, long dark tail often raised
Pale eye and pinkish legs, slender dark bill
Usually alone or in pairs, low in thickets, often near termite mounds

confuse.how: Also cocks a long tail, but its underparts are plain white with tawny flanks, no barring, and it has a pale eyebrow and rufous edges to the wing feathers.
Almost tailless, with plain buff-orange underparts, no barring.

voice: A loud, ringing, monotonous series of identical notes, often heard long before the bird is seen and giving its presence away. Field guides write it in various ways, for example 'pli-pli-pli-pli'.
behaviour: Very secretive: it forages mostly near the ground in the undergrowth and only moves up into the canopy when disturbed. It builds a ball-shaped nest with a side entrance from fine grass and plant down, stitched to the leaves with spider web.
memo: A tiny barred skulker that you hear before you see.

migration: In South Africa most birds are breeding visitors from further north, present from about October to April, but some stay all year. Breeds September to February. It is generally uncommon and easily overlooked.
size: 19-22 cm: about the size of a blackbird, but slimmer, with a longish rounded tail.
keys: Male all glossy blue-black, with a bright orange-yellow gape at the base of the bill
A few males show a yellow shoulder patch; most have none
Female very different, cuckoo-like: olive-brown above, finely barred, white below with neat black scalloping, and bright yellow edges to the wing and tail feathers
Quiet and unobtrusive in the mid-canopy, often in mixed bird parties

confuse.how: Deeply forked tail, red eye and no coloured gape; perches out in the open.
Dark eye and no orange gape; sallies to the ground from a low perch instead of gleaning leaves.
Bigger, with a long tail tipped white and no orange gape; the female cuckooshrike is told from cuckoos by her yellow-edged wing feathers.

voice: Mostly silent. The male's song is a dry, very high-pitched, insect-like trill.
behaviour: Gleans slowly through the leaves of the mid-canopy for insects, and is especially fond of hairy caterpillars that most birds avoid (Campephaga means “caterpillar-eater”). The female builds a small cup nest of moss and lichen bound with spider web in a high fork, camouflaged like a knot on the branch.
memo: A black bird with an orange smile, eating hairy caterpillars.

migration: Resident all year in pairs that defend fairly large territories (about 10-15 ha), mostly in riverine woodland and thickets. No seasonal movements recorded. Breeds August to December, peaking September to November, in a hole dug in the underside of a branch.
size: 20-23 cm: about the size of a starling, a medium-sized woodpecker.
keys: Underparts and throat heavily streaked black on pale yellowish-white (streaks, not spots)
Greenish, pale-barred back; golden-olive tail and yellowish flight-feather shafts
Male: red crown and red moustache stripe
Female: black forecrown spotted white, red only on the back of the head, and a black-and-white speckled moustache

confuse.how: Underparts spotted, not streaked, and often feeds on the ground; the female has a brown throat and cheek patch.
Much smaller (about 15 cm), with a brown forehead, a black moustache in both sexes and finer streaking; works thin twigs rather than larger branches.
Much bigger (about 25 cm), with a bold black moustache and ear-patch on a white face and barred, not streaked, underparts.

voice: A single loud, nasal, rather drawn-out “waaaa” or “weeea”, like a shout, given mostly by the male; also drums softly.
behaviour: Works slowly over a small area in the lower and middle parts of trees, tapping and hammering dead or rotten wood more than other Campethera woodpeckers, and picking out ants and termites with its long barbed tongue. Its nest holes are often taken over by honeyguides, which lay their eggs in them.
memo: Streaky chest, golden tail and a nasal “waaa!” from the riverine trees.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, living in pairs or small family groups that stay on their territory and only disperse locally. Breeds August to February, with a peak from October to December. Often nests in an old hole made by another woodpecker, such as a Bearded Woodpecker.
size: About 24 cm: a little smaller than a blackbird but stockier, with a strong straight bill.
keys: Feeds on the ground, on bare soil or short grass, which is unusual for a woodpecker
Pale yellowish underparts with round dark spots, not streaks. Back barred brown, yellow and white
Male: red crown and red moustache on a clean white cheek and throat
Female: black crown dotted white and a brown throat and cheek patch, unique among our woodpeckers

confuse.how: Underparts streaked, not spotted, and it forages in trees rather than on the ground; no plain white throat.
Much smaller (about 15 cm) with a streaked breast and a brown forehead; it taps on thin twigs, not the ground.
Much bigger, with a bold black moustache on a white face and a grey, finely barred belly.

voice: Fairly vocal: a chattering “wirrit-wirrit” and series of “wi-wi-wi-wi” or “kee-kee-kee” notes, often exchanged by members of a pair. It rarely drums, and then only softly.
behaviour: A woodpecker that lives on the ground: it hops about digging into underground ant nests and licks up ants, eggs and pupae with its sticky tongue. When disturbed it flies to the nearest tree, then drops back down once the danger has passed. Pairs greet each other by pointing their bills, flicking their wings and fanning their tails.
memo: The woodpecker that digs for ants on the ground, and the female wears a brown face.

migration: Sedentary all year, making only small local movements. Pairs break up into small coveys of up to about 12 outside the breeding season. Breeds in the rainy season, mostly late summer when the grass is tall and seeds are plentiful.
size: 20-25 cm: the smallest francolin in South Africa, about the size of a small bantam hen or a large dove.
keys: Male: plain ochre-buff to rusty head with a darker crown, contrasting with closely black-and-white barred underparts
Female: white throat edged with a thin black line, pale eyebrow with a black stripe above, plain tawny breast
Yellow legs and a black bill with a yellow base
Grey-brown back finely streaked buff; walks crouched with a low body and upright head

confuse.how: Bigger, with a dark cap and broad white eyebrow, red legs, a dark-tipped tail often cocked like a bantam's, and chevron-spotted breast rather than fine bars.
Much bigger, with a bright orange-red bill and legs and scaly, marbled underparts; usually in thickets near water.
Much bigger and darker brown, with bare red skin on the face and throat and black legs.

voice: The name is the call: a repeated two-note 'co-qui' (Afrikaans name Swempie), given mainly by the male; also a short series of cackling notes.
behaviour: Shy and secretive in long grass: it relies on camouflage and crouches motionless when danger approaches, then bursts up in a whirring flight at the last moment. More often heard than seen, calling from the grass at dawn and in the wet season.
memo: The little francolin that says its own name: 'co-qui, co-qui' from the long grass.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds across Europe and western Asia and spends the austral summer in Africa south of the Sahara. In South Africa it is mainly found in the Lowveld of Limpopo and Mpumalanga and northern KwaZulu-Natal, arriving between September and November and gone by April. Uncommon and easily overlooked.
size: 24-28 cm: about the size of a Laughing Dove, but with long pointed wings and a long tail.
keys: Grey-brown, bark-patterned plumage with fine dark streaks; no rufous collar
Roosts by day lying lengthwise along a tree branch, often high up, not on the ground
Male: white patch near the tip of the three outer primaries and white tail corners; female and young have no white
Thin pale moustache line and a buff band across the folded wing

confuse.how: Smaller and warmer, with a rufous collar and breast and a big white throat patch; roosts on the ground in leaf litter rather than along a branch.

voice: Mostly silent in Africa; the famous long, mechanical churring song is mainly heard on its European breeding grounds, and in flight it gives a sharp 'kwik'.
behaviour: Unlike our local nightjars, it spends the day flattened lengthwise along a tree branch, sometimes up to 20 m high, and often reuses the same roost for several years. At dusk and before dawn it flies out from a perch to catch beetles and moths in flight, and even drinks on the wing.
memo: The nightjar that sleeps along a branch, not on the ground: a European on holiday in the bushveld.

migration: Resident in the Lowveld woodland, with pairs returning to the same territory every year. Breeds in the late dry season, mainly August to October, often with two clutches. It sings most at dusk and dawn in the weeks before and during breeding.
size: 23-25 cm: about the size of a Laughing Dove.
keys: Rufous-chestnut collar on the nape and a rufous wash on the breast
Large white throat patch
Mottled grey-brown upperparts that vanish into leaf litter
Male: white spots on the four outer primaries and white tail corners; smaller and buffier in the female

confuse.how: Larger, greyer and colder, with no rufous collar; roosts lengthwise on a branch and is only here in summer.

voice: A beautiful, mellow, descending whistle, famously rendered 'Good Lord, deliver us', often preceded by a wind-up phrase and given from a raised perch at dusk.
behaviour: Spends the day motionless on the ground in leaf litter, trusting its camouflage, and lays two eggs on bare ground with no nest. At dusk and on moonlit nights it makes short sallies from a perch or a dirt road to catch moths and beetles. Chicks are fed only when they grasp the parent's bill.
memo: 'Good Lord, deliver us': the voice of the bushveld night.

migration: Resident and largely sedentary, but uncommon. In South Africa it occurs mainly in Limpopo, in mopane and broad-leaved woodland, sometimes riverine forest. Pairs keep their young with them until the next breeding season, which falls in spring and early summer.
size: 25-27 cm: a little smaller than a Fork-tailed Drongo, about the size of a dove but slimmer.
keys: Pale blue-grey upperparts and head, clean white belly and undertail
Black lores give a small dark mask in front of the eye; black bill and mainly blackish tail
Male has a darker grey throat and upper breast sharply cut off from the white; female's throat is paler grey, merging into the white
Moves slowly and quietly through the mid-canopy, alone or in pairs

confuse.how: Much smaller (about 14 cm), grey below as well as above, and flycatches in sallies from a perch rather than creeping through the canopy.
Broad black mask through the eye and forehead, black wings with a white patch, and perches upright on exposed perches to drop on prey.

voice: Usually quiet; the call is a soft, high, drawn-out whistle, with some trilled notes.
behaviour: Gleans caterpillars slowly from trunks, branches and leaves in the canopy, often in mixed-species bird parties. The female alone builds a tiny shallow nest decorated with old-man's beard lichen on a thick branch, and the pair destroy it after the chicks leave.
memo: A pale grey ghost with a white belly, picking caterpillars in the mopane.

migration: Intra-African migrant over most of South Africa: the bulk of the population arrives in July and August and heads north again between February and May. In the warm Lowveld some birds stay all year, so a few can be seen even in mid-winter. Breeds in summer, peaking September to November, often raising two broods.
size: 15-19 cm including the tail streamers: about the size of a Barn Swallow.
keys: Rufous-chestnut cap and sides of the head, glossy blue-black back
White underparts with heavy black streaks from throat to belly
Rufous-orange rump, deeply forked black tail with long outer streamers (shorter in the female)
Juvenile duller and browner, with shorter streamers

confuse.how: Dark blue head and back with a red throat and dark breast band; unstreaked buffy-white belly and no rufous rump.

voice: A nasal, descending series of squeaky notes, “zeh-zeh-zeh-zeh”, often given from a perch or wire; the song is a harsh, chattering twitter.
behaviour: Builds a retort-shaped mud nest of about a thousand mud pellets, with a long entrance tunnel, stuck under bridges, culverts, roof eaves, rock overhangs or big branches; the same nest is reused year after year. Flight is fluttery, with glides and short bursts of wingbeats, often low over water or open ground.
memo: Ginger cap, ginger rump, pinstriped belly: the swallow that builds a mud bottle under the eaves.

migration: Resident all year, in pairs on fixed territories in thickets, reedbeds and riverine bush. It is much more vocal in summer, when it breeds (September to February). The male builds a bulky nest in a thorn tree or tangle and does most of the incubating.
size: About 41-44 cm: the size of a small crow or a hornbill, with a long, heavy tail.
keys: Black head and long black tail, with fine pale bars on the rump
Rich rufous-chestnut back and wings, glowing in flight
Creamy-white underparts and a striking red eye
Juvenile: short pale eyebrow and streaky brown crown

confuse.how: Summer visitor to wet grassland: breeding adult is all black underneath with chestnut wings, not white below.
Much smaller and all black, with no chestnut or white; it calls from the canopy, not from thickets.

voice: A deep, bubbling “doo-doo-doo-doo” falling then rising, like water poured out of a bottle: hence the nicknames “water-bottle bird” and “rainbird”, as it calls a lot in humid weather around rain.
behaviour: A skulking predator that stalks through thickets eating grasshoppers, frogs, lizards, chameleons, mice and even doves and nestlings. When the grass is wet with dew or rain, it climbs to the top of a bush and spreads its wings and tail to dry in the sun.
memo: The bubbling water bottle in the thicket: a big rusty-winged cuckoo with red eyes.

migration: Scarce and local in the Lowveld, which is at the very edge of its range. It turns up mainly with the summer rains in tall, wet grass and vleis. Breeds December to March (peak January–February), and is hard to find or absent in the dry season.
size: 30-34 cm, female clearly bigger than male: about the length of a Red-eyed Dove, but with a long, broad tail and a heavier body. Smaller than Burchell's Coucal.
keys: Breeding plumage: head, body and tail all black, with bright rufous-chestnut wings
Non-breeding: dark brown above with rufous barring and pale streaks, buffy below, so it looks like a small, streaky coucal
Dark brown eye and black bill (Burchell's Coucal has a red eye)
Juvenile rufous, barred and streaked dark and pale

confuse.how: Larger and common all year in thickets, with a red eye and creamy-white underparts, never black below.

voice: The female calls from a grass stem with series of hollow, popping notes. They lack the long, liquid 'water-bottle' bubbling of Burchell's Coucal.
behaviour: Sex roles are reversed. The bigger female holds the territory and calls from exposed perches, and she mates with several males. Each male builds a deep grass cup and incubates and raises the chicks entirely on his own. Otherwise it creeps low through rank, wet grass, taking grasshoppers and other insects.
memo: The rainy-season coucal with a black belly and chestnut wings, whose mother calls the shots and whose father does the babysitting.

migration: Sedentary resident of savanna with bushes and grass, especially acacia and mixed bushwillow woodland. Pairs keep territories all year; eggs are laid September to January, peaking September to November.
size: 14-16 cm: about the size of a sparrow, but slimmer, with a longer tail.
keys: White eyebrow over a dark eye-stripe, white throat
Two clear white wing bars on dark wings
Whitish breast with dark streaks, flanks washed buff-rufous, rufous rump
Tail dark with white tips and corners, constantly cocked, flicked and fanned

confuse.how: Larger, with an orange-rufous unstreaked breast and a black moustache stripe; lives in denser riverine thicket.
Larger, with a black head and bright orange underparts and tail, without any streaks or wing bars.

voice: A loud, varied, thrush-like song of repeated phrases, sung all year from inside or on top of a bush; the alarm is a harsh “skirr”.
behaviour: Hops on the ground under bushes, turning over leaves and digging for termites, with drooped wings and cocked tail. Males display with the tail raised and fanned, and rivals sometimes grapple in mid-air over territory.
memo: Small brown robin with white brows and wing bars, tail always cocked.

migration: Sedentary resident of dense thickets, in territorial pairs, with no seasonal movements. Breeds from September to December.
size: 15-17 cm: about the size of a sparrow, but slimmer and longer-tailed.
keys: Bold face pattern: white eyebrow, black stripe through the eye, white crescent under it and a black “beard” (malar stripe)
White throat, orange-rufous breast and flanks, white belly, with no streaks on the breast
Dark olive-brown back and a dark tail with white tips, often raised and fanned
Sexes alike; juvenile paler and more mottled

confuse.how: Smaller and paler, with clear dark streaks on the breast, white wing bars and a rufous rump; it favours more open bush.
Larger, with a slate-grey back, a black face and an orange tail with dark central feathers, and no black beard.

voice: A loud song of rich, varied, melodious whistled phrases, often with mimicry, given from a perch in or above a thicket, especially at dawn; calls include a harsh “chrrrt” and a scolding “chuck”.
behaviour: Shy, it forages on the ground in the leaf litter under dense cover, flicking and fanning its tail, and often follows driver ant swarms to catch the insects they flush. It also takes sand baths.
memo: The robin with a black beard: a beautiful singer hidden in the riverine thickets.

migration: Resident all year wherever there is open water with small fish, such as rivers, dams and pans, making only short local moves when waters dry up or flood. In South Africa it breeds mainly August to November, digging a tunnel in a sandy riverbank.
size: 25 cm: about the size of a blackbird but with a big head, a crest and a long, dagger-like black bill.
keys: The only black-and-white kingfisher: white with heavy black spotting above, white below
Shaggy black-and-white crest, white eyebrow and long black bill
Male: two black breast bands, the lower one thin
Female: a single breast band, often broken in the middle

confuse.how: Much bigger (about 43 cm), with a slate-grey back finely spotted white and a chestnut breast (male) or belly (female). It hunts from a perch and rarely hovers.

voice: A sharp, high, chattering “kwik-kwik” or “chirruk-chirruk”, often given in flight and in noisy group squabbles.
behaviour: Hovers more than any other kingfisher: it hangs in the air a few metres above the water, tail down and bill pointing at the surface, then plunges head first. It can swallow small fish in flight and beats larger ones against a perch. It is a cooperative breeder: helpers, often last year's young males, assist the pair at the nest.
memo: The black-and-white kingfisher that hovers like a kestrel over the water.

migration: Resident in the Lowveld, where it is common in savanna woodland and gardens. It moves locally to follow flowering trees such as coral-trees and aloes. Breeds all year, mainly October to January.
size: 13-15 cm: smaller than a sparrow, with a long, strongly curved bill.
keys: Male: very dark velvety brown, almost black, with a bright scarlet breast shield
Male: metallic green crown and throat, visible in good light
Female: dull brown above, whitish below and heavily mottled and streaked dark brown
Young male: female-like, gradually gaining the red breast and metallic head

confuse.how: The male is metallic green with a purple and maroon breast band, never a black body with a red shield. The female is paler, with fine streaks on a yellowish belly.
Smaller with a shorter bill. The male has a white belly, and the female is plain grey-brown and pale below without heavy mottling.

voice: A loud, sharp “cheep” or “chip” note, and a short song of four or five notes followed by rapid repeated notes, which the male can repeat from a perch for an hour or more.
behaviour: Males defend flowering trees aggressively and chase rival males over long distances. Besides nectar, it catches insects and spiders in flight or on the ground. The female builds a hanging, pear-shaped nest bound with spider web and decorated with lichen, often placed next to an active wasp nest.
memo: A black sunbird wearing a red bib: it flashes from the coral-tree blooms.

migration: Resident and largely sedentary, often at the same site year after year. It makes local moves as dams and pans fill or dry up, and may leave some sites when the rains begin. Breeds mostly in the dry season, July to October, when muddy shores are exposed.
size: 18 cm: about the length of a starling, but slim and long-tailed, with longish wings.
keys: Two black breast bands separated by a white band, on otherwise white underparts
Red eye-ring and a red bill with a black tip
Grey face, white forehead and white eyebrows meeting at the back of the brown crown
In flight: thin white wing bar and a long tail edged white; juvenile duller and scaly, with a browner forehead
voice: A sharp, high, whistled “weet-weet” or piercing “pip”, often given as it flies off low over the water.
behaviour: Usually alone or in pairs on the bare muddy edge of a dam or pan, running a few steps, stopping, then picking at prey; it also trembles a foot on the mud to flush small animals. Pairs defend their stretch of shore by running or flying at intruders, and lay their eggs in a bare scrape near water.
memo: Two black necklaces and red “eyeliner”: the little plover of every muddy dam edge.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld and sedentary, staying in the same thickets. Breeds September to March, mostly October to December.
size: 20-22 cm: a little bigger than the Dark-capped Bulbul, about the size of a thrush.
keys: Olive-brown upperparts and bright yellow underparts from throat to vent
No black head and no crest, unlike the common bulbul
Reddish-brown eye with white upper and lower eyelids (a broken pale eye-ring)
Keeps low in dense tangled thickets, especially along rivers

confuse.how: Black head with a small crest, brown breast and yellow only under the tail.
All dull olive-green with a striking white eye, no bright yellow belly; mostly heard rather than seen.

voice: Loud, nasal, rather complaining calls, often repeated from inside a thicket.
behaviour: Forages in the lower canopy, often with other bulbuls, gleaning fruit, seeds and insects from leaves. It has even been recorded picking ticks off impala, duiker and nyala, and around camps it becomes bold and will steal fruit from tables.
memo: A bulbul without the black hat: olive above, lemon-yellow below, hiding in the riverine tangle.

migration: Resident all year, not migratory, in pairs that hold territories along wooded drainage lines and riverine bush. Breeds mainly October to December.
size: 17-19 cm: a little smaller than a Dark-capped Bulbul.
keys: Grey head with a yellow forehead and eyebrow and a black mask through the eye
Olive-green back, wings and tail
Bright yellow underparts with an orange wash on the breast
Female duller, with a less distinct mask; juvenile has a greyish head, no orange and faint barring

confuse.how: Bright red throat bordered by a black necklace and green upperparts with no grey head; skulks low in thickets.
Much bigger (about 25 cm) with a heavy hooked bill, pale eye and no yellow eyebrow or black mask.

voice: A far-carrying, whistled series of short notes ending in a long drawn-out one, known in South Africa as “Coffee, tea or meeeee?”, which earned it the nickname “air hostess bird”.
behaviour: Hunts insects (beetles, caterpillars, mantids, wasps) by gleaning quietly through the canopy of thorn trees and riverine woodland, so it is heard far more often than seen. Builds a flimsy, shallow twig nest on a horizontal branch or in a creeper tangle.
memo: “Coffee, tea or meeee?” from the treetops: the air hostess of the bushveld.

migration: Resident all year in pairs that cover large areas of woodland. Unusually, it breeds mainly in the dry winter: eggs from April to December, peaking May to August.
size: 24-27 cm: the size of a thrush, one of Africa's largest woodpeckers.
keys: Bold black-and-white face, with a broad black mask through the eye and a thick black “beard” stripe
Dark olive-grey underparts finely barred white, olive-brown back barred white
Male has a red patch on the back of the crown; female has no red (black crown speckled white)
Yellowish rump and tail tip, and a large, long chisel bill

confuse.how: Much smaller (about 15 cm), with a streaked breast and a brown, not black, cheek stripe.
Smaller, with spotted and streaked whitish underparts, not dark barred, and no bold black mask.
Spotted pale underparts and a pale face with no black stripes; often feeds on the ground.
