voice: A loud, sharp series of high “wik-wik-wik” clicks, speeding up toward the end; drums very loudly, a short roll ending in about four separate taps.
behaviour: Often heard before it is seen, from its loud calls, hammering and drumming, which carries up to 1 km and comes from the same high dead branch. It works one tree for a long time, then flies off far to another, and slips behind the branch when watched.
memo: The biggest drummer in the bushveld: a black beard and a roll that ends in four knocks.

migration: Intra-African migrant whose movements follow the rains. It arrives from central and East Africa in September-October, calls and breeds through the summer (eggs October to March), and leaves in March-April. Essentially absent in the dry winter months.
size: 18-20 cm: a small cuckoo, about the size of a bulbul but with a longer tail.
keys: Metallic green upperparts with a coppery-bronze sheen, white underparts with green-barred flanks
Broken white stripe above and behind the eye, plus white spots on the folded wing and the tail
Red eye and red eye-ring, black bill (male)
Female more coppery with a buff throat and more barring; juvenile has a distinctive coral-red bill

confuse.how: Only a small white patch behind the eye (no white stripe in front of it), no white spots on the wing, a dark eye, and a quite different call “meitjie”.

voice: The name says it all: a loud, plaintive, persistent “dee-dee-dee-deederik”, given for long periods from a perch, mostly in the morning and late afternoon.
behaviour: A brood parasite of weavers, bishops and sparrows: the female watches a colony, slips into a nest while the owners are away, removes an egg and lays her own, often chased off by angry weavers. The male courts the female by offering her hairy caterpillars, a food most birds avoid.
memo: Shouts its own name: “dee-dee-deederik!” from the weaver colony.

migration: Many birds arrive in September and October and leave around April. Klaas's Cuckoo is also the cuckoo most likely to stay through the winter in the low-lying Lowveld, where some pairs are resident. It calls from late winter onwards, and egg-laying peaks from October to January.
size: 16-18 cm: smaller than a Laughing Dove, about the size of a bulbul but slimmer.
keys: Male glossy emerald green above, plain white below with green patches on the sides of the breast
Small white spot behind the eye only, with no white in front of it
No white spots on the wings
Female bronze-brown above, white below finely barred bronze-brown

confuse.how: Has a white eyebrow in front of and behind the eye, rows of white spots on the wings, and (male) a red eye.

voice: A plaintive, repeated “mee-tjie, mee-tjie”, which gives it its Afrikaans name Meitjie.
behaviour: A brood parasite that lays one egg per nest, mainly in the nests of batises (Chinspot Batis) and sunbirds. The chick throws out the host’s eggs. It feeds high in the canopy, mostly on hairy caterpillars.
memo: A little emerald cuckoo crying “mee-tjie” from the treetops, even in winter.

migration: Intra-African migrant that breeds north of the equator in the Sahel rains (May to August), then flies south to spend the austral summer here without breeding. Arrives with the first good rains, mostly November-December, wanders nomadically after food, and gathers in big flocks before leaving between late February and early April.
size: 73-81 cm, the smallest stork in the region: smaller than a White Stork, with a wingspan of about 1.4 m.
keys: Glossy black head, neck, back and wings with a white belly and a white rump that shows well in flight
Short greenish-horn bill with a red tip
Bare blue-grey face with a red patch in front of the eye; brighter blue around the bill when breeding
Dull olive-grey legs with red 'knees' and feet; juvenile browner, duller, with a reddish bill

confuse.how: Bigger, with a bright red bill and red legs; black down to the chest with no white rump, and usually alone near water, not in flocks on dry grassland.
Mostly white body with black flight feathers, and a long red bill and red legs; often feeds alongside Abdim's at fires and locust swarms.
Fluffy white neck and white undertail, longer dark bill; usually in pairs near water rather than in big dry-country flocks.

voice: Mostly silent; at roosts and nests it gives weak, two-note whistles, also some bill-clattering.
behaviour: Walks slowly in loose, spread-out flocks across grassland, cultivated or freshly burnt ground, snapping up grasshoppers, locusts, caterpillars and termites. Gathers in the thousands at locust outbreaks, armyworm plagues and grass fires, and soars high in the midday heat. In Africa it is popularly said to bring the rain with it.
memo: The little 'rain stork': black above, white belly, here with the summer rains.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds in Europe and western Asia, leaves in August and September and reaches southern Africa from about October, travelling over land via Gibraltar or the Levant. It wanders in flocks during the austral summer, following insect outbreaks, and leaves northwards from March, with the last birds gone by about May.
size: 100-115 cm, wingspan up to about 2 m: taller and much bulkier than a Grey Heron.
keys: All-white body with black flight feathers, black on the wing both at rest and in flight
Long, straight, bright red bill and long red legs
Flies with the neck stretched out, often in large soaring flocks circling on thermals
Juvenile: duller, with a dark-tipped or orange-based bill and pinkish legs

confuse.how: Has a slightly down-curved yellow bill, a bare red face and a pinkish tinge to the white plumage, and is usually found at water.
Smaller, mostly black with only the belly and lower back white, and a greenish bill. The two often forage together in summer flocks.

voice: Almost silent. Adults greet each other with loud bill-clattering, head thrown back, but this is mostly heard at the nest in Europe.
behaviour: Gregarious in Africa: flocks, sometimes in the hundreds, walk slowly through grassland and burnt veld, snapping up locusts, armyworm caterpillars and other insects, and they gather where outbreaks occur. They travel by soaring on thermals and avoid crossing open sea.
memo: The baby-bringer from Europe: white, black-winged, red bill and legs, flocking in summer.

migration: Largely resident in eastern South Africa, where pairs breed with eggs laid August to December, in a stick nest high in a large tree. Elsewhere in southern Africa it is a non-breeding visitor, from about November to April, so numbers in the Lowveld may increase in summer.
size: 75-92 cm: a medium-sized stork, a little taller than a Hadada Ibis.
keys: Glossy black body with a fluffy, woolly white neck
Black cap on the crown and a dark face
White lower belly and undertail, long red legs, blackish bill with a red tip
Juvenile: browner and duller, with a feathered forehead

confuse.how: Entirely glossy black, neck included, with only the belly white. Bill and legs are bright red.
Smaller and has a black neck with no woolly white, plus a white lower back, a greenish bill and dull legs. Usually seen in flocks.

voice: Mostly silent. It gives two-syllable whistles and bill-clapping during displays at the nest.
behaviour: Usually seen alone or in pairs, walking slowly and deliberately along rivers, pans and dam edges, stabbing at frogs, insects and crabs. It is drawn to grass fires to catch fleeing insects and small animals.
memo: The bishop stork: black robes and a white woolly scarf.

migration: The southern African population is separate from the European migrants and is essentially resident, wandering locally between rivers and pools. It breeds in autumn and winter (eggs about April–September) on cliff ledges, when shrinking pools concentrate fish. Kruger and the surrounding Lowveld are its most reliable area in South Africa.
size: 95-100 cm, wingspan about 1.5 m: as tall as a White Stork, but much darker.
keys: Glossy black head, neck, breast and back, with a purple-green sheen in good light
Clean white lower breast and belly
Bright red bill, red legs and red skin around the eye
Juvenile: brown and dull, with grey-green bill and legs. In flight: black wings and front, white belly and armpits

confuse.how: Smaller summer visitor in flocks, with a grey-green bill, blue face and white lower back that shows in flight.
Fluffy white neck and white undertail, and a dark bill with a red tip.
Much bigger, with a huge red-black-yellow bill and white flight feathers showing in flight.

voice: Mostly silent away from the nest. At the nest it gives wheezy, raptor-like whistles and hisses, and clatters its bill.
behaviour: A shy, solitary hunter that wades slowly through shallow pools to stab fish and frogs. It is usually alone or in pairs, often at drying pools in the dry season. It nests on inaccessible cliff ledges and reuses the same nest for years.
memo: A black stork in a white vest and red stockings, fishing the last winter pools.

migration: Intra-African migrant that comes to breed. It winters in tropical Africa further north, arrives in the Lowveld from about September-October, and leaves from March to May. While here it moves around locally following fruiting trees.
size: 16-18 cm: smaller and slimmer than a Cape Starling, about the size of a House Sparrow but longer.
keys: Male: entire head, back, wings and tail glossy violet-amethyst that can look black, plum or coppery depending on the light
Male: pure white lower breast and belly, sharply cut off from the violet
Female: brown above with pale edges, white below heavily streaked dark brown, like a small thrush
Juvenile like the female but with more rufous fringes and a dark eye

confuse.how: Glossy blue-green all over, including the belly, with an orange-yellow eye; no white underparts.
Could suggest the streaky female, but it is bigger, grey above with a bold black-and-white face pattern, and feeds on the ground, whereas the starling stays in the canopy.

voice: Fairly quiet: soft, plaintive nasal whistles; the male's song is a short series of lively notes then whistles, rendered “tipee-tipee-teeeeuu”.
behaviour: Lives in the tree canopy and is rarely seen on the ground, feeding on fruit (figs, mistletoe, berries) and catching flying termites in the air like a flycatcher. Flocks are often made up mostly of one sex, so a party of streaky brown females may be seen without a single male.
memo: Amethyst on top, snow below: the jewel starling that brings summer.

migration: Mainly a bird of the escarpment, highveld gardens, forest edges and fynbos, resident in most of its range but partly migratory in the north-east. In the Lowveld it is at most a scarce visitor, probably dropping down from the nearby Drakensberg escarpment in the dry season when aloes flower.
size: About 14 cm including the long bill: about the length of a sparrow, but much slimmer.
keys: Male: glittering green head, throat and back
Broad scarlet breast band, wider than in the other double-collared sunbirds, edged above by a thin metallic blue line
Pale grey belly (not black or white), long down-curved black bill; yellow tufts at the shoulders show in display
Female: plain greyish-olive, paler below, with darker wings

confuse.how: Male has a purple-blue and maroon band, not red, and a black belly; female is yellowish and streaked below.
Male has a green head with a narrow purple-blue band and a clean white belly, no red; smaller and shorter-billed.
Male is mostly sooty black-brown with a scarlet chest and green forehead, not green above.

voice: A harsh, repeated “chut” call; the song is a fast, high-pitched jumble of tweets and twitters.
behaviour: Feeds on nectar, especially aloes in winter, and on small insects; males defend flowering plants aggressively and fluff out their yellow shoulder tufts when displaying.
memo: A wide red sash and a grey belly: a mountain sunbird visiting the bushveld.

migration: Resident all year in acacia and mixed bushveld, with some local wandering to follow flowering plants such as aloes and Kigelia (sausage tree). Breeds from July to February, mainly September to November.
size: 11-14 cm: a little smaller than a House Sparrow, with a long, curved bill.
keys: Male: glossy metallic green head, throat and back
Male: a thin violet-blue band and a wide maroon-purple band across the breast, above a black belly
Female: brown above, pale yellowish below with dark streaks on the throat and breast
Long, strongly down-curved black bill; immature male has a dark throat on a yellow, streaked breast

confuse.how: Smaller, with a shorter bill; the male has a white belly below the purple band, and the female is plain greyish-white below with no streaks.
Bigger and stockier; the male is velvety dark brown with a bright scarlet breast, the female dark and heavily mottled below.
Small, short-billed and green above with a yellow belly; the male has only a thin purple collar and no maroon band or black belly.

voice: A repeated sharp "chip-chip" call; the song is a long, fast jumble of chips, buzzes and trills that can go on for minutes.
behaviour: Hovers or clings at aloe, coral-tree and sausage-tree flowers, and also catches insects in flight. Males sing from treetops and hold vocal duels with rivals, and the female builds the nest and incubates alone.
memo: Green suit, maroon tie, black trousers: the bushveld's long-billed sunbird.

migration: Resident and sedentary in the Lowveld, moving only locally to flowering trees and aloes. Breeds over a long season, June to March, peaking September to December.
size: 10-12 cm: smaller than a House Sparrow, with a thin, curved bill.
keys: Male: glossy metallic green head, throat and back, with a narrow violet-blue band across the breast
Clean white belly, unique among the local green sunbirds
Female: plain grey-brown above and off-white below, without streaks
Medium, slightly curved black bill

confuse.how: Larger, with a longer, more curved bill; the male has a broad maroon breast band and a black belly, not white.
Smaller, with a short bill and a yellow belly.
The female is darker and heavily mottled below, not clean white; the male is velvety black with a red breast.

voice: A sharp, metallic chattering call; the male sings a fast, loud, rambling twittering warble from a treetop.
behaviour: Often the commonest sunbird in thornveld, visiting aloes, coral trees and wild dagga for nectar alongside other sunbirds. In the late afternoon it catches insects in flight and gleans them from leaves. The female alone builds the untidy oval nest of grass and spider web, sometimes next to a wasp nest.
memo: A green sunbird with a white belly: the bushveld's everyday nectar sipper.

migration: Resident in the Lowveld, though young and some adults wander widely (one ringed bird moved 2,100 km); movements are poorly known and it may be nomadic in places. Eggs can be laid almost all year, with a peak from October to January; a single chick fledges after about 100-110 days.
size: 66-78 cm, wingspan 160-185 cm: a big eagle, larger than a Tawny Eagle, with an outsized owl-like head.
keys: Uniform dark chocolate-brown, sitting very upright on a bare treetop or pylon
Large rounded, owl-like head with big yellow eyes
Long bare, pale greyish-white legs (no 'trousers')
In flight: silvery-white flight feathers contrasting with dark brown body and underwing coverts; tail dark with 3-4 narrow pale bars

confuse.how: Paler, tawny brown, with feathered 'baggy trousers' down to the feet, a flatter head and a dark eye.
Adult has a white belly and white underwings; the brown juvenile is more rufous below and has a paler, less uniform look.
The brown juvenile has a very short tail, short legs and a different, long-winged gliding silhouette.

voice: Usually silent; in display gives a hoarse, guttural “hok-hok-hok” series, sometimes ending in a crowing sound.
behaviour: A patient perch hunter: it sits for long periods on an exposed branch, then glides down onto a snake, crushes its head and swallows it whole, even cobras, mambas and puff adders. Its thick, scaly legs help protect it from bites, but it is not immune to venom.
memo: Chocolate eagle, owl's head, yellow eyes, bare white legs: the snake hunter on the dead tree.

migration: Partly migratory and nomadic, with movements that are not well understood. In the former Transvaal it is mainly a non-breeding visitor, and more birds appear in the dry winter months; in South Africa it lays its single egg mostly June to August.
size: 63-71 cm, wingspan about 1.8 m: a medium-large eagle, smaller than a Martial Eagle.
keys: Dark brown-black head, chest and back like a hood, sharply cut off from a clean white belly with no spots
Big round head with large lemon-yellow eyes, owl-like face
In flight: white underwings with three narrow black bars on the flight feathers and barred tail
Juvenile very different: rufous to cinnamon brown below, scaly brown above

confuse.how: Much larger, with dark spots on the white belly and dark brown underwings; the Snake Eagle's belly and underwings are pure white.
Same big-headed, yellow-eyed shape, but dark brown all over, including the belly and underwing coverts.

voice: Usually silent; occasionally a whistled “kwo-kwo-kwo-kweeoo”, sometimes in flight.
behaviour: One of the few eagles that hovers: it hangs in the wind high over open ground, then parachutes down feet first to grab a snake, cobras and puff adders included, and crush its head. Often seen perched in full view on a dead tree or pole.
memo: An eagle in a black hood and white trousers that hovers to hunt snakes.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, living in pairs or small family groups on a permanent territory. It is much more conspicuous in summer, when males sing from bush tops. Breeds October to April, peaking November to January.
size: 12-15 cm: about the length of a sparrow, but slimmer, with a longish tail.
keys: Rufous-brown crown and rufous edges to the wing feathers
Grey-brown back boldly streaked dark, plain unstreaked rump
Plain greyish face with a faint pale eyebrow, whitish underparts with buff-grey flanks
Sings from the top of a bush with the tail cocked; sexes alike, juvenile washed pale yellow below

confuse.how: Bigger and bulkier with a heavy, thick bill and no rufous cap; gives a croaking "chee-fro" rather than a rattle.
Smaller with a short, white-tipped tail and a streaked crown; calls "zit… zit" in a bouncing display flight over grass, not from a bush top.
Plain unstreaked back, clear white eyebrow, tawny flanks and a long tail waved and cocked high.

voice: A few sharp introductory notes followed by a dry trill, "chi-chi-chi-chrrrrr", repeated from a bush top; the rattle at the end gives the bird its name.
behaviour: Noisy and aggressive at intruders, scolding from a perch with a repeated sharp alarm note. Young from earlier broods often stay on as helpers that defend the territory with the breeding pair.
memo: The bushveld's rattler: a few sharp notes and a dry trill from every thornbush.

migration: Resident and sedentary, but very local: in the Lowveld it lives only in rank, tall grass and reeds along rivers, streams and marshy areas. Breeds October to March, mostly December to February, in a ball nest with a side entrance built less than half a metre above the ground.
size: 13-15 cm: a little smaller than a House Sparrow, with a longish tail.
keys: Plain, unstreaked grey-brown back and crown (no bold streaks, no rufous cap)
Warm rufous-orange face (lores, cheeks and around the eye), strongest outside the breeding season
Whitish throat and underparts, with buffy flanks
Always low in dense waterside vegetation

confuse.how: Streaked back and a rufous cap, lives in dry bushveld rather than waterside reeds, and gives a dry rattling song.
Has an obvious white eyebrow, rufous-edged wings and a long tail it often cocks and flicks, with no rufous face.
Smaller and heavily streaked above, with a short white-tipped tail; sings “zit-zit-zit” in a high display flight over grassland.

voice: A loud, ringing series of whistled notes that rise in volume, often given as a duet by the pair from inside the reeds.
behaviour: Skulks low in thick riverside grass and reeds, gleaning insects such as beetles, ants and flying termites; it is far more often heard than seen. The pair calls loudly to each other from cover, the best way to find it.
memo: The plain cisticola with a sunburnt face, hiding in the riverside reeds.

migration: Resident and largely sedentary in open and damp grassland. Breeds August to April, mostly November to February; it is conspicuous only while males display in summer.
size: 10 cm: a tiny warbler, much smaller than a sparrow, with a short tail.
keys: Buff-brown back heavily streaked black; whitish underparts with rufous flanks
Short, fan-shaped tail with a black band and white tip to each feather, best seen from below
Pale face with a pale eye, no rufous cap
Breeding male shows less streaking on the crown than the female

confuse.how: Bigger and plainer-backed, sings a harsh rattling song from bush tops in the bushveld, not in a bouncing song flight over grass.
Much bigger and bulkier, with a heavy bill and a croaking call.
Long, often cocked tail, plain unstreaked back and a pale eyebrow.

voice: In the song flight a dry, metallic “zit… zit… zit” repeated in rhythm, one note at each dip; the alarm is a sharp “tchep”.
behaviour: The male rises 15-30 m above the grass and flies in undulating circles, giving one “zit” at the bottom of each bounce, then drops back to cover. Otherwise it creeps through the grass like a mouse. It sews its pouch nest into a grass tuft with spider web.
memo: A tiny bouncing dot in the sky going “zit… zit… zit” over the grass.

migration: Resident and sedentary, living in rank, often damp grassland with scattered bushes. Breeds in summer, with eggs laid from October to March. Outside the breeding season it rarely leaves the grass, so it goes unnoticed in winter.
size: 13-17 cm, the largest cisticola, about the size of a House Sparrow. The male is clearly bigger than the female.
keys: Big, heavy-bodied cisticola with a stout, heavy bill
Grey-brown upperparts heavily streaked black, whitish underparts, no bright rufous cap
Chestnut panel in the folded wing
Broad, pale-tipped tail that it often flicks. Non-breeding birds are more tawny and finely streaked

confuse.how: Smaller and less heavily built, with a rufous-tinged cap and a dry rattling song given from a bush top, not a frog-like croak.
Much smaller (about 10 cm), with a short white-tipped tail and a sharp “zit… zit… zit” given in a high bouncing display flight.

voice: A loud, frog-like croaking “breep-breep” (or “krrrk”), surprisingly loud for its size and the easiest way to identify it.
behaviour: More often heard than seen, keeping low in the grass. In the breeding season the male makes short display flights and croaks in the air; males are polygamous, and the female hides a ball-shaped grass nest with a side entrance deep in a green grass tuft.
memo: A cisticola that croaks like a frog from the long grass.

migration: Breeding migrant that arrives in October and leaves by April; it spends the austral winter further north in Africa (up to Kenya, Sudan and Chad). Some southern African birds may come from India, but this has never been proven by ringing. A few stay all year.
size: 33-34 cm: about the length of a dove but slim, with a long graduated tail and a crest.
keys: Glossy black upperparts and a pointed black crest
Clean white underparts with no streaks
White patch on the wing and white tips to the long tail, obvious in flight
Dark morph all black except the white wing patch; juvenile duller with a small crest and buffy underparts

confuse.how: Bigger and longer-tailed, with heavy black streaks on the throat and upper breast; Jacobin's underparts are plain white.
Can suggest the dark-morph Jacobin, but has no crest and no white wing patch.

voice: Loud, ringing metallic whistles, “klee-klee-kleeuu, kleeuu”, often given in flight or in chases between birds.
behaviour: A brood parasite, mostly of bulbuls, especially the Dark-capped Bulbul, and also Sombre Greenbul and fiscals. The male calls loudly near the nest to distract the hosts while the female slips in to lay; the chick does not evict its nest mates but grabs most of the food. Hops through foliage picking off hairy caterpillars.
memo: A crested black-and-white monk that leaves its eggs with the bulbuls.

migration: Intra-African breeding migrant that winters in equatorial Africa. It arrives in southern Africa around October-November and leaves around March-April once breeding is over. Its Afrikaans name, Gestreepte Nuwejaarsvoël (“striped New Year bird”), reflects its summer presence.
size: About 38-39 cm, much of it tail: bigger and longer-tailed than a Laughing Dove, slim and crested.
keys: Glossy black upperparts with a spiky crest and a white patch at the base of the primaries
White underparts with a heavily black-streaked throat and upper breast
Very long, graduated black tail with white tips
Rare dark morph all black apart from the white wing patch; juvenile brown above with a buffy face and underparts

confuse.how: Smaller and shorter-tailed, with a plain white or greyish throat and breast, no streaks; dark morphs of the two are almost identical except for size.
All black without a crest or white wing patch, and calls a mournful rising “hoo-hoo-heee”.

voice: A loud, ringing, repeated “kuwu-weer, kuwu-weer…” and an excited, rapid “ku-wi-wi-wi-wi”.
behaviour: A brood parasite of babblers, notably Arrow-marked Babbler: the pair works as a team, one bird distracting the babbler group with showy flights while the female slips in to lay. The chick does not evict the host's eggs or young and grows up with its foster siblings. It feeds largely on hairy caterpillars, including mopane worms.
memo: A crested black-and-white cuckoo with a pinstriped bib that lays its eggs on the babblers.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds in eastern Europe and western Asia and crosses at the Bosphorus and through Egypt to winter in Africa, south to north-eastern South Africa. It arrives in southern Africa in October, most in November, and most leave in March.
size: 57-64 cm, wingspan 145-170 cm: a medium-sized eagle, smaller than a Tawny Eagle, with a small head and bill.
keys: Plain dark brown, with paler brown wing coverts and head, and a pale yellowish eye in the adult
Long legs in tight, narrow feathered “stovepipe” trousers (not baggy) and round nostrils
In flight: pale flash at the base of the primaries above and a pale crescent on the rump
Juvenile darker, with rows of cream spots on the wing coverts forming thin pale lines across the wing, and a dark eye

confuse.how: Bigger and heavier-billed, with baggy trousers, oval nostrils and a gape that extends to the back of the eye; plumage often tawny rather than dark brown.
Smaller, with a small crest and a long, narrow, square-ended tail; soars on straight, flat wings and is here mainly August to March as a breeder.

voice: Mostly silent in Africa; on its breeding grounds it gives a high, dog-like yelp, “yuk-yuk”.
behaviour: In southern Africa it lives largely on flying termites: after rain, when the alates swarm, it gathers with other eagles and kites, walking on the ground or hunting from a perch to snap them up. It also raids Red-billed Quelea colonies for chicks, and takes rodents and frogs.
memo: A plain brown eagle in tight stockings that comes from Europe to feast on termites after the rains.

migration: Resident all year and largely sedentary, with family groups wandering locally to fruiting trees. Can breed in almost any month, with egg-laying mainly September to January.
size: 30-36 cm, of which more than half is tail: the body is about the size of a bulbul.
keys: Drab mousy-brown bird with a shaggy crest and a very long, stiff, graduated tail
Blackish face and throat, no red skin on the face
Bicoloured bill: black above, whitish to silvery below
Juvenile: shorter crest and tail, browner eye

confuse.how: Has a bare red mask around the eye, greyer plumage and flies fast and straight in tight groups, while the Speckled flutters weakly from bush to bush.

voice: Noisy in groups but without a real song: buzzing, harsh contact notes and a 'tsu-tsu' in flight, with a sharp 'tisk-tisk' alarm.
behaviour: Creeps through thickets like a mouse, often hanging from branches by its feet, and groups sunbathe with fluffed bellies on a branch. At night they roost in tight clusters and can drop into torpor on cold nights.
memo: A brown mouse with a crest and a long tail, creeping in the thicket.

migration: Sedentary resident, but flocks commute daily, sometimes 20-25 km, between roosts and feeding areas. Breeds in any month, often mainly in the dry season.
size: 32-35 cm: the size of a feral town pigeon.
keys: Rufous-maroon back and wings heavily spotted with small white triangles
Bare red skin around a pale yellow eye
Blue-grey head and belly, neck streaked brown and white
Juvenile: browner, with dull brownish eye skin

confuse.how: Has a black half-collar on the hindneck, pinkish-grey plumage and no white spots on the wings.

voice: A loud, fast, rising series 'doo-doo-doo-doo', higher and quicker than a feral pigeon's coo.
behaviour: Originally a cliff and rocky-outcrop bird, it now nests readily on buildings, under eaves and on roofs, so look for it around lodges and staff villages rather than in open bush. Feeds on seeds on the ground, often in flocks.
memo: The cliff pigeon with red glasses and white spots.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, holding territories even outside the breeding season. After breeding it may disperse locally, returning when the rains start. Eggs are laid August to February, mostly September to December, in an old tree hole or a termite mound.
size: 28-30 cm, or 36-38 cm with the tail streamers: about the size of a dove, but with a big head and a strong bill.
keys: Lilac throat and breast, turquoise-blue belly
Greenish crown, whitish face and chin, rufous-brown back
Long black outer tail streamers; in flight dazzling cobalt and turquoise wings
Sexes alike; juvenile has a rufous-buff, white-streaked breast and no streamers

confuse.how: Summer visitor with an all-blue head and underparts, no lilac on the breast and no tail streamers.
Bigger and dull, with a lilac-brown breast streaked white, a white eyebrow and a square tail.
Cinnamon-brown with a short, broad yellow bill and no long streamers; hunts insects high in the air at dusk.

voice: A harsh, grating, crow-like “rak-rak-rak” or “kraak”, mostly in flight during territorial displays.
behaviour: Sits on an exposed perch such as a dead branch, pole or termite mound, then drops onto insects, scorpions or lizards and usually returns to the same perch to eat. In display it climbs high, then dives steeply, rolling from side to side while calling harshly, hence the name “roller”. It also comes to bush fires to catch the animals fleeing the flames.
memo: Lilac bib, turquoise wings, two black ribbons: the bushveld's jewel on every dead branch.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds from North Africa and Spain to Central Asia and spends the austral summer in African savannas. In South Africa it is concentrated in the Lowveld of Limpopo and Mpumalanga, arriving in October-November and leaving in March-April. A bird tracked from nearby Timbavati started its migration on 28 March and crossed 720 km to Gorongosa in three and a half days.
size: 29-32 cm: about the size of a Eurasian Jay; stocky, slightly shorter than a Lilac-breasted Roller, with no tail streamers.
keys: Turquoise-blue head and underparts with no lilac or purple on the breast
Plain rusty-brown back
Square-tipped tail without streamers
In flight, bright blue wings with black flight feathers; juvenile duller, greener and with a streaked breast

confuse.how: Lilac throat and breast, green crown, rusty cheeks and long tail streamers; resident all year.
Larger and bulkier, with a purplish-brown breast streaked white and a white eyebrow; looks much drabber.
Smaller and darker, cinnamon-brown with a short bright yellow bill; hunts flying termites at dusk.

voice: Mostly quiet in Africa; its calls are harsh, crow-like or magpie-like rasping notes.
behaviour: A sit-and-wait hunter: it perches in full view on a dead branch, pole or wire like a big shrike, then drops to the ground for beetles and grasshoppers. Usually alone or in loose groups here, though it migrates in flocks of hundreds. Its name comes from the tumbling display flight it performs on its breeding grounds.
memo: The roller without lilac or streamers: all blue and rust, back from Europe for the rains.

migration: Mostly resident in the Lowveld in territorial pairs, with some local, nomadic movements depending on conditions. Breeds mainly from October to April, in a tree cavity.
size: 35-40 cm: the largest roller, about the size of a pigeon but more heavily built, with a big head.
keys: Broad white eyebrow and a white spot on the nape
Pinkish-lilac underparts heavily streaked with white
Olive-brown back and crown (southern race), dark square tail without streamers
In flight, purple-blue wings that are duller than in other rollers

confuse.how: Plain lilac breast, unstreaked, turquoise belly and bright blue wings, with two tail streamers.
Head and underparts all turquoise blue, chestnut back. A summer visitor only.
Smaller, cinnamon-brown with a short, broad yellow bill and no white eyebrow.

voice: A harsh, grating “kaa-kaa-kaa” repeated steadily, given non-stop during display flights.
behaviour: Hunts from a high perch, often a dead tree or a wire, and drops onto grasshoppers, scorpions and small lizards. Its display flight is spectacular: it climbs above the trees, then rocks from side to side and tumbles down calling loudly. It fiercely chases crows, small raptors and other rollers.
memo: The heavy, streaky roller with a white eyebrow: the dullest roller, but the biggest.

migration: Mostly sedentary, making only short local moves after drought or local rain. Breeds September to November, building a large twig nest in a tall isolated tree or on a telephone pole. Its range and numbers are growing in South Africa, helped by farms, roads and towns.
size: 45-50 cm: a large crow, the size of a Carrion Crow, much bigger than a pigeon.
keys: Glossy black bird with a white “waistcoat”: white breast, collar and upper back
Strong black bill, black legs, dark eye
In flight, black wings with white underwing coverts and a white band across the body
Juvenile duller black, with the white faintly spotted dark
voice: A harsh, repeated “karh-karh-karh” and a deeper “kla-kla”, often with head bobbing and tail movements.
behaviour: A clever, bold omnivore that scavenges carrion and roadkill, raids bins and robs other birds' nests of eggs and chicks. It even kills snakes such as puff adders and attacks roosting fruit bats. It mobs and chases raptors much bigger than itself.
memo: A crow in a white waistcoat: the scavenger of roads and villages.

migration: Resident all year wherever there is permanent water with reeds or overhanging vegetation. Outside the breeding season it wanders locally in search of food, and young birds disperse widely, sometimes flying at night. Breeds over a long season in southern Africa, roughly August to May, often timed to low water so the burrow is not flooded.
size: 13-14 cm: a little smaller than a House Sparrow, with a big head and a long bill.
keys: Bright red-orange, long dagger bill and red legs
Turquoise crown barred black, running down to the eye, with a shaggy crest usually held flat
Deep blue back, orange-chestnut face and underparts, white throat and a white patch on the side of the neck
Sexes alike; juvenile duller and darker, with a black bill that slowly turns red

confuse.how: Slightly smaller, no crest, an orange eyebrow and a violet wash on the cheeks, the dark blue crown stopping above the eye; lives in woodland, often far from water.
Much bigger and black and white with a black bill; hovers over open water rather than sitting low in reeds.

voice: Fairly quiet; a thin, high-pitched squeaky note, usually given as it whirrs low over the water.
behaviour: Sits motionless on a reed stem or low branch just above the water, bobbing its head and flicking its tail, then plunges steeply to catch a small fish near the surface. It beats the fish on the perch and swallows it head first. When flushed it zips away low over the water like a blue spark and soon perches again.
memo: A jewel on a reed: red bill, turquoise cap, blue spark over the water.

migration: Sedentary resident of riverine forest, dense thickets and gardens, holding a territory of about 1 ha. In southern Africa it lays from August to January, peaking in November, and often raises two broods.
size: 19-20 cm: about the size of a thrush (like Kurrichane Thrush).
keys: Black head with a long, bold white eyebrow from the bill to the nape
Bright orange-rufous underparts and collar, olive-grey back
Orange rump and outer tail feathers with dark brown central feathers, seen as it flies into cover
Juvenile: brown head, faint eyebrow, mottled and duller

confuse.how: Has a white throat and a white wing bar, with orange only on the breast sides and flanks; it prefers drier thickets.
Much smaller and brown, with white wing bars and a streaked breast, and a dark tail tipped white rather than orange.

voice: A rich, loud song that starts softly and swells in a crescendo, phrases repeated many times, often in duet at dawn and dusk; often rendered as “don't-you-do-it, don't-you-do-it, DON'T-YOU-DO-IT”. The alarm is a guttural “takata-kata-kata”.
behaviour: Shy and stays hidden, hopping on the ground and flicking through leaf litter in shade, but the male's loud crescendo song from deep in cover gives it away. It also chases emerging termites in the air and is a frequent host of the Red-chested Cuckoo.
memo: Black hood, white brow, orange belly: the dawn crescendo of the riverine thicket.

migration: Nomad that follows insect outbreaks, especially locusts and caterpillars, so flocks turn up and vanish unpredictably. In the summer-rainfall areas it breeds mostly January to March, in colonies that are abandoned if the insects run out.
size: 21 cm: about the size of a Cape Starling, with a shorter tail and pointed wings.
keys: Pale grey-brown starling with black wings and tail
Whitish rump, obvious when the flock takes off
Breeding male: bare yellow head with black wattles on the forehead and throat; it can look half bald
Non-breeding male, female and juvenile: feathered head with a small bare yellow patch behind the eye and a dark moustache stripe; female's wings and tail browner

confuse.how: All glossy blue-green with a bright orange-yellow eye, no grey body and no white rump.
The female is brown above and white below with heavy dark streaks, not plain grey, and has no white rump.

voice: Wheezy, grating calls like a European starling, especially a drawn-out “ssreeeeo”; flocks keep up a squeaky chatter.
behaviour: Very gregarious, often in large flocks mixed with other starlings, feeding on the ground among grazing game and livestock. It perches on animals' backs to pick off ticks and catch the insects they flush. Known as the “locust bird” because it gathers to feed and breed at locust swarms.
memo: A grey starling with a white rump; the breeding male is bald and yellow with black wattles.

migration: Intra-African migrant that comes south to breed when the rains have grown enough grass cover. Present in southern Africa from about October to April, then returns to equatorial Africa, flying mostly at night. Lays from October to March, peaking in January and February.
size: 20-23 cm: a little smaller than a blackbird, but plump, short-tailed and long-legged.
keys: Blue-grey face, throat and breast, with a white line from the bill to above the eye
Flanks and belly boldly barred black and white
Upperparts blackish, streaked olive-brown; short reddish bill and red eye
Juvenile duller, with a dark bill, grey eye and less barring

confuse.how: Smaller, with a short stubby bill, buffy plumage with an orange breast and no black-and-white barred belly; flushes on whirring wings without trailing its legs.
All black with a bright yellow bill and red legs, and lives at the water's edge rather than in dry grass.

voice: The male's territorial call is a long series of rapid, grating “krrr-krrr-krrr” notes, two or three per second, repeated for minutes, mostly in the rainy season.
behaviour: A crake of grassland rather than reedbeds, active by day and especially at dusk or in light rain. Usually seen only when flushed from long grass, flying a short way with its legs dangling before dropping back in.
memo: A grass crake with a zebra belly that only shows up when the rains have made the grass tall.

migration: Resident all year and among the commonest birds of the lowveld (Kruger holds an estimated 65,000). It wanders only locally for fruit and water, gathering in flocks of 20-30 at fruiting trees and waterholes in the dry season. Can breed in any month, with a peak in spring and summer.
size: 47-51 cm including the long tail: bigger than a dove, about the length of a magpie.
keys: Plain smoky grey all over, darkest on the throat
Long, shaggy, wispy crest, raised and lowered with its mood
Long tail and short black bill
Juvenile with a shorter crest and a buffy wash

confuse.how: Same shape and long tail, but colourful: green body, purple crest and bright red flight feathers in flight.

voice: A loud, nasal, drawn-out 'kweh' or 'kay-waaay', often rendered 'go-away', which gives it its English name and the Afrikaans kwêvoël.
behaviour: The bush's alarm system: it calls loudly from treetops at any intruder, and 19th-century hunters complained that it warned game of their approach. Mostly eats fruit, flowers and buds in the canopy, and runs and bounds along branches more than it flies.
memo: Grey, crested and shouting 'go-away!' from the treetops.

migration: Resident and largely sedentary in the Lowveld, though small groups wander locally after seeds, especially in the dry season. Breeds September to April, mostly December to March.
size: 11-13 cm: smaller than a House Sparrow, a small finch with a short tail and stubby bill.
keys: Bright yellow forehead and broad yellow eyebrow on a grey-olive crown
Dark eye-stripe and a bold black moustache stripe framing a yellow face
Bright yellow underparts and a deep yellow rump that flashes as it flies off
Female duller with a weaker face pattern; juvenile greyer-headed, with a streaked breast

confuse.how: Females and non-breeding males are much bigger, with a long pointed bill, a red eye and no black moustache stripe.

voice: Short bursts of sweet, lively, twittering song with trills, much like a domestic canary; males sing a lot, several together in a flock.
behaviour: Feeds mostly on the ground in pairs or small flocks, often with waxbills, flying up into a bush when disturbed. It perches on grass stems and bends them down with its weight to reach the seeds.
memo: A tiny yellow finch with a black moustache and a yellow rump: the bushveld's wild canary.

migration: Intra-African migrant that comes to breed in southern Africa. It arrives from tropical Africa in September and October and calls a lot until about December or January, then goes quiet. It leaves northwards by March, or April at the latest.
size: About 30 cm: the size of a dove, slim, with a long, rounded tail.
keys: All black with a faint gloss, no crest and no white wing patch
White tips to the tail feathers, visible from below or in flight
Dark bill and eye, no red eye and no coloured gape
Female sometimes faintly barred pale brown on the underparts

confuse.how: Deeply forked tail and red eye; perches openly and hawks insects, while the cuckoo has a rounded, white-tipped tail and skulks in the canopy.
Smaller (about 20 cm) with an orange gape and sometimes a yellow shoulder; it gives a dry high trill, not a mournful whistle.
Has a crest and a white patch in the wing, and is usually white below.

voice: A mournful, far-carrying, three-note whistle “hoo-hoo-heeee”, with the last note rising and drawn out, repeated endlessly and known as “I'm so siiick”. Also a wild, excited “whirly-whirly-whirly”.
behaviour: Much easier to hear than to see: it calls from high in a leafy canopy and is hard to locate. A brood parasite of boubous (Laniarius shrikes), including the Southern Boubou. Its chick throws the host's eggs out of the nest a few days after hatching.
memo: “I'm so siiick!” from the treetops: the all-black cuckoo you rarely get to see.

migration: Intra-African migrant that breeds in southern Africa. It arrives from equatorial Africa around September and leaves around March or April. Lays from September to December, peaking in October and November.
size: About 32 cm: the size of a dove, but slim and long-tailed, with pointed wings and a flight that makes it look like a small falcon or sparrowhawk.
keys: Plain grey head, throat and breast; white belly finely barred dark grey
Yellow bill with a dark tip: the yellow covers much of the bill
Yellow eye-ring and yellow legs
Long grey tail with complete pale bars and a white tip; sexes alike

confuse.how: Has a rufous-orange chest and a mostly dark bill, and calls a three-note “piet-my-vrou”, not two notes.
A true hawk with a short hooked bill, red eye and rufous-barred breast; it perches upright and does not call “hoop-hoop”.

voice: The male gives a soft two-note “hoop-hoop” or “coo-coo”, the second note higher, easily mistaken for an African Hoopoe; the female gives a bubbling “kwik-kwik-kwik”.
behaviour: A brood parasite that relies almost entirely on the Fork-tailed Drongo: the male draws the drongos away from their nest while the female removes an egg and lays her own. Lives mostly on hairy caterpillars gleaned from the foliage.
memo: The grey cuckoo with a yellow bill that calls “hoop-hoop” and fools the drongo.

migration: Intra-African migrant that comes here to breed. It spends the austral winter further north in tropical Africa and returns in late September or early October, roughly with the first rains (South Africans call it the “rain bird”). It calls a lot until January, then falls silent and goes unnoticed, and leaves around March-April.
size: About 30 cm, the size of a dove. Slim, with a long tail and pointed wings; its shape recalls a small sparrowhawk.
keys: Rufous-orange chest contrasting with the grey throat and slate-grey upperparts
Creamy belly barred black, long grey tail spotted white
Yellow eye-ring and legs, dark bill
Female has a duller, often barred chest. Juvenile almost black, scaled white

confuse.how: No rufous chest: the breast is grey then barred, and the base of the bill is bright yellow. Its call is a two-note “hoop-hoop”.
The dark juvenile Red-chested Cuckoo can suggest it. The adult Black Cuckoo is all black and gives a mournful “hoo-hoo-heee” with a rising last note.

voice: Three loud, descending notes repeated endlessly: “Piet-my-vrou” in Afrikaans, “Pete-my-wife” or “it-will-rain” in English. Heard from early morning into the night.
behaviour: Heard everywhere but rarely seen, as it calls hidden deep in the foliage. A brood parasite: the female lays an egg in another bird's nest, mostly robin-chats and thrushes. At about two days old, the chick throws out its hosts' eggs or young.
memo: “Piet-my-vrou!” on repeat from October: the rain is coming, and the singer stays invisible.

migration: Resident all year, never far from palms; in the Lowveld it is closely tied to Lala palms and planted ornamental palms around camps and towns. Breeds all year with a peak from August to November. Its range in South Africa has expanded with palm planting.
size: 16 cm: about as long as a Barn Swallow, but much slimmer, with very thin wings and tail.
keys: Very slender, pale grey-brown swift with no white rump or throat patch
Long, thin, scythe-shaped wings
Long, deeply forked tail, usually held closed into a single fine point
Almost always flying around palms, often in small groups

confuse.how: Stockier and blackish, with a big white rump and a short square tail.
Blackish with a narrow white rump band and a white throat; tail forked but shorter and broader.
Bigger and darker, with broader wings and a shorter, only shallowly forked tail.

voice: A thin, high-pitched, shrill twittering scream, given in flight around the palms.
behaviour: It nests on a palm frond: a small pad of feathers and plant down glued on with saliva, and the 1-2 eggs are glued to the pad as well. The incubating bird clings vertically under the hanging leaf, so the eggs never fall out even in wind.
memo: The pencil-thin swift that glues its eggs to a palm leaf.

migration: Largely resident, but flocks move locally between dams and pans, sometimes 100 km or more, following rain and good feeding sites. Numbers on a given dam can change a lot from month to month. Nesting starts with the rainy season.
size: 38-48 cm: a medium-sized duck, a little smaller than a Mallard, with long legs and an upright stance.
keys: White face and forecrown contrasting with a black hindhead and nape
Chestnut neck and breast, black belly, flanks finely barred black and white
Stands very upright on long grey legs, often in a tight group at the water's edge
Long dark bill; juvenile has a dull greyish head without the clean white face

confuse.how: Much bigger, with white head and underparts speckled black, glossy dark wings and, in the male, a knob on the bill; it does not whistle.

voice: Very noisy: a clear, three-note whistle “swee-swee-sweeoo”, given on take-off, in flight and while feeding, often by the whole flock in chorus.
behaviour: Gregarious: flocks stand upright and packed together on the shore, rest through the heat of the day and feed mainly at dawn, dusk and even at night. Pairs bond for life and spend a lot of time preening each other.
memo: A white mask and a whistle: the duck that sings in chorus at dusk.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld. Pairs stay together and defend a territory all year, and each bird roosts alone in a tree hole at night. Lays mainly from July to December, peaking August to October.
size: 14-16 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow, the smallest woodpecker in the region.
keys: Tiny woodpecker with an olive-brown back finely barred white (barred, not spotted)
White face with a dark moustache stripe, whitish underparts heavily streaked black
Male: brown forehead and red hind crown and nape; female: same brown forehead but black hind crown and nape
Juvenile duller and greyer; young males already show some red on the crown

confuse.how: The only other local woodpecker with streaked underparts, but much bigger, with a spotted (not barred) back and golden tail shafts.
Much bigger (about 25 cm), with a bold black-and-white face and finely barred grey underparts, not streaked.
Bigger, with spotted (not streaked) underparts and a red cap; forages mostly on the ground for ants.

voice: A high-pitched, dry rattling series of "krrrek-krrrek" notes. It drums softly and regularly, and is often found by the faint tapping it makes while feeding.
behaviour: Works thin, often dead twigs and stems low in trees and shrubs, hanging under branches and pecking rapidly from every angle to dig out beetle larvae with its long sticky tongue. Often joins mixed bird parties moving through the woodland.
memo: Sparrow-sized woodpecker tapping on twigs: barred back, streaked front, red nape on the male.

migration: Resident all year and sedentary. Pairs keep to the same thickets, in drainage-line bush, thorn scrub and wooded gardens. Breeds September to January, mainly October and November, with a cup nest on or near the ground.
size: 17-18 cm: a little smaller than a blackbird, about the size of a White-browed Robin-Chat.
keys: Bold white eyebrow over a black face mask, with a pure white throat and upper breast
Slate-grey crown and back with a white bar on the shoulder, against black wings
Orange-buff lower breast and belly. Orange rump and tail with a dark centre and dark tip
Juvenile: mottled brown, without the white wing bar

confuse.how: Also has a white eyebrow and an orange tail, but its throat and breast are orange all the way up, and it has no white bar on the wing.
Brown above with streaked underparts and two white wing bars. Cocks and fans a dark tail with white tips, not an orange one.

voice: A varied, high warbling song of whistled phrases, often with imitations of other birds' calls.
behaviour: Shy and ground-loving. It hops through the leaf litter under thickets, flicking leaves over for beetles, termites and ants, and dives back into cover when disturbed. Fruit and small vertebrates are a small part of its diet.
memo: A white bib and a white shoulder flash: the thicket robin-chat that the White-browed one lacks.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, where it is one of the commonest birds. In winter it only makes small local moves to follow food. Breeds mainly September to November.
size: 23-26 cm including the tail: about the size of a blackbird, but slimmer, with a long tail.
keys: All black with a blue gloss, perched in full view on a bare branch
Long, deeply forked tail with the tips flaring outwards
Dark red eye and a stout, slightly hooked black bill
In flight the wings look pale, almost translucent. The juvenile is brownish black with pale spots, a less forked tail and a brown eye

confuse.how: Smaller and slimmer, with a dark (not red) eye, a small unhooked bill and a square or barely notched tail.
The male has a rounded tail with no fork, an orange gape and often a yellow shoulder patch. Keeps more hidden in the foliage.

voice: Very vocal, often the first to sing at dawn and the last at dusk. Mixes metallic, grating and whistled notes, and is an excellent mimic of raptors such as Pearl-spotted Owlet or African Goshawk.
behaviour: A pirate: it mimics the alarm calls of other animals, meerkats or babblers, to scare them off and steal their prey. It follows elephants, giraffes and bush fires to catch the insects they flush, and fearlessly mobs raptors, hornbills and even snakes.
memo: Black, red eye and a fishtail: the savanna's little mimic and bully.

migration: Strictly resident: pairs hold the same territory of a few hectares all year and rarely move more than about 10 km. Breeds mainly September to January.
size: 16-18 cm: a little smaller than a Dark-capped Bulbul.
keys: Male: glossy blue-black cap and back, pure white underparts, black wings with white edges
Bright red eye
Fluffy white rump and lower back, puffed out into a white 'snowball' in display
Female duller, with a white line above the dark lores, a greyer back and an orange eye. Juvenile buffy, with a brown eye

confuse.how: Bigger, skulks low in thickets, has buff-pink flanks, a dark eye and no puffy white back.
Smaller and stockier, with a white eyebrow and a rufous stripe along the flanks.
Black underparts, not white, with a pale eye.

voice: A sharp click followed by a loud whistle, 'chick-weeu', repeated many times, often in duet with the female's harsh rasping calls.
behaviour: Moves restlessly through the tree canopy in pairs, gleaning insects, and often joins mixed bird parties. In display the male puffs out his long white back feathers into a ball and flies about calling, sometimes snapping his bill.
memo: The black-and-white canopy shrike that puffs up a snowball on its back.

migration: Generally resident on permanent water in South Africa, but it moves nomadically to fill temporary pans after rain, so numbers at a given dam fluctuate. Breeds August to March in mixed colonies with other herons, in trees or reeds over water.
size: 55-65 cm: a slim white heron, clearly bigger than a Hadada Ibis in height but much lighter.
keys: All-white, slender heron with a thin black dagger-shaped bill
Black legs with bright yellow feet (“golden slippers”)
Breeding adult has two long thin plumes on the nape and lacy plumes on the back; lores turn pinkish-violet in courtship
Juvenile has duller, greenish-yellow feet

confuse.how: Much larger (about 90 cm) with a very long kinked neck, a yellow bill outside breeding and all-black feet; the dark gape line extends behind the eye.
Smaller and stockier with a short thick yellow bill and short neck; usually feeds in dry grass near game, not in water.

voice: Mostly silent; a harsh croaking “kraah” when disturbed, and gurgling croaks at the breeding colony.
behaviour: An active hunter in shallow water: it walks briskly, dashes after small fish and stirs the mud with one yellow foot to flush prey before stabbing. It also follows hippos, cormorants or spoonbills to snap up what they disturb.
memo: The white egret in golden slippers, stirring the shallows with its feet.

migration: Not a true migrant, but highly mobile: it moves around following rodent booms, and females wander more than males (one ringed bird was found 915 km away). Common on the open highveld, it is only irregular and scarce in the Lowveld's bushveld, mostly in open grassy areas, where numbers rise and fall with rodent populations.
size: About 30-33 cm, wingspan about 80 cm: roughly the size of a dove, but with long pointed wings.
keys: Pale grey above, pure white below, with a striking black shoulder patch on the folded wing
Large forward-facing red eyes under a black 'eyebrow' smudge, giving an owl-like stare
Short, square white tail; yellow legs. In flight from below: white with black wingtips
Juvenile: chestnut wash on the breast, scaly brown-edged back and dark eyes

confuse.how: Also grey and white, but a passerine with a broad black mask across the forehead, black wings without a shoulder patch and a long black-and-white tail. Never hovers.

voice: Mostly silent; gives a thin, high whistle or squeal, mostly near the nest or at roosts.
behaviour: Hovers like a kestrel about 10 m above open grass, legs dangling, before parachuting down onto a mouse; rodents make up over 80% of its diet. When perched on a pole or treetop it often jerks and wags its tail up and down.
memo: The grey ghost with red eyes and black shoulders, hanging in the air over a mouse.

migration: Partially migratory: some birds stay all year, others make local or longer seasonal moves linked to rainfall and altitude (one bird ringed in South Africa was found in Zimbabwe). In South Africa it breeds from October to April, peaking in December and January, when singing males are most conspicuous.
size: 13-15 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow.
keys: Head boldly striped black and white
Warm cinnamon-brown underparts with no white
Male: black throat; female: browner head stripes and a smaller greyish throat patch
Usually on bare stony ground, rocky outcrops or road verges
voice: A short, fast, high-pitched trill of chirpy notes, such as "chip-chip-ip-ereee", sung from a rock or bush top; each male repeats one song type, ending in a typical whistle.
behaviour: Feeds on the ground among rocks, moving in short hops (its legs are too short to walk), picking up seeds and some insects, and needs regular access to water. Usually alone, in pairs or in small family groups. Drawn to freshly burned areas to pick up insects killed by the fire.
memo: A cinnamon sparrow in a striped hat, hopping on rocks.

migration: Resident and sedentary all year: pairs hold large home ranges along rivers and pans. They move locally when droughts or floods change the food supply, and young birds disperse to temporary pans. Breeding can happen almost all year, but mostly from August to March.
size: About 145-150 cm tall with a 2.4-2.7 m wingspan: the tallest stork in Africa, rivalled only by the Marabou.
keys: Huge red bill with a broad black band and a yellow “saddle” at the base
Glossy black head, neck, wings and tail against a white body; in flight the wings are white with black bands
Black legs with pink-red “knees” and feet
Male: dark brown eye and small yellow wattles under the bill. Female: golden-yellow eye, no wattles. Juvenile greyish with a dull bill

confuse.how: Much smaller, with a black breast and back and a plain red bill with no black band or yellow saddle.
White body with pinkish tones, a bare red face and a slightly drooping yellow bill, and black only in the wings and tail.

voice: Almost silent: its only real sound is bill-clattering, mainly at the nest.
behaviour: Hunts like a heron, standing still or wading slowly through shallow water, stabbing at fish and frogs. It swallows fish head first and then takes a gulp of water. Pairs stay together for life and reuse the same huge stick nest at the top of a tall tree year after year.
memo: A red, black and yellow bill on a giant: the stork of the Big Six.

migration: Resident all year but local in the Lowveld, tied to rank grass and reeds near water. Flocks wander locally to follow seeding grasses. In the summer-rainfall north it lays mostly from November to May, peaking December to February.
size: 11-13 cm including the long tail: smaller than a House Sparrow, about the size of a Blue Tit.
keys: Bright red, waxy bill and a red stripe through the eye (the 'mask')
Grey-brown body finely barred with dark brown all over, whitish cheeks and throat
Pink wash on the underparts with a red patch on the belly, dark undertail; long graduated tail
Female paler with less red on the belly; juvenile duller with a black bill

confuse.how: The male is largely pinkish red on the head and body with no barring; the female is plain brown with a red rump, and neither has a red eye-stripe.
The female and non-breeding male also have a red bill, but a streaked back and boldly striped buff-and-black head, with no fine barring or red mask.

voice: Noisy flocks keep up a buzzing, twittering contact call (a nasal 'zep'); the short song is harsh and nasal with a drop at the end, often written 'cher-cher-preee'.
behaviour: Moves in noisy, low-flying flocks of 20-40 or more that cling to grass stems to pick seeds straight from the heads. Builds a ball-shaped grass nest with a long downward entrance tube, and the male roosts in a rough 'cock's nest' on top. Nests may be parasitised by the Pin-tailed Whydah.
memo: A barred brown mouse with a red-wax bill and a red mask, hanging off grass stems.

migration: Sedentary and resident all year, in territorial family groups. Breeding peaks October-November, at the start of the rains.
size: About 24 cm: slightly bigger than a blackbird, stocky, big-headed and long-tailed.
keys: Bright white crown and forehead above a broad black mask through the eye to the side of the neck
Ash-brown back, darker brown wings and tail, off-white underparts with a buff wash on the breast
Strong black hooked bill; sexes alike
Juvenile: crown greyish and mottled, not white

confuse.how: Grey bristly crest instead of a smooth white cap, yellow eye-wattle and black-and-white wings with a white wing bar.
Glossy black with white wing patches and a very long, thin tail; no white crown.

voice: Groups keep up shrill, squeaky, rather bleating calls, often given together while perched or flying from tree to tree.
behaviour: Lives in tight groups of 3-6 birds that sit up on prominent perches, then drop to the ground to grab beetles, caterpillars or termites. A cooperative breeder: helpers join the pair to build a neat grass cup bound with spider web on a horizontal fork, and help feed the chicks. Sometimes follows hornbills to catch the insects they flush.
memo: A white cap and a black bandit's mask, always in a small gang.

migration: Intra-African migrant that comes to the Lowveld to breed in the wet season, then moves north towards the equatorial belt for the dry season. Arrives from about mid-October and leaves by late February or March.
size: 27-30 cm: about the size of a pigeon, but stockier, with a big head.
keys: Bright yellow, very broad and short bill: often the first thing you notice
Cinnamon-brown head and back, lilac-purple throat and breast
In flight: deep blue wings and blue tail contrasting with the brown back
Juvenile: duller, with a paler breast

confuse.how: Larger, with a dark bill, a white eyebrow and a heavily white-streaked purplish breast.
Black bill, turquoise belly, lilac only on the throat and long tail streamers.
Black bill and turquoise-blue head and underparts, not brown and lilac.

voice: A harsh, snarling, rolling cackle, “k-k-k-krrrrr”, often given in flight or when chasing intruders.
behaviour: Sits quietly on a high dead branch most of the day, but in the late afternoon it hawks swarming flying ants and termites, sometimes in groups of up to 100. It nests in tree holes and aggressively chases other birds from its territory.
memo: The yellow-billed dusk hunter: brown bird, blue wings, and a snarl.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds in south-east Siberia, Mongolia, north-east China and Korea, then spends the austral summer in southern Africa, more than 11,000 km away. It crosses India, then flies non-stop over the Indian Ocean to East Africa. The first birds reach the region in early November, a few weeks after the Lesser Kestrels, and most leave in April, the last by early May.
size: 28-30 cm, wingspan 65-75 cm: about the size of a dove, slimmer, with long pointed wings.
keys: Male: all dark slate-grey with chestnut thighs and vent
Bright orange-red legs, cere and eye-ring in both sexes
In flight the male flashes white underwing coverts that contrast with the dark flight feathers
Female: grey above, grey crown, black moustache, white cheeks and creamy underparts heavily spotted and barred black; juvenile browner with buff feather edges

confuse.how: Like the female, it has a black moustache, but its feet and cere are yellow, the underparts are streaked lengthwise (not barred and spotted) and the adult has rufous 'trousers'.
Much bigger and bulkier, with a broad black hood, finely barred underparts and yellow feet; does not hunt in flocks or hover over grassland.

voice: Mostly silent away from its roosts; there, flocks give rapid, shrill, nasal 'kiu-kiu-kiu' notes.
behaviour: Gregarious: flocks sit in rows on wires and dead trees, hover over open grass and swoop down on emerging termites after rain. At night they gather with Lesser Kestrels in huge communal roosts in tall trees, sometimes tens of thousands of birds.
memo: A grey falcon with orange socks and white armpits, all the way from Siberia.

migration: Scarce at Pidwa. The resident African race (minor) lives all year near cliffs, such as on the nearby Drakensberg escarpment, and lays from late July to early November. Palearctic birds (race calidus) visit southern Africa from October to March and use more open country, so summer brings the best chance of one passing through.
size: 34-50 cm, wingspan 95-115 cm: a compact, powerful falcon, the female about the size of a pigeon or bigger, the male a third smaller.
keys: Black hood with a broad, thick black “moustache” on a white cheek and throat
Slate-grey upperparts; whitish underparts finely barred black (the African race is darker and more rufous below)
Long, pointed wings with a broad base, short tail, quick shallow wingbeats
Juvenile brown above, buff below with brown streaks rather than bars

confuse.how: Smaller and slimmer, with heavily streaked (not barred) underparts and rufous thighs and vent; a summer visitor that hunts insects at dusk.
Smaller. The male is plain dark grey with a chestnut vent and orange-red legs and cere. The female has a thin moustache and white underwing coverts, and both often travel in flocks.

voice: Mostly silent away from the nest; when agitated it gives a harsh, repeated “kek-kek-kek” or “kré-kré-kré”.
behaviour: Hunts birds in the air, climbing high above the prey and then stooping down at great speed to strike it from behind with its feet. A dive has been reliably measured at 184 km/h, and claims of over 300 km/h have not been confirmed by radar. Doves, swifts and starlings are typical prey.
memo: A black helmet with thick sideburns: the fastest dive in the sky.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds across Europe and Asia, leaves in August-October and spends the austral summer in Africa, reaching southern Africa from October. Uncommon in the Lowveld from October to April, returning north in March-May.
size: 29-36 cm: about the size of a kestrel but slimmer, with a short tail and long scythe-shaped wings, like a giant swift.
keys: Slate-grey upperparts, dark cap and a neat black moustache on white cheeks
White throat, whitish underparts heavily streaked black
Rufous “trousers” (thighs and undertail)
Juvenile browner above, creamier below, thighs buff not rufous

confuse.how: Male uniformly dark grey with orange-red legs, cere and vent and white underwings; female has a barred (not streaked) belly, and it usually hunts in flocks or hovers.
Bigger and bulkier with a broader moustache, finely barred (not streaked) underparts and no rufous thighs.

voice: Mostly silent in Africa; the alarm is a sharp, repeated “kew-kew-kew”.
behaviour: A pure aerial hunter that catches swallows, swifts and big insects such as dragonflies in fast flight, then eats the insects on the wing, passing them from foot to bill. Often hunts where swarms of termite alates and dragonflies emerge after rain, which in turn attract swallows and swifts.
memo: A swift-shaped falcon with a moustache and red trousers, snatching swallows from the summer sky.

migration: Mostly resident in riverine woodland and dense thickets. Some birds move downhill from the escarpment in winter, so it may be slightly commoner in the lowveld in the dry season. Breeds October to December.
size: 13-15 cm: a little smaller than a House Sparrow, slim and upright.
keys: Plain blue-grey upperparts, very pale grey breast and white belly
'Spectacles': black line in front of the eye, white stripe above it joining a narrow white eye-ring
Sits upright in mid-canopy, plain dark tail with no white edges
Juvenile brownish with buff spots above and mottled underparts

confuse.how: Brownish-grey, not blue-grey, with a finely streaked crown and breast and no white spectacles.
Dull pale brown, sits lower in open woodland, and lacks the black-and-white mark in front of the eye.
Smaller, perches more horizontally and constantly fans a tail edged with white.

voice: A thin, high song of 5-7 notes that drops and rises again, often sung from a treetop before dawn; by day short staccato twitters and peeps.
behaviour: Restless: it sallies out from a perch to snap insects in the air or glean them from leaves and bark, mostly in the upper canopy, sometimes with mixed bird parties. Besides insects, it occasionally takes berries and even small geckos.
memo: A grey flycatcher wearing white spectacles.

migration: Resident; no regular movements are described. Localised and uncommon in southern Africa, in woodland and riverine forest. Lays August to January, mostly October to December, in tree holes.
size: About 14 cm: a little bigger than a sparrow but slimmer, the size of a small flycatcher.
keys: Plain grey above, paler whitish-grey below
Short white spectacles around the eye
Black tail with white outer feathers, constantly fanned and swung from side to side
Leans forward horizontally with the tail cocked, like a tit, not upright like a typical flycatcher

confuse.how: All-dark tail with no white edges, upright posture, and it sallies from a perch instead of fanning its tail while gleaning.
Brownish rather than grey, with no white in the tail. Sits upright on low perches and drops to the ground.

voice: A plaintive, two-note whistle, written as “tree-troo” or “teee-reee”.
behaviour: Gleans caterpillars, beetles and termites in the canopy, constantly opening and closing its tail like a fan, which probably flushes insects. This habit gave it its old name, Fan-tailed Flycatcher (Waaierstertvlieëvanger in Afrikaans). It nests in old barbet or woodpecker holes.
memo: The grey flycatcher that fans its white-edged tail like a tit.

migration: Resident and largely sedentary, but it moves when water levels change, so it can appear on a dam after rains and leave when it dries up. Breeds all year, with a peak from August to March in South Africa.
size: 30-38 cm: about the size of a small chicken or a large pigeon, but with long legs and toes.
keys: Blackish-slate bird with a red frontal shield and a red bill with a yellow tip
White line along the flanks
White undertail with a black centre, flashed as it flicks its tail
Long greenish-yellow legs and long toes. Juvenile brown-grey with a pale throat and dull bill, no red shield

confuse.how: Much smaller (about 20 cm), all black with a lime-yellow bill, bright red legs and no white on the flanks or undertail.
Smaller, dumpy and tail-less, with a short dark bill and no red shield; it dives constantly instead of picking food from the surface.

voice: A sudden, gargling “krrruk” and a series of sharp “kik-kik-kik” notes, heard by day and at night.
behaviour: Swims with a jerky, head-bobbing action, tail raised and flicking to show the white undertail. Walks over floating plants on its long toes, and when alarmed it pattering-runs across the water to the reeds. Young from earlier broods often help to feed the next one.
memo: Red shield, yellow tip, white flank line: the bobbing hen of the dam.

migration: Sedentary in pairs or small family groups, moving from tree to tree within its territory. In the rains it may wander a little further from the riverine forest into nearby woodland. Lays from August to February.
size: 42-46 cm: about the size of a pigeon but with a much longer tail.
keys: Glossy violet crest and green head, with red skin around the eye
Crimson flight feathers, hidden at rest and blazing in flight
Green-pink breast and dark blue-violet tail
Keeps to the canopy of riverine trees such as figs and jackalberries

confuse.how: The same turaco family and shape, but all plain grey with a pointed crest and no red in the wings.

voice: A loud series of croaking “kok-kok-kok” notes that rise and speed up, then run into lower, grumbling notes. Neighbouring birds often answer in chorus.
behaviour: Mostly hidden in the canopy, where it runs and bounds along branches like a squirrel to reach fruit at the tips, especially figs. When it flies from one tree to the next, the hidden red wings flash suddenly. It is the national bird of Eswatini, whose royal family wears its crimson feathers.
memo: Green and purple in the treetop, then a flash of red when it flies.

migration: Resident, with pairs holding a territory all year. Calls most before breeding and lays from August to November in tree holes, often old woodpecker or barbet holes. The young stay near the nest for months after fledging.
size: About 20-22 cm: about the size of a thrush, a little bigger and more round-headed than a Pearl-spotted Owlet.
keys: Round head with no ear tufts, finely barred buff-white on brown; yellow eyes
No 'false eyes' on the back of the head
Breast finely barred brown; belly and flanks white with rows of brown spots
Long white line along the folded wing (scapulars)

confuse.how: Smaller, with white spots (not bars) on the head and back, a streaked breast and two black 'false eyes' on the nape; its call is a rising series of whistles ending in falling 'peeoo' notes.
Grey bark-like plumage with ear tufts, and a single frog-like 'prrrp' repeated at night.

voice: A series of 6-8 evenly spaced, slightly falling whistled or purring notes, about one per second, mostly at dusk and dawn; also purring trills when excited.
behaviour: Partly active by day: it often sits in the open to watch for prey, then drops onto beetles, caterpillars, scorpions, lizards and small birds. When small birds find it, they mob it loudly, which is often the best way to locate one. Generally the least heard of the little owls, and more often found in riverine woodland.
memo: The barred owlet: bars where the Pearl-spot has spots, and no eyes on the back of the head.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, in pairs that defend the area around their nest. Breeds in old barbet or woodpecker holes, laying mainly August to November (peak September-October). Calls most before breeding and goes quiet while nesting.
size: 17-20 cm: about the size of a starling, but chunky, round-headed and short-tailed. One of Africa's smallest owls.
keys: Tiny round-headed owl with no ear tufts, often seen by day on an open branch
Cinnamon-brown back, crown and tail sprinkled with small white spots (the “pearls”)
Two black “false eyes” edged with white on the back of the head
White eyebrows, yellow eyes, whitish belly streaked brown; sexes alike

confuse.how: Head and back finely barred, not spotted, with no false eyes on the nape; rarer, in denser riverine woodland.
Grey and bark-patterned with ear tufts, active only at night, and gives a soft purring “prrrp” rather than whistles.
Much bigger (about 25 cm), grey with a white face framed in black, ear tufts and orange eyes.

voice: A series of piercing whistles that rise and speed up, followed by a few long, falling “peeoo” notes; pairs often duet, and it calls by day as well as at night.
behaviour: Hunts by day as well as by night, pouncing from a perch on insects, scorpions, solifuges, lizards and even birds its own size. Small birds mob it noisily, and its fake face on the nape makes it look like it is watching you from behind. When nervous it flicks its tail from side to side.
memo: The owl with eyes in the back of its head: a whistling pocket owl, out in daylight.

migration: Resident: adults stay all year but travel long distances each day looking for carcasses, while young birds wander up to about 1,500 km before settling. It breeds in the dry season, laying about April to July in tree-top stick nests, often in loose groups along rivers.
size: 78-98 cm, wingspan about 2.1 m: a large vulture, smaller than Cape Vulture and much bigger than Hooded Vulture.
keys: Brown to pale buff body with blackish flight feathers and tail; old birds can look almost cream
White lower back and rump, visible when it banks or lands (hence the name)
Blackish bare face and neck with white down and a white ruff, dark brown eye
In flight from below: pale underwing coverts contrasting with the dark flight feathers. Juvenile darker brown and streaked, with no white back

confuse.how: Larger and paler cream, with a pale yellowish eye and blue bare skin at the base of the neck; rare in the Lowveld.
Much smaller and all dark brown, with a thin bill and a bare pink face.
Much bigger, with a huge bill, a bare red wrinkled head and white thighs.

voice: Usually silent; at a carcass it gives hissing, cackling and grunting calls, like squabbling pigs.
behaviour: The commonest vulture at Lowveld carcasses and often one of the first to arrive, after watching other vultures and scavengers drop. It feeds in squabbling crowds on the soft insides, as its bill is too weak to open tough hides. It is Critically Endangered, mainly because of poisoned carcasses.
memo: The everyday Kruger vulture: dark eye, white back, first to the kill.

migration: Endemic to southern Africa and not migratory, but it ranges very widely: adults can travel up to about 750 km from their colony, and immatures wander even more. The nearest colony is Manoutsa, on the escarpment cliffs near Hoedspruit (one of the largest anywhere), where eggs are laid mainly from May to June. The few birds seen in the Kruger area are mostly immatures and non-breeders.
size: 96-115 cm long, wingspan 2.3-2.6 m, 7-11 kg: clearly bigger than the White-backed Vulture it usually feeds with.
