keys: Pale creamy-buff body and wing coverts contrasting with black flight and tail feathers
Adult has a pale yellow (honey) eye, unlike other vultures here
Bare bluish skin on the face and neck, and two bare blue patches at the base of the neck
Juvenile darker and streaked, with a brown eye and a reddish neck

confuse.how: Smaller, with a dark eye and a blackish face. The adult shows a white lower back in flight. The far commoner vulture at Pidwa.
Even bigger and dark brown, with a bare pink-red head and a huge bill. It is the only vulture that dominates the Cape at a carcass.
Smaller, with a white head, a red bill with a blue base and a white belly contrasting with the dark breast.

voice: Silent in flight. At a carcass it hisses, grunts and cackles loudly while squabbling.
behaviour: At a carcass it pushes aside almost every other vulture except the Lappet-faced, and it can swallow about 1.5 kg in five minutes. So full, it needs a breeze or a long run to take off again. It breeds in colonies on cliffs and spots food from great heights.
memo: The big pale one with a honey-coloured eye: a cliff-nester from the escarpment visiting the Lowveld's carcasses.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, in pairs that hold the same territory. It makes no regular migration, only small local moves. Breeds mainly September to December, in a burrow it digs about a metre deep into a riverbank, gully or road cutting.
size: 22-24 cm: about the size of a blackbird but stockier, with a big head and a big red bill.
keys: All-red bill with a dark tip, red legs
Brown head finely streaked darker, with a pale buffy collar
Black back (dark brown in the female) contrasting with the turquoise-blue wings and the bright azure rump, which flashes in flight
Buff-washed breast with a few dark streaks, cinnamon underwing in flight. Juvenile duller, with a brownish bill and scalloped underparts

confuse.how: Plain grey, unstreaked head and a bright chestnut belly; the Brown-hooded is buff below with a streaky brown head.
Two-tone bill (red above, black below) and bright blue back; summer visitor only, absent in winter.
Smaller (18 cm), with a mostly dark two-tone bill and a broad dark eye-stripe; much less blue.

voice: A loud, ringing, descending trill, “ki-ti-ti-ti-ti”, often given with the wings flicked open; the alarm is a sharp “cheerit”.
behaviour: A dry-land kingfisher: it sits motionless for long periods on a low perch, often far from water, then drops onto crickets, beetles, lizards and even small snakes on the ground, beating them on the perch before swallowing them whole.
memo: Red bill, streaky brown hood, blue rump: the kingfisher that hunts lizards, not fish.

migration: Resident and sedentary all year: pairs hold the same territory of a few hectares year-round. Breeds in tree holes in spring, with laying peaking in October and November.
size: 16-18 cm: a small kingfisher, about the size of a sparrow but with a big head and bill.
keys: Two-tone bill: blackish upper mandible, red lower mandible
Dull grey-brown above with a streaked crown, a black stripe through the eye and a whitish collar
Bright blue on the rump, wings and tail, which mostly shows in flight or when it opens its wings
Whitish underparts with fine dark streaks on the breast and flanks; male has a black bar on the wing, juvenile has a duller bill

confuse.how: Bigger (22 cm), with an all-red bill and a tawny breast; its back is blackish, not grey-brown.
Bigger, with a bright turquoise back and a red-and-black bill, and it is only here in summer.

voice: A loud, high, far-carrying “cheer-cherrrrrr”: a sharp note followed by a descending trill, often given at dusk and usually the first sign that the bird is around.
behaviour: A dry-bush kingfisher that does not need water: it hunts grasshoppers and other insects from a perch about 3 m up, drops to the ground and returns to beat its prey. Pairs sit facing each other in a treetop, tails cocked, and call while flicking their wings open and shut to flash the blue and white underwing, especially at dusk.
memo: A small grey kingfisher with a striped crown that winks its blue wings at dusk.

migration: Intra-African migrant: it winters in central and eastern Africa, north of Zambia, and comes to the far north-east of South Africa to breed. It migrates at night, arrives from September and lays mainly October-November. Most leave in March-April, though some reports say breeders leave as early as January.
size: 20-22 cm: about the size of a blackbird but stockier, with a big head and a long, dagger-shaped bill.
keys: All-red bill (bright orange-red), straight and dagger-shaped
Pale grey head and breast, black back
Chestnut belly, the best mark when the bird faces you
Bright cobalt-blue wings, rump and tail. Juvenile duller, with little chestnut below and a darker bill

confuse.how: Streaky brown head, buff flanks instead of a chestnut belly, and a red bill with a dark tip. Much commoner and present all year.
Two-tone bill (red above, black below), turquoise back and a whitish belly with no chestnut.
Smaller (18 cm), mostly grey-brown with a streaked crown and a dark two-tone bill; very little blue.

voice: A weak, high, sibilant trill, “ji-ji-ji-ji-chi”, and a sharp “tchk-tchk-tchk” in alarm. Much less striking than the Woodland Kingfisher's song.
behaviour: A dry-land kingfisher: it sits still on a low branch for long periods, bobs its head, then drops onto grasshoppers, other insects or small lizards on the ground. It digs its nest tunnel in a riverbank or erosion gully, and in display the pair spread and quiver their wings to flash the blue. It dive-bombs monitor lizards that come near the nest.
memo: Grey hood, red dagger, chestnut belly: the summer kingfisher of the dry riverbeds.

migration: Intra-African migrant that breeds here in summer. Birds fitted with trackers in Limpopo wintered in South Sudan, some 4,000 km away. They travel only at night, leave between late March and mid-April and return between mid-November and early December. In the Lowveld its song announces summer: guides bet on the date it returns, around early November.
size: 23 cm: about the size of a blackbird but stockier, with a big head and a big bill.
keys: Two-tone bill: red upper mandible, black lower mandible
Bright turquoise-blue back, wings and tail; greyish-white head and underparts
Short black line behind the eye and black shoulders (coverts)
Sexes alike; juvenile duller, with a brownish bill

confuse.how: All-red bill, streaky brown head and blackish-brown back: only the rump and wings are blue.
All-red bill, grey head and chestnut belly; Woodland Kingfisher has a white belly.
Smaller (18 cm), with a mostly dark two-tone bill, a streaked crown and mostly brown and grey plumage, little blue.

voice: The song starts with a sharp note followed by a long trill that descends and fades: “tjip-trrrrrrrrr” (or “kri-trrrrr”). Often compared to running a fingernail along the teeth of a comb. THE sound of summer in the Lowveld.
behaviour: Hunts from a perch on an open branch, often far from water, dropping onto insects and small lizards on the ground. When singing it spreads its wings wide, flashing the white underwing and the blue above. Very territorial, it may attack intruders, people included.
memo: A sharp “tjip” then a long falling trill: summer has just arrived in Kruger.

migration: Resident: pairs stay together year-round on a stretch of river or a dam, with only some dispersal after breeding. Young birds wander widely until they settle. Breeds in the dry season, laying mainly in May and June (April to August), when the water is low.
size: 63-75 cm, wingspan about 2-2.4 m, the female being larger: a big eagle, much bigger than a Yellow-billed Kite.
keys: Snow-white head, breast and short tail
Chestnut belly and shoulders, black wings
Bare yellow face and a yellow, black-tipped bill
Juvenile brown and streaky with a pale face and a broad whitish chest band; full adult plumage takes about 5 years

confuse.how: Can be confused with a brown juvenile Fish Eagle, but is uniform tawny-brown with feathered legs, no whitish chest band, and is not tied to water.
Also a brown raptor perched near rivers, but with a big round owl-like head, large yellow eyes, bare whitish legs and plain dark-brown plumage.

voice: A loud, ringing “weee-ah, hyo-hyo-hyo” thrown back with the head flung right back, often by a pair in duet; known as “the voice of Africa”.
behaviour: Hunts from a riverside perch, swooping down to snatch a fish from the surface with only its feet entering the water; a fish too heavy to lift is towed to shore, the eagle rowing with its wings. It also steals catches from herons and other birds.
memo: White head, chestnut belly, and the cry that says “Africa”.

migration: Resident in South Africa from the Eastern Cape coast to the Lowveld and escarpment of Mpumalanga and Limpopo, mostly in riverine and forest-edge vegetation. Breeds mainly in spring and summer: eggs can be laid almost all year, peaking September to January.
size: About 10 cm: one of the smallest birds in the bush, smaller than a waxbill-sized sunbird such as Marico, with a short tail.
keys: Very short, only slightly curved bill (Afrikaans name "short-billed sunbird")
Male: glossy metallic green head, throat and back, a narrow purple-blue band across the breast, bright yellow belly
Female: glossy green above and entirely yellow below, with no green throat or breast band
Usually in dense riverine trees and thickets, often in pairs or in mixed bird parties

confuse.how: Longer, curved bill; the male has a white belly and the female is greyish-white below, not yellow.
Bigger, with a longer curved bill and a broad red breast band below the green throat; the belly is grey, not yellow.
Bigger, with a long, strongly curved bill; the male has a blackish belly below a blue and maroon breast band, and the female is pale and streaked below.

voice: Soft, high calls and a short twittering song.
behaviour: Feeds more on insects and spiders than nectar, gleaning them from leaves and often perching rather than hovering at flowers. In winter it visits flowering aloes, for example at Skukuza. The female alone builds an untidy hanging nest with a side entrance, often next to a wasp nest.
memo: Tiny, short-billed and yellow-bellied: the green-and-gold jewel of the riverine thickets.

migration: Intra-African migrant that breeds here: it arrives in August-September and leaves in March-April, spending the austral winter north of the equator (Sudan, Chad, Nigeria). A tracked female flew more than 8,800 km in nine months between Namibia and Chad.
size: 53-61 cm, wingspan about 1.3-1.45 m: a small eagle, roughly the size of a Yellow-billed Kite but stockier.
keys: Plumage very variable: usually dark brown, but pale (creamy below) and intermediate morphs exist, unrelated to sex
Small pointed crest on the nape, dark brown eye, yellow cere and feet, legs fully feathered
In flight: straight-edged, parallel wings and a long, narrow, square-cut tail held closed, giving a cross-shaped silhouette
Flight feathers and tail grey below with fine barring

confuse.how: Bigger and heavier, with a bigger bill, gape reaching behind the eye, no crest, and a shorter rounded tail in flight.
Yellow bill and a forked, constantly twisting tail instead of the eagle's straight square tail.
Bigger, with a large owl-like round head, staring yellow eyes and bare whitish legs.

voice: Fairly vocal around the nest: a long, thin whistled “kleee-ah”, repeated, often given in flight.
behaviour: Hunts from a perch or while soaring, dropping steeply on lizards, birds, squirrels and other small prey, and may follow bush fires. Each pair builds a small stick nest lined with green leaves in a tall tree, often a Jackal-berry or Knob-thorn along a dry riverbed, and raises a single chick.
memo: The little brown eagle with a square tail that comes back with the spring heat.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds across Europe and Asia and spends the austral summer in southern Africa, after a journey of about 10,000 km. The first arrive in September, most in October to December, and they leave in late March and April, gathering in large flocks before departure.
size: 17-19 cm including the tail streamers: smaller than a sparrow in body, but long-tailed.
keys: Glossy steel-blue upperparts and a dark blue breast band
Brick-red forehead and throat, off-white to buffy underparts
Deeply forked tail with long, thin outer streamers (shorter in the female)
Juvenile and moulting birds, common here in summer: duller, with a pale rusty throat and no streamers

confuse.how: Orange-rufous head and rump, and white underparts heavily streaked black, with no blue breast band.
Plain brown above, with a brown throat, no blue gloss and only a shallow notch in the tail.
Sooty black with a white throat and a broad white rump, square tail and stiff, flickering wingbeats; never perches on wires.

voice: Fairly quiet on its wintering grounds: a short “vit” or “witt” in flight, and a sharper “tsi-vitt” in alarm.
behaviour: Hawks insects low over grass and water, following game, people and vehicles to catch what they flush, and drinks by skimming the surface. At dusk huge numbers gather in communal roosts in reedbeds; one near Durban holds around three million birds.
memo: The swallow of Europe: blue band, red throat, streamers trailing behind.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, but uncommon and thinly spread. Males call from traditional song posts mainly September to March, when females come to them to mate; otherwise it is quiet and easily overlooked.
size: About 20 cm: a little smaller than a blackbird, close to a Dark-capped Bulbul.
keys: Male: pink bill, black throat and white cheek patch, grey-brown above, whitish below, often a small yellow shoulder patch
Broad white outer tail feathers, flashed in flight
Female: plain grey-brown with a dark bill, no black throat
Juvenile: olive-brown above with a striking yellow throat and breast

confuse.how: The plain female can suggest a bulbul, but the bulbul has a blackish head with a small crest, a yellow vent and no white in the tail.

voice: The male's song is a loud, far-carrying “vic-tor” or “whit-purr”, repeated from a high perch; when guiding it gives an excited rattling chatter, and displaying males make a drumming sound with their tail.
behaviour: Famous for leading people to wild bee nests with its chattering call, then eating the wax left behind; it can digest beeswax. It is also a brood parasite: the female lays in holes of barbets, woodpeckers, bee-eaters or starlings, and the chick kills the host's young with the hooks on its bill.
memo: “Vic-tor!”: the bird that guides you to the honey and eats the wax.

migration: Intra-African migrant that breeds here in summer. It arrives in September-October and leaves in March-April for tropical Africa further north (up to around the equator). It is thought to migrate mainly at night.
size: 12 cm: Africa's smallest kingfisher, smaller than a House Sparrow.
keys: Tiny, with a red-orange bill and red legs
Deep blue crown and back, with orange eyebrow and lilac-violet wash on the cheeks
Rufous-orange underparts with a white throat; white patch on the side of the neck
Juvenile has a black bill

confuse.how: Slightly bigger, always by water, with a barred turquoise crest reaching down to the eye and orange cheeks; no orange eyebrow or violet cheek.

voice: A thin, high, insect-like “tsip-tsip”, mostly given in flight.
behaviour: Despite its name it hardly ever eats fish: it hunts insects, spiders and small lizards in woodland, often far from water, dropping from a low perch to the ground and back. It bashes its prey on the perch before swallowing it. It nests in a tunnel dug into an earth bank or a termite mound.
memo: A flying jewel no bigger than a thumb, hunting grasshoppers, not fish.

migration: Intra-African migrant and uncommon summer visitor: in South Africa it occurs mainly in the November-April wet season, arriving from October to December and leaving in March-April for equatorial Africa. Breeds in the rains (eggs November to April, peak January-February), when pans and flooded areas fill.
size: 25-30 cm: a tiny heron, a little bigger than a Laughing Dove, and much smaller than a Striated Heron.
keys: Uniform dark slate-grey crown, back and wings, with no pale wing patch
Buff throat and underparts boldly streaked with black stripes
Yellow or greenish-yellow legs (orange in courtship), dark bill with a yellow lower mandible
Female paler with a more rufous belly; juvenile buffier with rusty underparts

confuse.how: Larger, with a black cap, grey unstreaked underparts and pale-edged wing feathers; Dwarf Bittern has uniform dark upperparts and heavily streaked underparts.
Buff-brown above and shows bright white wings in flight; Dwarf Bittern is dark slate above and stays dark in flight.

voice: Usually silent and poorly known; gives a loud croak when flushed.
behaviour: Mostly active at dusk and at night, standing motionless or creeping slowly through flooded grass and reeds to catch frogs, fish, crabs and insects. When disturbed it flies slowly a short distance into a bush or tree, or freezes in a stretched bittern posture to blend in.
memo: A small dark ghost of the summer floods: slate back, striped chest, yellow legs.

migration: Resident and sedentary, but some birds move about locally after breeding, and family groups have been recorded wandering in the dry season in north-eastern South Africa. Most records there are from April to August. Breeds September to November.
size: 35-37 cm: a small, stocky raptor, about the size of a pigeon but with a bigger head.
keys: Single black vertical stripe down the middle of the white throat: unique among raptors
Plain grey head, back and breast, white belly finely barred grey
Black tail with one broad white band (rarely two) and a white tip; white rump in flight
Red cere and short red legs, dark red-brown eye. Juvenile browner, with orange-yellow cere and legs

confuse.how: Slimmer, with long legs and a longer tail with several dark bars, and no black stripe on the throat.
Much bigger and longer-legged, with a grey throat with no stripe and a tail barred, not with a single white band.
Smaller and slimmer, with a yellowish to red eye, rufous-barred underparts and no throat stripe.

voice: Usually silent; at the start of the breeding season (September-October) it gives a clear, melodious whistle 'kleeeo-klu-klu-klu' from a perch, and a buzzard-like 'peee-oo'.
behaviour: Sits still for long periods on a branch 6-10 m up, then drops or glides into the grass onto lizards, grasshoppers, rodents and even snakes. Flies between perches low down with an undulating, thrush-like flight, rarely rising above the trees.
memo: A grey hawk with a black 'tie' down a white shirt: watch the grass, then drop on a lizard.

migration: Resident all year: pairs keep the same large territory and roosts for years. Breeds in the dry season (eggs mainly May to September), and the young may stay with the parents for up to two years.
size: 60-66 cm: the largest owl in Africa, much bigger than a Spotted Eagle-Owl; the female can weigh over 3 kg.
keys: Bright pink eyelids around dark brown eyes, which are easiest to see in good light
Pale, milky grey-brown plumage, finely barred below, with a whitish face boldly rimmed black
Short, often flattened ear tufts and a pale creamy bill
Juvenile browner, with smaller ear tufts and a less distinct facial disc

confuse.how: Much smaller (about 45 cm), with yellow eyes, no pink eyelids and prominent ear tufts.
Much smaller (about 25 cm), with bright orange eyes and a white face edged black.

voice: Deep, irregular grunts “gwonk, gwok-gwok”, among the lowest of any bird and carrying up to 5 km, with the white throat puffed out; the female and young give long, piercing begging whistles.
behaviour: An opportunistic apex predator that takes anything from beetles to young warthogs, monkeys and other raptors. It is known for leaving the skins of hedgehogs it has eaten under its perch. It doesn't build a nest but takes over old nests of Hamerkops, vultures or eagles, and roosts by day in big shady trees, often near rivers.
memo: Pink eyeshadow on dark eyes: Africa's giant owl, grunting like a pig in the night.

migration: Resident and sedentary in the Lowveld, living in pairs or family groups that move only short distances. It can breed in any month, with a peak in summer from December to April after the rains.
size: 10-11 cm: a little smaller than a House Sparrow, the size of a waxbill.
keys: Male pinkish red all over, head included (no grey cap), paler and more rosy than other firefinches
Black vent and undertail, black tail with a red rump
Dark blue-grey bill, not red
Female duller and browner, pinkish below with red lores and rump

confuse.how: Has a red bill and a yellow eye-ring, and the male has a brown back and a pale brown, not black, vent.
The male has a slate-grey crown and nape and is a deeper crimson below, with the black of the vent reaching onto the belly.

voice: A fast, dry trill or rattle, especially in alarm, and a few soft tinkling notes when feeding.
behaviour: Feeds on the ground on fallen grass seeds in thick grass along bushy watercourses, and darts quickly into a tangle when disturbed. It is the only host of the Purple Indigobird, which lays its eggs in its nests.
memo: A rosy firefinch with a grey bill and a black bottom.

migration: Resident and sedentary in the Lowveld, living in pairs or small family groups all year. It keeps to dense, moist cover such as rank grass and tangles along rivers and drainage lines. Breeds late in the rains, from November to June, peaking January to April.
size: 10-11 cm: smaller than a House Sparrow, a tiny long-tailed seedeater.
keys: Male deep crimson below with tiny white spots on the sides of the breast
Grey crown and nape, olive-brown back, red rump
Dark slate-grey (bluish) bill and a black vent and undertail
Female paler and duller red; juvenile brown without red underparts, apart from the rump

confuse.how: Red bill and yellow eye-ring, brown head, and a buff-brown (not black) undertail; usually in more open, drier places such as camps and gardens.
Very similar with a dark bill and black vent, but paler and pinker overall, with a pink-washed head and back instead of a grey crown and brown back.

voice: A rising, ringing trill and a loud “tui-tui-tui-tui”; the alarm is a harsh ticking from inside the cover.
behaviour: Feeds on the ground on grass seeds, close to cover, and darts back into a thicket at the slightest alarm. Its nests are parasitised by the Dusky Indigobird, whose chicks mimic the firefinch's own young.
memo: A crimson spark with a dark bill and black vent, always just about to vanish into the thicket.

migration: Resident all year, in pairs or small groups; in winter it often joins mixed flocks of seedeaters. Breeds almost all year round, mainly December to June.
size: 9-10 cm: much smaller than a sparrow, about the size of a waxbill.
keys: Male: pinkish-red head, breast and rump, with brown wings and back
Pink-red bill and a thin pale yellow eye-ring; tiny white dots on the sides of the breast
Female: brown with a red spot in front of the eye and a red rump
Juvenile: like the female but without red on the face, and with a dark bill

confuse.how: Bluish-grey bill, no yellow eye-ring and a black vent; the male is a deeper rosy pink, including the back.
Dark slate-grey bill, grey crown and nape, and a black belly and vent; keeps to denser cover.

voice: A soft, fluty, rising "pweet" or "queet" contact call, and a hard "chik" in alarm.
behaviour: Tame and confiding, it hops on bare ground near cover and around camps and lodges, picking up fallen grass seeds. It is the host of the Village Indigobird, whose chicks copy the firefinch chicks' mouth markings and whose males copy the firefinch's song.
memo: A tiny red spark with a red bill and a yellow eye-ring.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld. Outside the breeding season it gathers in noisy flocks, often mixed with other starlings, and shares big communal roosts. Breeds August to January, peaking October-November, in tree holes left by woodpeckers and barbets.
size: 21-24 cm: about the size of a Common Starling, stocky with a short tail.
keys: Glossy blue-green all over, with a dark blue patch on the ear coverts like a mask
Bright yellow to orange eye
A row of black spots across the greener wing coverts
Belly and flanks deep blue to violet; juvenile duller, with sooty-brown underparts and a dark eye

confuse.how: Ear patch the same green as the head, so no dark mask, and a greener belly and flanks without the deep blue-violet sheen.
The male is violet above with a clean white belly; the female is brown above and streaked below.

voice: A nasal, drawn-out “squee-ar” or “skweer”, mixed with harsh chatter and more musical warbles; flocks sing in chorus from treetops.
behaviour: Bold and opportunistic: in Kruger rest camps and picnic sites it hops around tables scavenging scraps. It feeds mostly on the ground, hopping rather than walking, and sometimes rides on game or cattle to catch the insects they flush.
memo: The glossy starling with the dark blue “earmuffs” and the golden eye.

migration: Resident all year, with no regular migration. It breeds from September to February in tree holes. Outside the breeding season it forms bigger flocks that wander locally.
size: About 25 cm: the size of a blackbird, but stockier and shorter-tailed.
keys: Fairly uniform glossy blue-green plumage, with no dark ear patch
Bright yellow-orange eye
Green sheen on the belly and flanks, the same as the back
Juvenile duller and matt, with a grey eye that turns yellow at about two months

confuse.how: Has a contrasting dark-blue ear patch and a blue-violet sheen on the belly and flanks. The Cape Starling looks evenly green-blue all over, with no ear patch.
The male is violet above and pure white below. The female is brown and heavily streaked, never glossy green.

voice: A long, rambling warbling song, which can include imitations of other sounds around it.
behaviour: Feeds mostly on the ground, running and hopping after insects, often next to other starlings, and it also accompanies antelope to pick off their ticks and catch the insects they flush. It breeds cooperatively: a pair can have up to six helpers, and the nest hole is sometimes lined with snake skin.
memo: Glossy green all over, a yellow eye, and no blue ear patch: that's the Cape.

migration: Resident and sedentary all year in the Lowveld. Pairs seem to keep the same territory for life, usually in dense thickets along drainage lines. Breeds mainly September to December.
size: 20-23 cm: about the size of a blackbird, with a strong hooked bill.
keys: Glossy black upperparts with a long white stripe along the wing
White underparts shading to rufous-orange on the flanks, belly and under the tail
Strong black hooked bill, black eye (brown in the female)
Female greyer above with more rufous below; juvenile mottled buff above and barred below

confuse.how: Smaller (about 17 cm), with a red eye, clean white underparts with no rufous, and a grey-white rump the male puffs out. Feeds high in the canopy, not on the ground.
Very long black tail, all-black underparts and white wing patches. Sits in the open on top of bushes, in noisy groups.

voice: Loud, carrying duets: the pair answers back and forth in liquid whistles and harsher notes, such as an “ooo-whee-ooo” that can be mistaken for Black-headed Oriole. The alarm is a muted cluck. Much more often heard than seen.
behaviour: A skulker: it hops about on the ground under cover, flicking leaves aside, and takes insects, snails, lizards, mice and even the eggs and chicks of other birds. It rubs the sting off bees and cracks snail shells on a branch before eating them.
memo: Black on top, white below, orange under the tail: heard duetting from the thicket long before it shows.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds in Europe and western Asia, leaves there in August and September, and travels down through East Africa. Most arrive in the Lowveld in November, a few in late October, and they leave mainly in the first half of April.
size: 16-18 cm: a bit bigger than a sparrow, with a longer tail.
keys: Male: blue-grey crown and nape, black mask through the eye, chestnut back
Male: pinkish-white underparts and a black tail with white sides at the base
Female: brown above with a dusky brown mask, whitish below with fine dark crescent bars
Sits upright on top of a bush, often fanning or wagging its tail

confuse.how: Larger, with a grey (not chestnut) back, a black forehead joining the mask and a big white wing patch.

voice: Mostly silent in Africa; gives harsh "chack" or "tek" alarm notes, and sometimes a quiet scratchy song with imitations of other birds.
behaviour: Hunts from an exposed bush top, dropping onto insects on the ground. Like other shrikes it sometimes impales surplus prey on thorns as a "larder". In Africa males tend to use more open bush and females denser thornveld.
memo: Grey cap, black mask, chestnut back: the little "butcher" from Europe on every summer thornbush.

migration: Resident and sedentary, living all year in groups that hold a territory; some local movement in the dry season. Breeds in the rainy season, laying mainly October to January, often raising two broods.
size: 40-50 cm including a very long tail (body about the size of a starling).
keys: All black with a very long, graduated black tail
White patches on the shoulders (scapulars) and white tips to the wing feathers; greyish-white V-shaped rump
Female has a white patch on the flanks and a slightly shorter tail
Juvenile duller and browner, with buffy scaling

confuse.how: The breeding male also has a long black tail, but is tiny, with a red bill and white underparts.
Black and white too, but with a short tail, white or buffy underparts and a skulking habit.
All black with no white at all, and a forked, not long graduated, tail.

voice: Loud, melancholy whistles 'kee-oo, kee-oo' or 'tee-loo', often from several birds together; pairs duet, and the alarm is a harsh 'tchzzrrr'.
behaviour: Lives in noisy groups of up to a dozen that perch high on Acacia tops and drop to the ground for insects, lizards and small rodents. A cooperative breeder: young from the previous brood help feed the chicks. Groups display with bowing, tail-spreading and wing-raising.
memo: A black-and-white shrike with a tail as long as its body, whistling in a gang.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds in southern and eastern Europe and western Asia, leaves in late August and is one of the latest migrants to arrive, reaching southern Africa from late November to December. Most of the world population winters in the dry savannas of southern Africa; it leaves again in March-April.
size: 19-23 cm: about the size of a starling, a little bigger than Red-backed Shrike.
keys: Pale grey crown and back with a broad black mask that crosses the forehead above the bill
Black wings with a white patch at the base of the primaries, black tail with white sides
White underparts washed pink on the breast and belly
Female a little duller, with less black on the forehead; first-winter birds lack the black forehead and look browner

confuse.how: The male has a chestnut back and only a thin mask that does not cross the forehead; females and young are brown and finely barred.
Much bigger and browner, with a white crown and white throat, living in noisy groups.

voice: Mostly quiet in Africa; gives harsh 'tchek' calls, and its song is a soft warbling chatter full of imitations.
behaviour: Sits upright and conspicuous on a bush top or wire in open thornveld, drops to the ground to catch beetles and grasshoppers, then flies back to a perch. Unlike most shrikes, it rarely impales its prey on thorns.
memo: A grey shrike with a black bandit mask across the forehead and a blush-pink belly.

migration: Resident and nomadic in the Lowveld, moving in response to local rain, carcasses and drying pools where fish get trapped. Can turn up in any month but numbers vary a lot. Breeds in colonies in the dry season, laying mainly June to September.
size: 115-152 cm tall, wingspan up to about 2.9 m: bigger than a Grey Heron, one of the largest flying birds.
keys: Bare, scabby pink-and-black head and neck with a dangling pink throat pouch
Huge, thick, pale wedge-shaped bill
Dark slate-grey back and wings, white underparts and white neck ruff
Long legs that look whitish; in flight the neck is pulled in like a heron's. Juvenile browner with a smaller bill

confuse.how: Soaring together over a carcass; the Marabou shows long legs trailing beyond the tail and a massive bill tucked in on its pulled-in neck.
Glossy black and white with a red-and-black bill with a yellow saddle and a long outstretched neck; no bare head or pouch.
Smaller and mostly white with a red face, a yellow down-curved bill and black flight feathers.

voice: Almost silent; the main sound is loud bill-clattering, especially in courtship, plus grunts made with the throat pouch.
behaviour: The "undertaker of the bush": it soars on thermals to find carcasses, then waits behind the vultures, hyenas and jackals and snatches the scraps at the end. It is also an opportunist hunter, stabbing fish in drying pools, catching flying termites and raiding the chicks of quelea and other colonial birds.
memo: Bald head, pink pouch, giant bill: the undertaker waiting at the back of the queue.

migration: Resident in the Lowveld, where it occurs singly in tall grassland and open savanna, sometimes moving locally after rain. Breeds October to February. Males are most conspicuous then, displaying and calling from termite mounds.
size: 58-65 cm: taller than a Helmeted Guineafowl, with a long, thin neck and long legs. The male is much heavier than the female.
keys: Long thin neck and long legs, standing tall above the grass
Male: black underparts with a thin black line running down the front of the neck
Upperparts tawny-buff with black chevrons. The male's wings show large white patches in flight
Female plainer buff with a white belly and fine wavy barring on the neck

confuse.how: Smaller and shorter-necked, with no black line down the front of the neck and bold cream V marks on the back. The male tumbles out of the sky in display.

voice: The male's display call is a rising, wheezy whistle followed after a pause by a short 'quock' or 'plop', likened to a cork popping or a burp.
behaviour: The displaying male stands on a termite mound, stretches up his neck, then snaps his head back onto his back and pops. He also flies slowly with exaggerated wingbeats and glides down with his wings raised to show off the black belly. The female alone incubates the 1-2 eggs and raises the chicks.
memo: Long legs and a black belly: the bustard that pops a cork on a termite mound.

migration: Palearctic migrant that breeds in eastern and central Europe and winters in inland southern Africa, from the Zambezi to north-eastern South Africa. It leaves Europe in July-August, travels via north-east Africa and Kenya, and only reaches southern Africa in December-February. It leaves in late March or early April. Rare and very localised, and often returns to the same spot each year.
size: 14-16 cm: bigger than a Willow Warbler, about the size of a sparrow, with a broad, rounded tail.
keys: Plain, unstreaked olive-brown upperparts and a faint pale eyebrow
Throat and breast diffusely streaked or spotted brown on a whitish background
Long brown undertail coverts with broad pale tips, giving a scaly pattern
Creeps low in thick cover with its body held horizontal; juvenile more yellowish or rusty

confuse.how: Smaller and slimmer, yellowish-green with a clear eyebrow and no breast streaks. It flits actively through the canopy instead of creeping on the ground.

voice: A hard “tchik” or “zrr” call. The song is a long, mechanical, insect-like reeling that sounds like a sewing machine, mostly given at dusk and at night.
behaviour: A real skulker: it creeps like a mouse through tangles of dense bush such as num-nums and grewias, feeding mostly on the ground. It is almost impossible to see unless it comes up to sing.
memo: A brown ghost from Europe in the thickets: listen for the sewing machine.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, in pairs that keep the same territory. Outside the breeding season it may gather in small groups of up to about 20 birds that move about locally. Egg-laying starts after the first good summer rains and peaks in October and November.
size: 45-51 cm including the long bill and tail: about the size of a magpie, slightly smaller than the Yellow-billed Hornbill.
keys: Dull grey-brown hornbill: dark grey head and neck with a broad whitish stripe above the eye
Dark brown back, each feather edged white, and a whitish belly
Male: dark bill with a creamy-yellow base and ridge on the upper mandible; female: yellow upper mandible with a red tip
Juvenile: bill smaller and mostly dark, without a casque

confuse.how: Big bright yellow bill and crisp black-and-white plumage, with no grey-brown.
Slim, all-red bill, white face and neck, and wings boldly spotted white; no grey-brown.

voice: A plaintive, piping whistle, a long series of “pee-o pee-o pee-o” notes that speeds up then falls away, quite unlike the clucking of the other small hornbills. In flight, a single far-carrying “pleu”.
behaviour: When it calls it points its bill up and flicks its half-open wings in time with the notes. Unlike the Yellow-billed Hornbill it feeds mostly up in the trees, flying from bush to bush and snatching grasshoppers and other insects. At the nest the female seals herself into a tree hole with her own droppings, leaving only a slit for the male to feed her.
memo: The grey hornbill that whistles instead of clucking: “pee-o pee-o” from the treetops.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, living alone or in pairs in bushveld. It makes only small local moves following rain and food. Breeds October to April, mainly October-November in the old Transvaal; the nest is a bare scrape on the ground under a bush or grass tuft.
size: About 50 cm and 650-700 g: the size of a hen, with longish yellow legs.
keys: Mottled upperparts covered in cream V-shaped (arrowhead) marks
Black belly; white patches on the sides of the breast
Male: blue-grey head and neck; the red nape crest is hidden and shows only in display
Female and young: browner head and neck, with a broad white band across the lower breast

confuse.how: Taller and long-necked, with a thin black line down the front of the male's neck and plain sandy back without cream chevrons; prefers tall open grassland.
Also walks in the grass, but is round, slate-grey spotted white, with a bare blue head and a bony casque, and lives in flocks.

voice: The territorial song is a series of dry clicks, “tik-tik-tik”, that speeds up and turns into loud, piercing whistles; pairs also duet. Heard far more often than the bird is seen.
behaviour: The “suicide bird”: the male rockets almost vertically to about 20 m, then tips backwards and plummets like a shot bird, opening his wings only at the last moment before the ground. He then raises his red crest and puffs out his throat for the female.
memo: Clicks, whistles, then a kamikaze nosedive: the bushveld's “suicide bird”.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld and fully sedentary: pairs or small family groups hold the same territory and roost together in tree holes. Breeds mainly September to February, when the duets are loudest.
size: 17-20 cm: a little smaller than a blackbird, but much stockier, with a big head and a heavy bill.
keys: Bright red face, forehead and throat, framed by a broad black collar across the breast
Pale yellowish belly; back and wings brownish with yellow edging
Heavy, dark, slightly notched bill on a big head
Sexes alike; juvenile duller and browner, with little or no red on the face. A rare yellow-faced form also exists

confuse.how: Larger, with a shaggy crest, a yellow face speckled with red and black, and a black breast band spotted white; no solid red face.
Smaller and black-and-white streaked, with only a small red forehead patch and a black throat, not a red face.

voice: A loud, ringing duet usually written “too-puddly, too-puddly, too-puddly”: one bird sings “too” and its mate instantly answers “puddly”, so perfectly timed that it sounds like a single bird.
behaviour: The pair duets face to face, bowing and flicking their wings. Groups dig their nest hole on the underside of a dead branch, often in a fig, and may reuse it for years; extra group members help feed the chicks.
memo: Red face, black collar, and two birds singing as one: “too-puddly”.

migration: Resident and sedentary, in pairs on territories in grassland and at vlei edges. Breeds September to March, mostly November to January, nesting on the ground in tall grass.
size: 20-22 cm: about the size of a thrush, a stocky pipit-like bird.
keys: Bright yellow throat and underparts with a black necklace across the chest
Bold yellow eyebrow on a streaky olive-brown back
Very long hind claw, often seen on birds walking on tracks
Female and immature duller, buffier below, with a narrower brownish necklace

confuse.how: Similar shape and walk, but brown and buff all over with a streaked breast and no yellow or black necklace.

voice: A loud whistled phrase of 4-5 notes, repeated many times from a treetop, bush or fence or in flight; also shrill whistles and buzzy calls when flushed.
behaviour: Walks through the grass with long strides, flushing insects. Flies slowly and jerkily with stiff wingbeats and the tail spread, showing white tail corners, then lands on a bush top to sing. Its colours and habits mirror the American meadowlarks, though the two are unrelated.
memo: A yellow throat with a black necklace singing from a bush over the grassland.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, where pairs hold large territories in thick woodland and riverine bush. Apart from limited wandering after breeding, it doesn't move. Breeds mainly September to November (eggs from August to January), and the young may stay in the parents' territory for up to a year.
size: 23-26 cm: a little bigger than a blackbird and much stockier. It is the largest bushshrike in South Africa.
keys: Huge, heavy, hooked black bill on a big grey head, with a white spot in front of the eye
Staring pale yellow eye
Olive-green back and wings, bright yellow underparts washed orange on the breast
Juvenile: paler, with a brownish bill, brown eye and a mottled crown

confuse.how: Much smaller (about 18 cm), with a slender bill, a dark eye, a yellow forehead and eyebrow and a black mask.
Smaller, with a bright red throat edged by a black collar and a dark eye. It skulks low in thickets.

voice: A long, drawn-out, mournful hoot “hoooooop” on one note, often repeated for long periods from a high perch, which gives it the Afrikaans name “Spookvoël” (ghost bird). It also gives clicks and bill snaps.
behaviour: A shy predator that is heard far more often than seen. It hops through the canopy gleaning big insects, but also kills lizards, chameleons, snakes, small birds and mice, and may impale prey on thorns. A ranger at nearby Timbavati once saw one kill a fruit bat.
memo: The ghost bird: an eerie hoot from the thicket, and a yellow-eyed shrike with a hatchet for a bill.

migration: Resident all year along permanent rivers and larger dams in the Lowveld, usually in pairs that hold a long stretch of bank. It only makes local moves along the river, for example to pools left in a drying riverbed. Breeds September to January in South Africa, digging a tunnel about 2 m long in a riverbank.
size: 42-46 cm: Africa's largest kingfisher, about the size of a pigeon but with a huge dagger bill. Roughly five times the weight of a Pied Kingfisher.
keys: Massive black dagger bill and a big shaggy crest
Slate-black upperparts finely spotted white
Male: rufous-chestnut breast, white belly barred dark
Female reversed: breast black spotted white, belly and flanks rufous-chestnut

confuse.how: Much smaller (about 25 cm), pure black and white with no chestnut at all, and often hovers over the water before diving.

voice: A loud, harsh, far-carrying “wak-wak-wak” or “kek-kek”, often given in flight as it flies low along the river when disturbed.
behaviour: Hunts from a perch 2-4 m above the water, usually a shaded branch rather than an exposed one, plunging in and often vanishing completely underwater. It beats crabs against the perch to break off their claws and swallows fish head first.
memo: A kingfisher the size of a pigeon: if the chest is chestnut it's a he, if the belly is chestnut it's a she.

migration: Resident all year in Lowveld woodland, with no known migration. Breeds May to January, peaking September-October, nesting in tree hollows or behind loose bark.
size: 19-22 cm: about the size of a bulbul, a little smaller and slimmer than a Fork-tailed Drongo.
keys: All black with a faint blue gloss, slim and upright on a low perch
Square or barely notched tail, never deeply forked
Dark brown eye and a small, thin black bill with no hook
Juvenile dark brown spotted with buff

confuse.how: Bigger, with a red eye, a heavier hooked bill and a long, deeply forked tail.
Male has a rounded tail, an orange-yellow gape and often a yellow shoulder, and creeps through the canopy instead of sallying from a perch.
Smaller and dumpier, with white edges in the wing, and gleans busily along branches in groups.

voice: Fairly quiet: thin, high sibilant notes and a soft song, sometimes including imitations of other birds.
behaviour: Waits on a low branch or fence post and drops to the ground or sallies into the air for beetles, termites and grasshoppers. Often forages alongside Fork-tailed Drongos, which makes it easy to overlook as one of them.
memo: The quiet drongo look-alike: square tail, dark eye, small bill.

migration: Resident all year in broad-leaved woodland, especially Combretum (bushwillow); group territories, though groups may range up to 10 km a day. Breeds August to January, mainly September to November.
size: 15-16 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow.
keys: All black tit with a blue gloss (male) and clear white edges on the wing feathers
Female duller, underparts tinged dark grey
White tips to the outer tail feathers
Juvenile dark brown above

confuse.how: Bigger and slimmer, all black with no white in the wing, sits still and upright then sallies for insects.

voice: Noisy, harsh, buzzy calls such as a repeated “jee-jee-jee” and a churring “chrrr-chrrr-chrrr”.
behaviour: Small noisy groups glean along branches and bark, often in mixed bird parties, eating many tiny wasps from bushwillow pods. A cooperative breeder: helpers from earlier broods feed the incubating female and the chicks, and the female at the nest hole hisses like a snake to scare predators.
memo: A little black tit with white wing stripes, scolding in a family gang.

migration: Resident and sedentary in tall broad-leaved bushveld (knob thorn, marula, mopane), only partly nomadic in the dry season or during droughts. Breeds in the dry season: eggs from July to November, peaking August to October; young disperse at the start of the next breeding season.
size: 42-50 cm, wingspan about 1 m: a little bigger than a feral pigeon, standing tall on long legs.
keys: Dark grey head, breast and upperparts; belly finely barred grey and white
Long orange-red legs and orange-red cere
Rump finely barred grey (not plain white); tail with broad black-and-white bars
Upright posture on an open perch. Juvenile brown with a streaked breast and barred belly, grey cere, yellow eye

confuse.how: Much smaller (about 30 cm), with a clean white rump obvious in flight and less upright stance.
Smaller and stockier, with a white throat split by a black central stripe and a single broad white band across the black tail.

voice: Mostly silent outside breeding; in the breeding season the male gives a long, melodious piping chant (“wheee-wow” or a speeding-up series of fluty notes), mainly at dawn and dusk, which gives the bird its name.
behaviour: Hunts from a perch, dropping onto lizards, rodents, birds and insects on the ground. An opportunist that follows honey badgers, ground hornbills, dogs and even people, as well as bush fires, to grab small animals they flush.
memo: The grey hawk on orange stilts that chants at dawn and shadows honey badgers.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds in southern Europe, North Africa and western Asia, then spends the austral summer in the Lowveld. The first arrive in late September, most in October, and they leave in late March and April. Virtually absent from May to August.
size: 27-29 cm including the tail streamers: about the length of a blackbird, but slimmer.
keys: Bright yellow throat edged with a thin black collar, turquoise blue-green belly
Chestnut crown and back, with golden-yellow shoulders forming a pale V in flight
Black mask through the eye, whitish forehead, two short points in the middle of the tail
Female slightly duller, with greener shoulders; juvenile dull, without tail points

confuse.how: Resident along riverbanks. White forehead, bright red throat and green back, no yellow on the throat.
Much smaller (about 16 cm), green back and ochre belly. Hunts low from a bush, not high up in flocks.

voice: A soft, liquid, rolling “prrrup… prrrup”, given non-stop by flocks in flight. Often heard before it is seen.
behaviour: Very gregarious: noisy flocks hunt high in the sky or sit in rows on dead branches and wires. Before swallowing a bee or wasp, it beats it several times against its perch to remove the sting.
memo: A rainbow from Europe: yellow throat, chestnut back, and that “prrrup” falling from the summer sky.

migration: Resident all year; it only makes local movements, with no true migration. Lays mainly in early summer (August to November) in colonies dug into riverbanks and erosion gullies.
size: 23 cm: about the length of a blackbird, but slimmer, with a square tail.
keys: Bright red throat below a white chin and a white forehead
Black mask edged below by a broad white stripe
Green back and wings, buff-cinnamon chest and belly, deep blue vent and undertail
Square tail with no central streamers; juvenile duller

confuse.how: Yellow throat with a black collar, chestnut back and blue belly; a summer visitor that hunts high in flocks.
Much smaller (16 cm), with a yellow throat and a black gorget, no white on the face.

voice: A nasal, squeaky “gaa” or “kwaank”, often in conversational groups; the alarm is a sharper, piercing call.
behaviour: Lives in clans: a breeding pair is often helped by 1 to 5 helpers, usually its own young from earlier years, and pairs with helpers raise about twice as many chicks. It eats almost only bees and wasps (honey bees alone are about 70% of its diet), hunting by sallies from a perch near the colony.
memo: Red throat, white forehead: the riverbank bee-eater that raises its family with the help of its older kids.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld and does not migrate; it only makes small local moves linked to rainfall. Breeds mainly September to December, digging its own tunnel in a sandy bank.
size: 16-17 cm: the smallest African bee-eater, smaller than a sparrow in body but slimmer, with a longer tail.
keys: Bright green upperparts with a broad black mask through the eye
Yellow throat bordered below by a black bib, then a rich cinnamon-brown breast fading to buff on the belly
Square tail, slightly notched, with no central streamers; black bill
Juvenile lacks the black bib, with a pale throat and greenish breast

confuse.how: Much bigger (27-29 cm), with a chestnut back, turquoise belly and tail points; summer-only and hunts high in noisy flocks.
Larger, with a white forehead and a bright red throat; lives in colonies along riverbanks.

voice: Quiet when hunting; a soft “sip” or “seep”, repeated when two birds greet each other, and a sharper “tsp-tsp-tsp” in alarm.
behaviour: Hunts from a low perch, often a grass stem or bush about 1 m up, darting out after bees and wasps and beating them on the perch to remove the sting before swallowing. At night, small groups roost huddled shoulder to shoulder in a row on a branch.
memo: A tiny green bee-eater with a yellow throat and black bib, always on a low twig.

migration: Resident, but moves about locally with the water: in the dry season it gathers on rivers such as the Olifants and on permanent dams, and it spreads to pans and seasonal pools after the rains. It breeds in colonies at any time of year, often in trees standing in water.
size: 50-60 cm, wingspan 80-90 cm: about the size of a small duck, but slimmer with a long tail.
keys: Small all-dark cormorant with a fairly long tail and a short stubby bill
Breeding adult: glossy black, wing coverts silvery grey scaled black, small tuft on the forehead, yellow to red facial skin
Non-breeding adult and juvenile: brown above, whitish or buffy underparts
Often perches upright on a snag over water with wings spread out to dry

confuse.how: Much longer, thin snake-like neck with a kink, dagger-shaped pointed bill and rufous neck stripe; often swims with only the neck above water.

voice: Mostly silent; gives hisses and cackling “ha-ha-ha” calls at colonies and roosts.
behaviour: Swims very low with only its head and bill showing, then dives and chases fish underwater using its feet. Its plumage gets waterlogged, so afterwards it perches with wings held open to dry. It roosts in groups in trees standing in water, often alongside herons and darters.
memo: The little black cormorant drying its wings on a dead branch above every Lowveld river and dam.

migration: Mainly sedentary, usually alone or in pairs; young birds wander and disperse. In South Africa it breeds mainly from September to January, nesting in the fork of a thorn tree.
size: 28-36 cm: the male is about the size of a Laughing Dove, the female clearly bigger.
keys: Broad, clean white rump, obvious in flight
Plain grey head, throat and upper breast; belly finely barred grey and white
Red cere and long red legs, dark eye
Dark morph (about a quarter of birds) all black with no white rump; juvenile brown, streaked and barred, with yellowish cere and legs

confuse.how: No white rump; underparts finely barred rufous, red eye and yellow legs.
Also has a white rump, but stockier with a white throat split by a black central stripe and a single broad white tail band.
Much larger, with a finely barred grey rump, not pure white, and sits upright in the open.

voice: Usually quiet; in display and as contact or alarm it gives shrill, piping 'kee-kee-kee' whistles.
behaviour: A dashing bird hunter that chases prey persistently through the trees, even on foot into thick cover, and raids weaver colonies, tearing into nests or hovering at them for the chicks. It adds webs of live social spiders to its nest; the spiders keep spinning until the web cloaks the nest.
memo: Small grey hawk, red legs, white rump: the weaver-colony raider with a spider-web nest.

migration: Intra-African breeding migrant. It arrives in the north and east of South Africa from July-August (most by September), breeds August to December, and leaves in March, a few lingering into April. It winters in tropical Africa further north.
size: About 55 cm, wingspan around 1.4 m: a medium raptor, smaller and much slimmer than a Tawny Eagle.
keys: Long, shallowly forked tail, constantly twisted as it flies; looks notched, not square
Plain rufous-brown plumage with fine dark streaks below
Adult: all-yellow bill and dark eye
Juvenile: dark bill with a yellow cere, paler and more streaked

confuse.how: Also a summer migrant and brown, but the tail is straight-edged and square, not forked, and the bill is dark.
Shorter, rounded fan-shaped tail, broad wings held in a shallow V, and soars in circles rather than drifting low and twisting.

voice: A high, quavering whistled whinny, given in flight, especially near the nest.
behaviour: An agile opportunist that drifts low and swoops down to snatch prey from the ground or water surface without landing: small birds, rodents, lizards, frogs, termites and locusts, plus carrion. In courtship the male dives at the female, who rolls over to lock talons with him in mid-air.
memo: A brown kite with a forked, twisting tail and a banana-yellow bill: the swallow-tailed scavenger of summer.

migration: Resident all year, in territorial pairs tied to rivers, dams and lodge grounds. It only disperses locally, and outside the breeding season small groups can gather at good feeding spots. Lays almost all year, with peaks from August to November and from February to April, often raising two or three broods.
size: About 20 cm including the long tail: a little longer than a House Sparrow, but slimmer.
keys: Bold black and white: black upperparts, white underparts with a broad black breast band
Broad white eyebrow on a black head, white throat
Big white patch on the folded wing, very obvious in flight
Long tail constantly wagged up and down; juvenile duller, greyish-brown instead of black, with dirty-white areas
voice: Loud and musical: a ringing “wee-wee-wee” or “tseet-tseet-tseet” with a higher last note, and a varied, whistled song.
behaviour: Walks and runs briskly on sandbanks, lawns and rocks at the water's edge, bobbing its tail and snatching flies, sometimes in the air. Very territorial, it chases intruders and is known to attack its own reflection in car mirrors and windows. Often nests on buildings, bridges or boats.
memo: The black-and-white tail-wagger of the riverbank and the lodge lawn.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds in Europe and western Asia and winters in sub-Saharan Africa. Arrives in southern Africa from mid-October to late November and leaves from mid-March to early April.
size: 13-15 cm: about the size of a sparrow, but slimmer and more upright.
keys: Plain grey-brown above, off-white below, no wing bars
Fine brown streaks on the crown and breast
Upright stance on an open, low perch, with short black legs and a broad, pointed bill
Juvenile: spotted pale above (rarely seen here)

confuse.how: Larger and paler brown, with an unstreaked crown and breast.
Blue-grey above and pale grey below with no streaks, and a white line above the lores.

voice: Mostly quiet in Africa: a thin, high 'tseee' falling slightly in pitch, and a 'tsee-tik' alarm.
behaviour: Sits upright on an exposed perch, darts out to snap a flying insect and often returns to the same perch, flicking its wings and tail.
memo: Streaky grey sparrow that sallies out and always comes back to the same twig.

migration: Wanders according to water levels and fish supply, so numbers vary from year to year. More common in the austral summer (about October to April), when pans and dams fill; a few may stay through the dry season on permanent water. Breeds in colonies, mostly late in the dry season and early summer, often outside the Lowveld.
size: 95-105 cm tall, wingspan about 1.5-1.65 m: about the size of a White Stork.
keys: White body with a pink wash on the back and wings when breeding
Long, deep yellow bill that curves slightly down at the tip
Bare red face; black flight feathers and a short black tail
Juvenile greyish-brown with a dull yellowish bill and a dull orange face

confuse.how: Straight red bill, red legs, fully feathered white head without bare red skin; usually in flocks in open grassland, not wading.
Taller, with a black head and neck and a huge red-and-black bill with a yellow saddle.

voice: Usually silent; at the nest it gives hissing, falsetto squeals and clatters its bill.
behaviour: Wades slowly through shallow water with its bill half open and submerged, snapping it shut by touch, and stirs the mud with one foot to flush out fish. It sometimes follows crocodiles or hippos to catch the prey they disturb.
memo: A white stork with a red face and a yellow bill, fishing by touch with its foot stirring the mud.

migration: Resident and sedentary; in South Africa essentially restricted to Kruger and the adjoining private reserves of Limpopo and Mpumalanga. Immatures wander locally. Breeds in the dry winter, laying mainly June to September, in a stick nest high in a big riverside tree such as a Jackalberry.
size: 65-75 cm, wingspan about 1.6-1.8 m: the smallest vulture in Kruger, roughly half the size of a Lappet-faced Vulture.
keys: Long, thin, slender bill (other vultures have heavy bills)
Bare pink face and throat that flushes red-purple when excited at a carcass
Uniform dark brown plumage, pale beige downy 'hood' on the back of the head and neck
Juvenile darker and plainer, with a pale bluish-grey face

confuse.how: Bigger, with a heavy red bill with a blue base, a white downy head and (adult) white belly.
Huge, with a massive bill and folds of red skin on the head and neck, and white thighs.
Bigger and paler, with a heavy black bill and a dark grey face; the juvenile is brown but still has a heavy bill.

voice: Almost always silent; at most thin squeals at a carcass or at the nest.
behaviour: Usually alone or in a pair, often first at a kill because, being light, it can fly before strong thermals form. Easily bullied off by bigger vultures, it darts in to snatch scraps and retreats, slips between hyenas' legs, and pecks at the ground like a chicken; its thin bill reaches bone crevices others miss.
memo: The little pink-faced vulture with a pencil bill: first in, last out at the carcass.

migration: A highly mobile diving duck that turns up on Lowveld dams and pans unpredictably, following water levels rather than a fixed calendar. Ringed South African birds have been recovered more than 3,000 km away in Zambia, Malawi, Tanzania and Kenya. Southern African birds lay over a long season, mostly in summer after rains.
size: 48-51 cm: a medium-sized duck, a little smaller than a Mallard, compact with a rounded head.
keys: Male: very dark chocolate-brown, almost black head and neck, with a bright red eye
Blue-grey bill on a plain, dark body; sits low in the water when feeding, tail pointing down
Female: brown with a pale crescent from the throat up behind the cheek and a pale patch at the bill base
In flight both sexes show a broad white bar along the whole trailing wing

confuse.how: Upright stance with a white face, barred flanks and a chestnut breast; dabbles and whistles loudly instead of diving quietly.
Much smaller, with a tiny pointed bill, a chestnut neck in breeding plumage and no white wing bar.
Much bigger, glossy black above and white below with a speckled head; the male has a knob on the bill.

voice: Usually silent; displaying males give a nasal, buzzing "perr-perr" and females a low, short "quarrk".
behaviour: A true diver: it feeds mostly on water-lily seeds, sedge seeds and other aquatic plants, diving for them in deep clear water, mainly early and late in the day. It needs a long pattering run across the surface to take off.
memo: The dark duck with a red eye that dives on the dam and flashes a white wing bar.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, in pairs holding large territories (about 35 ha). Outside the breeding season it often joins mixed bird parties moving through the woodland. Lays from about August to January.
size: 12-15 cm: about the size of a sparrow, a small, compact shrike.
keys: Male: black crown and back, broad white eyebrow and black eye-stripe
White underparts with a rufous-chestnut stripe along the flanks
Black wings with a long buff-white stripe; black tail with white outer edges
Female duller and browner, with fine streaks below and less rufous; juvenile mottled brown, barred below

confuse.how: No white eyebrow and no rufous flanks, and it has a red eye; the male puffs out a white rump.
Grey back and a black or chestnut breast band, with no rufous flanks; the Brubru is bigger and shrike-like.

voice: A far-carrying, rolling “prrrrrrrp” like an old telephone ringing, often answered by the female's softer “eeeu” in duet.
behaviour: Unobtrusive: it hops through the leafy upper canopy of big trees gleaning insects, so it is far more often heard than seen. Its neat cup nest of twigs and spider web, decorated with lichen, is so well camouflaged it looks like a knot on the branch.
memo: The old phone ringing in the treetops: “prrrrrp”, a small shrike with a white eyebrow and rusty flanks.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld and sedentary: flocks wander up to about 10 km a day on foot, but do not migrate. In the dry season they live in flocks of 20-50 or more. With the rains the pairs leave the flock to breed, with laying mainly October to March.
size: 53-58 cm, about 1.3-1.5 kg: the size of a farmyard chicken, round-bodied with a small head.
keys: Round slate-grey body covered in small white spots
Bare blue head and neck with red-tipped wattles
Yellowish-horn bony casque (the 'helmet') on top of the head
Keets (chicks) are cryptically striped brown; sexes alike, males with bigger head ornaments
voice: Loud, harsh, grating cackles; the flock's alarm is a rattling “kek-kek-kek-kek-kaaarrr”, often triggered by a leopard, snake or raptor.
behaviour: Walks the veld in noisy flocks, scratching for bulbs, seeds, termites and ticks, and prefers running to flying. At dusk the flock flies up into a tall tree to roost together. When a predator attacks, the adults retreat while the keets scatter into the grass, then the adults come back to gather survivors.
memo: A polka-dot hen with a blue face and a helmet: the bush's noisy alarm bell.

migration: Resident all year, with some local wandering to follow fruiting and flowering trees; numbers may rise in north-eastern South Africa from July to September. Breeds September to February, mostly September to December.
size: 20-22 cm: about the size of a blackbird.
keys: Glossy black head and upper breast contrasting with brilliant yellow underparts
Coral-red to pinkish bill and red eye
Olive-yellow back, black wings with pale edges, yellow tips to the black tail
Sexes alike; juvenile has a dark olive head, streaked throat and breast, and a dark bill

confuse.how: Summer visitor only; the male has a yellow head with just a black line through the eye and jet-black wings, the female is greenish with a streaked whitish belly; no black hood.
Smaller, with a conical seed-eater bill and only a black mask on the face, not a whole black head and breast; lives at its nest colonies, not high in the canopy.

voice: A loud, liquid, fluty whistle (eBird writes it “wholeuooo”), mixed with a harsh, drawn-out alarm screech; a good mimic. Usually heard before it is seen.
behaviour: Despite its brilliant yellow it stays hidden in the canopy of tall trees, giving away its presence only by its liquid call. Its cup nest hangs in a fork near the end of a branch, high up, camouflaged with lichen (old-man's beard) and cobweb.
memo: A yellow bird with a black hood hiding in the treetops, betrayed by its liquid whistle.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds in Europe and western Asia and leaves from July to September, travelling mostly at night via the eastern Mediterranean. Reaches southern Africa late, mostly from November, and leaves in March-April. Uncommon in the Lowveld, more frequent in northern Kruger.
size: 24 cm: about the size of a blackbird.
keys: Male: bright golden-yellow head and body with all-black wings and a black tail tipped yellow
Black only on the lores (bill to eye), no black head
Dark pinkish-red bill
Female and young: greenish above, whitish below with fine dark streaks, wings brownish; some old females are almost as yellow as males

confuse.how: Resident, with the whole head and throat black, a pinkish-red bill and a yellow-green back; wings largely edged yellow-green, not all black.

voice: A loud, fluting whistle, “weela-wee-ooo” (the old English name “or-i-ole” comes from it), plus a harsh cat-like “kweeaahk” call; in Africa mostly the harsh call is heard.
behaviour: Shy and hidden in the canopy of tall trees, rarely coming down. Usually seen only as a flash of gold and black dashing between trees, in strong, slightly undulating, thrush-like flight. Feeds on insects and fruit, especially figs.
memo: A flash of gold with black wings from Europe, no black hood: not our resident oriole.

migration: Sedentary all year in pairs or small family groups of up to about seven. In South Africa it breeds from October to March, with the rains; in winter the diet switches mainly to bulbs, shoots and berries.
size: 30-35 cm: about the size of a bantam hen; the male is bigger than the female.
keys: Broad white eyebrow under a dark cap, white throat; dark crest raised only now and then
Long dark-tipped tail held cocked up like a bantam's
Red legs and black bill
Rufous-brown back with clear cream streaks (finely vermiculated in the female); breast with dark chevron spots

confuse.how: Bigger and greyer, with a bright orange-red bill as well as legs, finely scaled underparts, no white eyebrow, and does not cock its tail.
Bigger and plain dark brown, with bare red skin on the face and throat and black legs.
Smaller, with yellow legs and finely barred underparts; male has a plain buff head with no white eyebrow.

voice: A loud, rhythmic, metallic cackle, rendered 'cheer kirk-kik' or 'kerra-kreek', usually given as a duet by a pair. Often one of the first calls of the dawn chorus and very vocal again at dusk.
behaviour: Struts along tracks with its tail cocked like a little bantam, and slips into the roadside bush when a vehicle slows. Prefers to run rather than fly, and unusually for a francolin roosts at night in trees or shrubs.
memo: The bush bantam: white eyebrow, red legs and a cocked tail.

migration: Resident all year, without real seasonal movements. Pairs are not very territorial and may nest close together. Lays in tree holes in late winter and spring (June to November in southern Africa).
size: 15-19 cm: Kruger's smallest owl, about the size of a starling.
keys: Tiny grey-brown owl, streaked and mottled exactly like tree bark
Small ear tufts, raised when alarmed or roosting, flat when relaxed
Grey facial disc with a thin black rim, and yellow eyes
Some birds are browner or more rufous

confuse.how: Round head with no ear tufts, white-spotted brown plumage, two false “eyes” on the nape, and often active and calling by day.
Much bigger (about 25 cm), with a bright white face boldly rimmed black and orange eyes.

voice: A short, purring “prrrp”, repeated every 5 seconds or so through the night; pairs sometimes duet.
behaviour: Strictly nocturnal. By day it presses against a trunk, raises its ear tufts and narrows its eyes to slits, turning into a broken stub of branch, so it is easily overlooked even at close range. At night it drops onto insects, scorpions and spiders from a perch.
memo: Heard all night, seen almost never: a “prrrp” from a bark-coloured stick.

migration: Resident all year and sedentary, with only local wandering in flocks outside the breeding season. Breeds from September onwards, mainly December to April.
size: 15-16 cm: like a House Sparrow, slightly bigger.
keys: Plain grey head with no black bib and no eyebrow
Chestnut-brown back, rump and wings
Small white spot on the shoulder
Bill black when breeding, horn-coloured otherwise; sexes alike

confuse.how: The male has a black bib and a chestnut stripe on the side of a grey crown; the female is brown with a pale eyebrow. Both sexes have a streaked back, unlike the plain grey head and chestnut back here.

voice: Simple chirps, a sparrow-like “chip” or “cheep”, given singly or in a short series.
behaviour: Feeds mostly on the ground, often in mixed flocks with other seed-eaters, and comes to camps and bird feeders. Nests in holes: old barbet or woodpecker holes, fence posts, eaves, old swallow or swift nests, and even chambers in Red-billed Buffalo Weaver colonies.
memo: The bush sparrow: plain grey head, chestnut back, a white dot on the shoulder.

migration: Introduced from Eurasia: Indian birds released at Durban and European birds at East London around 1890-1900, spreading explosively from the 1950s. Sedentary and resident, tied to buildings, so at Pidwa look around lodges and staff quarters rather than in the bush. Breeds all year, peaking September to December.
size: 14-16 cm: a small, chunky seed-eater with a thick conical bill.
keys: Male: grey crown, chestnut band from eye to nape, whitish cheeks and a black bib
Brown back streaked black, white wing bar, grey rump
Female: plain buff-brown with a pale eyebrow stripe behind the eye, no bib
Always near buildings

confuse.how: Whole head plain grey with no black bib or chestnut face pattern, and lives in the bush as well as around houses.
Female and non-breeding birds also look streaky brown but have a bright red bill and travel in big flocks in the veld.

voice: Repeated chirps, “tchirp, tchirp” or “chissip”; no real song, and a fast rattling trill when alarmed or quarrelling.
behaviour: Lives alongside people, nesting under eaves, in thatch or holes in walls, and builds an untidy ball of grass and feathers. Hops on the ground picking up scraps and seeds, and dust-bathes in groups.
memo: The black-bibbed sparrow that came with the settlers: look for it at the lodge, not in the bush.

migration: Resident all year in stable family territories, with young birds often settling next to where they hatched. It can breed in any month, with peaks around the rains.
size: 32-40 cm including the long tail: longer than a blackbird, slim, with a long tail like a magpie's.
keys: Long, thin, curved bright red bill and short red legs
Dark plumage glossed green and blue-violet, looking black at a distance
White bar across the wing and white spots near the tip of the long, graduated tail
Juvenile duller with a dark (black) bill; female has a shorter bill

confuse.how: Smaller, with a black, much more strongly curved bill and black legs, and usually seen singly or in pairs, not noisy groups.
Cinnamon-orange with a fan-shaped crest and black-and-white barred wings; feeds on the ground.

voice: Groups give a loud, rising, cackling chorus 'kuk-uk-uk-uk' that sounds like laughter; the Afrikaans name Rooibekkakelaar means 'red-billed cackler'.
behaviour: Lives in family groups of up to about 12 birds that move from tree to tree, clinging under branches and propping on their tails like woodpeckers. When neighbouring groups meet, they rock back and forth, fan their tails and cackle in a noisy 'rally'. Only one pair breeds; the other group members feed the female and the chicks, and the group roosts together in tree holes at night.
memo: A red-billed gang that laughs its way through the trees.

migration: Palearctic migrant: breeds across northern Europe and Siberia, and some eastern birds fly up to 12,000 km each way. The first reach the north of the region in late September, more in October to December. It leaves in March and April, with a few stragglers into May.
size: 11-12.5 cm: much smaller than a sparrow, a slim little leaf warbler.
keys: Plain olive-green to grey-brown above with no wing bars, whitish below with a yellow wash on the throat and breast
Clear pale yellowish eyebrow and a dark line through the eye
Pale, pinkish-brown legs
First-year birds are much yellower below

confuse.how: Has a bold white ring around the eye and greener upperparts, and moves in chattering flocks.
Looks almost tailless, with a long curved bill, and is buffy below without yellow.
Darker brown, with no yellow, and a long scaly-tipped undertail. It skulks low in dense cover instead of moving through the canopy.

voice: A soft, sweet cascade of whistled notes that drops down the scale, often heard in Africa before it leaves in late summer. The call is a two-note “hoo-eet”.
behaviour: Restless and active in the canopy of acacias and other trees, picking insects off leaves, often hovering briefly at a leaf tip. It often joins mixed feeding parties.
memo: A tiny yellowish leaf warbler with pale legs that flew from Siberia to your thorn tree.

migration: Nomad that wanders between wetlands in response to local rainfall and water levels, so it can turn up at any dam or pan in any month and then vanish again. Ringed birds have moved hundreds of kilometres. In southern Africa it breeds mainly from July to November, in colonies in reedbeds or trees over water.
size: About 90 cm: as tall as a Grey Heron's body, much bigger than a Little Egret.
keys: All-white wader with a long grey, flat, spoon-shaped bill (pinkish-red edges)
Bare red face and long red legs
No crest, unlike the Eurasian Spoonbill
Juvenile: no red face, yellowish bill, black tips to the wings

confuse.how: Also big and white, but has a pointed yellow bill, black legs and a feathered face; it stalks and stabs instead of sweeping.
Much smaller and slimmer, with a thin black pointed bill, black legs and yellow feet.

voice: Usually silent; at most a low grunting “aark-ark” when alarmed or at the colony.
behaviour: Wades slowly through shallow water sweeping its half-open bill from side to side like a scythe, snapping it shut on any fish or invertebrate it touches. It sometimes follows hippos and crocodiles to catch animals they disturb. Flies with neck and legs stretched out.
memo: A white heron carrying a spoon, scything the shallows.

migration: Present all year, but it wanders between waters. Many birds make a dry-season moult migration to large dams and pans (on the Highveld and in the Free State), so numbers on Lowveld dams fluctuate and may dip in winter. Breeds mainly November to April in the former Transvaal, with a peak in January and February.
size: 75-100 cm (male much larger than female): bigger than a farmyard goose, the largest waterfowl in Africa.
keys: Huge and mostly glossy black with green-bronze sheen; southern birds show only a little white on the belly and face
Bare red face and red bill; the male has a knob on the forehead and more bare skin
Long pinkish-red legs
In flight: big white patch on the leading edge of the black wing

confuse.how: Much smaller, white head and neck speckled black, white underparts, grey legs, and the male's knob is black, not red.
Smaller and brownish-buff, with a dark-brown eye patch and a chestnut breast spot; white wing patches show in flight too.

voice: Usually silent. The male gives a weak, bubbling 'cher-wit' when taking off or alarmed.
behaviour: Grazes on banks and in fields and rests by water in the middle of the day; also perches in trees. It has a sharp spur on the bend of the wing, used in fights during the breeding season. Some birds that eat blister beetles store their toxin, cantharidin, in their flesh, so their meat can poison people.
memo: A black giant with a red face and a spur hidden in its wing.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, usually near water and tall trees. Outside the breeding season it wanders locally in flocks and roosts communally. Breeds in colonies from August to April, with peaks in September-October and January-February.
size: 15-17 cm: a little bigger than a House Sparrow, stocky, with a strong conical bill.
keys: Breeding male: black face and throat, but forehead and crown yellow (the black mask stops at the base of the bill in the southern race)
Back mottled black and yellow (old name 'Spotted-backed Weaver'), yellow underparts
Red eye, black bill, pinkish legs
Female and non-breeding: olive-yellow head with a yellow eyebrow, streaky grey-brown back, pale yellow to whitish below; juvenile has a brownish eye
