confuse.how: Plain, lightly streaked green back with no black spotting, and in the breeding male a narrow black band across the forehead above the bill.
Smaller, with a pale whitish eye, and the male's black mask extends over the forehead onto the crown.

voice: A sparrow-like “tjip” call; the song is a buzzing, swizzling chatter of liquid notes ending in drawn-out sizzling whistles, given non-stop at the colony.
behaviour: Nests in noisy colonies of up to a few hundred birds in one tall tree, often over water. Each polygynous male weaves several kidney-shaped nests from green grass or reed strips and displays hanging under them, flapping his wings, to attract a female; only accepted nests get an entrance tunnel and a lining.
memo: Black face, yellow crown and a spotted back: the colony weaver with the red eye.

migration: Resident, but after breeding the birds leave the colonies and roam in flocks to find food. Breeds in colonies from August to March, peaking October to January.
size: About 13-14 cm: the size of a House Sparrow, slightly smaller than Southern Masked Weaver.
keys: Breeding male: yellow with a black mask that reaches up over the forehead onto the crown
Pale, whitish-cream eye (in both sexes) in a black face
Blue-grey legs, not pinkish
Female and non-breeding male olive-yellow, with the same pale eye

confuse.how: Breeding male has a red eye, pinkish legs and only a narrow black band on the forehead, with the mask pointing down onto the throat.
Larger, with a red eye, a heavier bill and a back boldly mottled black and yellow.

voice: A drawn-out buzzing, sizzling song broken by chattering notes; colonies are very noisy.
behaviour: Nests in colonies, often over water and alongside Village Weavers. The male weaves several kidney-shaped nests with a short entrance tube pointing down and displays upside down below them, fluttering his wings; females inspect them and choose. Often parasitised by Diederik Cuckoo.
memo: Pale eye, black cap, grey legs: the masked weaver with the mask pulled up over its head.

migration: Resident all year. In winter it moults out of breeding plumage, gathers in flocks with other seed-eaters and roosts communally in reedbeds or trees. Breeds in colonies mainly September to February, often over water.
size: 11-14.5 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow.
keys: Breeding male: bright yellow with a black mask that reaches only a thin band above the bill, plus a black throat
Red eye in the male, pinkish-brown legs
Plain yellowish-green back with faint streaks
Female and non-breeding male: dull olive-yellow, streaked above, pinkish-brown bill; non-breeding male keeps the red eye

confuse.how: Pale yellowish eye (not red), the black mask extends onto the crown, and the legs are blue-grey.
Bigger, with a back spotted black and yellow, not plain green.
Non-breeding birds are smaller and browner, with a big red bill, and travel in huge swarms.

voice: A harsh, buzzy “swizzling” song, given by males hanging from their nests; sharp “chuk” alarm.
behaviour: The male weaves many kidney-shaped grass nests in a season (about 25 by one estimate) and displays under them, wings flapping, to attract females. A female inspects them and lines the one she chooses with soft grass and feathers. One male may have several females.
memo: Yellow, red eye and a black mask that stops at the forehead: the colony's builder.

migration: Resident and sedentary, staying all year in woodland with mistletoe. Lays from July to February, mainly October to March in South Africa.
size: 10-12 cm: smaller than a sparrow, a plump little barbet with a big head and a short tail.
keys: Yellow-orange spot on the forehead
Bold black-and-white striped face
Black back heavily streaked with yellow and white, lemon-yellow rump and underparts
Sexes alike; juvenile has a dark crown without the yellow spot

confuse.how: Bigger, with a red (not yellow) forehead, a black throat and a white belly.
Much bigger and more colourful, with a shaggy crest, a yellow-and-red face and a black breast band.

voice: A monotonous run of metallic “tink-tink-tink” notes, about 100 a minute, repeated for long periods from cover. More often heard than seen.
behaviour: Feeds mainly on mistletoe berries, which it swallows whole. Within minutes it regurgitates the sticky seed and wipes it onto a nearby branch, which makes it the main planter of mistletoe in its range. It digs its own nest hole in a dead branch, which Acacia Pied Barbets sometimes steal.
memo: A tiny tinker hammering “tink-tink” all day, and the mistletoe's gardener.

migration: Resident in the Lowveld, moving locally in pairs and small groups after seasonal seeds and fruit; up to 50 may gather where food is plentiful. Breeds in the dry season, roughly April to October, in old woodpecker or barbet holes.
size: 22-25 cm: about the size of a dove, but stocky with a short square tail and a big head.
keys: Bright green body with a plain brownish-grey head
Pale yellow eye; bill grey above, paler below
Bright yellow underwing coverts flash in flight (the 'hidden yellow' of its scientific name)
Juvenile duller with a dark eye

confuse.how: Also green in fruiting trees, but greyish-green with a red bill base, red legs and yellow 'trousers'; it coos and whistles rather than shrieking.

voice: A loud, harsh, shrieking flight call, the notes rising in pitch, usually heard before the birds are seen; softer chattering while feeding.
behaviour: Well camouflaged and quiet while feeding high in the canopy, it is mostly noticed as a pair or small group screeching past in fast, direct flight. Uses its bill like a third foot when clambering in trees and cracks hard seeds of trees such as sjambok pod, bushwillows and jackalberry.
memo: A screech, a flash of green and yellow underwings: the Lowveld's only parrot.

migration: Resident in territorial pairs with very large home ranges (about 144 km² per pair in Kruger); only young birds wander far. Lays mostly in the dry season (around April to June), raising a single chick, and pairs often breed only every second year.
size: 78-96 cm, wingspan up to 2.4-2.6 m: Africa's largest eagle, clearly bigger than a Tawny Eagle; females much heavier than males.
keys: Dark brown head, upper breast and back, like a hood
White belly and legs sparsely spotted with dark brown
Flat-topped head with a short crest and piercing yellow eyes; feathered legs
Juvenile: pale grey above, all white below with a dark eye; adult plumage takes about seven years

confuse.how: Smaller and round-headed with big yellow eyes, an unspotted white belly and bare whitish legs; in flight nearly white flight feathers and narrower wings.
Smaller and more slender, with white underparts streaked (not spotted) black and a mainly white underwing with a black trailing edge.
Uniform tawny to brown all over, with no white spotted belly; feathered legs and a yellow gape.

voice: Usually silent; mates keep in touch with a soft whistle, and during display flights it gives a loud ringing call.
behaviour: Spends hours soaring very high and can spot prey several kilometres away, then stoops in a long dive and often kills on impact. In Kruger it takes guineafowl, spurfowl, Egyptian Geese and monitor lizards, and it is the only bird considered a real predator of young antelope.
memo: The flying hood: dark head and chest, spotted white belly, Africa's heaviest eagle.

migration: Resident in the moist eastern woodlands, including the Lowveld, where pairs hold territories all year; it is more nomadic only in arid areas further west. Breeds from August to December, peaking September to November, in a stick nest high in a tall tree.
size: 60-66 cm, wingspan up to 1.5 m: about the length of a Common Buzzard, but with longer, broader wings and a long tail and a small head.
keys: Pale grey all over, with a white belly finely barred black
Small head with a bare face that is normally yellow and flushes red or pink when the bird is excited
Black tail crossed by one broad white band; broad grey wings with a black trailing edge
Juvenile: dark brown, blotchy and very variable, but already showing the small head and bare face

confuse.how: Also grey with a barred belly, but has long orange-red legs and cere, a feathered face, and perches bolt upright on open treetops.
Much smaller (35 cm) and stocky, with a white throat crossed by a black vertical stripe, though it also has a single white tail band.

voice: Mostly silent; in the breeding season gives a plaintive, drawn-out whistle, “su-eeeee-oo”, often while pairs soar together.
behaviour: Its “double-jointed” knees bend both ways, so it can reach deep into tree holes and cracks. It clambers up trunks and hangs upside down from weaver nests with its wings flapping, pulling out eggs and chicks, often with a crowd of weavers mobbing it.
memo: The grey hawk that blushes and hangs upside down from weaver nests.

migration: Resident and sedentary all year, in territorial pairs or small family groups. Breeds mainly in the rains: eggs in almost any month, peaking November to March.
size: 11-12 cm, about half of it a long tail: smaller and much slimmer than a House Sparrow.
keys: Long, narrow, graduated tail, often cocked upright or waved from side to side
Plain grey-brown above, with a pale eyebrow and dark lores
Whitish throat and breast, warm tawny-buff flanks and vent
Juvenile washed pale yellow below, with a yellowish bill; the tail is longer outside the breeding season

confuse.how: Stockier, with a shorter tail that is not waved about, a streaky back and a rufous crown, and it sings a harsh rattling song.
Also has a long cocked tail, but the white underparts are barred black right across.

voice: The song is a long, monotonous series of sharp, high notes, “tsip-tsip-tsip-tsip…”, often from an exposed perch with the tail cocked; the call is a short, wheezy note repeated quickly.
behaviour: Small, noisy family groups move through tall grass and tangles, hopping on the ground and in the undergrowth, tails jerking and waving. It weaves a ball-shaped nest with a side entrance from strips of green grass, and is often a host to parasitic indigobirds and whydahs.
memo: A tiny brown bird with tawny flanks, waving its tail like a metronome.

migration: Resident in groups that hold territories, breeding in broad-leaved woodland (mopane, miombo, Burkea) in spring and summer. In the dry season groups wander more widely, into acacia savanna and even gardens.
size: 19-25 cm: a little smaller than a thrush, stocky.
keys: Black and white: black back and wings with white wing bars, white underparts and collar
Bright yellow wattled eye-ring around a yellow eye
Grey-white bushy, curly crest on the forehead and crown
Orange-red legs; always seen in noisy groups of several birds

confuse.how: Mostly black and brown, with a red bill, red eye-ring and red legs, and no white collar or crest.
Bigger, with a white crown and a brown back, and no yellow eye-ring; sits still in small groups on open perches.

voice: A noisy group chatter of rolling churrs, whistles and bill-snapping, with a fast “cherow-cherow”; the pair calls back and forth.
behaviour: Groups of 5-12 move restlessly from tree to tree one after another, always chattering. They are cooperative breeders: the whole group helps build the nest, incubate and feed the chicks, and defends the territory noisily against other groups and predators.
memo: The yellow-spectacled gang: a chattering black-and-white troop that never sits still.

migration: Sedentary resident in groups that hold territories in tall broad-leaved woodland. Outside the breeding season groups wander more widely, into riverine forest, acacia savanna and gardens. Breeds from October to November as the trees come into leaf.
size: 19-24 cm: a little smaller than a blackbird, stocky.
keys: Black head and underparts, dark brown back, white vent and white tips to the tail
Red bill with an orange tip
Orange-yellow eye ringed with a red fleshy wattle; red legs
Juvenile browner, with little or no red on the bill, legs and eye-wattle

confuse.how: Grey-and-white with a pale crest and black-and-white wings, a black bill and a yellow eye-wattle, not a dark bird with red bare parts.

voice: Groups keep up a varied mix of grating, whistling and nasal notes, together with bill-snapping.
behaviour: Lives in close-knit groups of about 2-15 that move together through the canopy, one tree after another, gleaning insects. The whole group helps the breeding pair build the nest, incubate and feed the chicks, and noisily mobs rival groups and predators. It is a host of the Thick-billed Cuckoo.
memo: A gang of dark birds with red bills and red-rimmed eyes, chattering through the canopy.

migration: Sedentary resident, in pairs or small coveys that stay in the same thickets all year. Breeds mainly December to May in South Africa, although eggs have been found in every month.
size: 30-38 cm: about the size of a small domestic hen, the male clearly bigger and heavier than the female.
keys: Orange-red bill with a yellow base and red-orange legs
No bare skin around the eye or on the throat (the only spurfowl in its range without it)
Dark grey-brown head and back; underparts white closely scaled with black, densest on throat and breast
Juvenile duller with a buff wash, greenish bill and flesh-coloured legs; female lacks long spurs

confuse.how: Bare bright red skin around the eye and on the throat, blackish bill and dark legs, and brown streaky underparts, not white scaled black.
Smaller, with a bold white eyebrow, dark crown it raises as a crest and a tail cocked like a bantam's.

voice: Loud, raucous cackling series such as “ker-kik-kik-kik” and a ringing “kwali-kwali-kwali”, mostly at dawn and dusk; a short “kik” when alarmed.
behaviour: Shy and never far from thick cover, especially riverine thickets and bushy rocky slopes near water. Scratches through animal dung for undigested seeds, and roosts in trees at night. Prefers to run to cover rather than fly.
memo: Orange bill, orange legs, scaly belly, and no red face: Natal, not Swainson's.

migration: Resident all year, sedentary in pairs and small groups. Eggs can be laid in any month, with a peak from February to May, after the main rains.
size: About 38 cm: a large, chicken-like gamebird, a bit smaller than a Helmeted Guineafowl.
keys: Bare bright red skin around the eye and on the throat
Bill black above with a red lower mandible; legs dark, blackish
Plain grey-brown plumage with dark streaks, finer on the head and neck and coarser on the flanks
Female smaller and darker below, with no spurs; juvenile paler brown

confuse.how: Has an orange-red bill and red legs, no red bare face, and white underparts scaled black.
Much smaller, with a dark cap, a white eyebrow and a tail often cocked like a bantam's; no red on the face.

voice: A loud, harsh, grating crow, a series of “kwaaark-kwaaark-kwaark” calls that fade at the end, mostly at dawn and dusk; it gives an explosive “qua-qua-quak” when flushed.
behaviour: At dawn and dusk the male climbs a termite mound or low branch, stands bolt upright and puffs out his throat to crow. Shy, it would rather run to cover than fly, and groups come to drink at favoured spots in the morning and late afternoon.
memo: Red face, dark legs, crowing from a termite mound at sunrise.

migration: Sedentary resident with only local dispersal. Lays mainly August to November, usually in an old stick nest of another bird.
size: 22-28 cm: a small owl, about the size of a dove but much stockier, clearly bigger than the African Scops Owl.
keys: White face edged with a bold black rim
Large bright orange eyes
Short ear tufts with black tips
Grey upperparts with fine dark streaks and a row of white spots on the shoulder; juvenile has a greyer face

confuse.how: Much smaller and cryptic grey-brown, with yellow eyes and no white black-rimmed face.
No ear tufts, yellow eyes, brown spotted plumage and two black false eyes on the nape; often active by day.

voice: A fast, stuttering, bubbling series of notes ending in a longer, higher hoot, "bu-bu-bu-bu-hooo", repeated at night; pairs often call together.
behaviour: Hunts mostly small mammals, especially mice and shrews, dropping onto them from a perch and seizing them with its talons; it also takes birds up to dove size and large insects. It sometimes evicts small raptors from their own stick nests to breed there.
memo: A white face framed in black with flaming orange eyes.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, one of the commonest birds in camps and riverine bush. Mostly sedentary, it wanders only locally in the dry season to find fruit. Breeds in pairs from about September to April, peaking September to December.
size: 18-20 cm: a little smaller and slimmer than a blackbird, with a longish tail.
keys: Blackish-brown head with a slight peaked crest, looking darker than the body
Plain grey-brown back and paler brownish-grey breast and belly
Bright yellow patch under the tail (the vent)
Dark eye with no coloured eye-ring; sexes alike, juvenile duller in the face

confuse.how: Plain olive-green all over with a striking white eye, no dark cap and no yellow vent; usually hidden in dense thickets and heard rather than seen.
Olive-brown above with the whole underside yellowish, not just the vent, and no dark head; moves in groups low in thick riverine bush.

voice: Loud, cheerful, chattering phrases, often rendered “doctor-quick, doctor-quick, be-quick, be-quick”; also a sharp, harsh alarm chatter. Often one of the first birds singing at dawn.
behaviour: Bold and noisy, in pairs or small groups, and quick to come to picnic sites for scraps. It scolds snakes and other predators with long, agitated alarm calls, so a fussing bulbul is worth checking. Rival males can fight so hard they lock claws in mid-air and tumble to the ground.
memo: Black cap, yellow pants: “doctor-quick, be-quick!”

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, in pairs or family groups that stay in the same thickets and make only small local moves. It can lay in any month, but breeding peaks late in the rains, January to May.
size: 12-14 cm: a little smaller than a House Sparrow, but with a longer tail.
keys: Male: bright red face, chin and throat contrasting with a grey crown and nape, and a red bill
Olive-green back and wings, with a red rump and tail that show when it flies off
Underparts barred grey and white, with an olive-yellow wash across the breast
Female: plain grey head with no red, and barred underparts right up to the throat. Juvenile duller, with little barring
voice: Quiet and easy to miss: a few soft, water-drop notes followed by a trilled, falling “prrreeeooo”, given from cover.
behaviour: Feeds on the ground on grass seeds and termites, often on tracks and in clearings, and flicks back into a thicket at the slightest alarm. It is the host of the Long-tailed Paradise Whydah: the whydah lays in its nest, and the young male whydahs grow up copying the pytilia's song.
memo: Red face, green wings, zebra belly: a jewel that hops off the track into the thicket.

migration: Nomad following the rains and grass seeds. Seen almost all year in the Lowveld, but numbers vary hugely from year to year. Big flocks arrive in summer, a few weeks after the first rains, and breed in colonies from December to March. In the dry season they are more scattered, often around water.
size: 12 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow.
keys: Big, bright red conical bill, obvious even on the brown non-breeding bird
Breeding male: black mask framed by a head and breast washed yellow, pink or red, varying between birds
Female and non-breeding: brown and streaky like a sparrow, red or yellowish eye-ring; breeding female has an orange-yellow bill
Yellow edges to the wing feathers, and almost always in a flock, often a huge one

confuse.how: Females and non-breeding males are bigger, yellowish and only faintly streaked, with a dark or horn bill, never bright red.
The female also has a brown-streaked back, but a greyish bill; lives around buildings and does not form swarms.

voice: Endless chattering from the flock. The male gives a short chattering phrase then a warbling “tweedle-toodle-tweedle”. A flock in flight makes a roar of wings.
behaviour: Flies in swarms of thousands that swirl like smoke. On the ground the birds at the back leapfrog over those in front to reach the seeds, so the flock moves like a rolling cloud. They come to drink en masse at waterholes, and the colonies attract raptors, marabous and snakes. Said to be the most numerous wild bird in the world.
memo: A red-billed sparrow that travels in a cloud of smoke.

migration: Resident all year; established pairs hold territories year-round and only some individuals wander. Breeds in spring and summer in tree cavities, often reusing the same hole for several years.
size: 26-30 cm including the long tail: a bit longer than a blackbird, but very slim and light (35 g).
keys: Long, thin, strongly down-curved black bill (sickle-shaped)
Black plumage with a blue-violet gloss, short black legs
Bold white bar across the wing, very obvious in flight; small white tips to the outer tail feathers
Female and juvenile browner on the face and breast, with a shorter bill

confuse.how: Bigger, with red legs and a red, less curved bill (black and straighter in the juvenile), and it travels in noisy cackling groups.

voice: A short series of 3-5 high, mournful, rather ventriloquial whistles, “pwee-pwee-pwee”, given from a treetop.
behaviour: An acrobat of the branches: it climbs up and down trunks and hangs upside down to probe its sickle bill behind loose bark and into crevices for insects. Usually alone or in pairs, often joining mixed bird parties; the female incubates alone while the male feeds her at the nest hole.
memo: A black sickle with a white wing stripe, hanging upside down under the bark.

migration: Present all year in the Lowveld, but secretive and uncommon. A resident breeding population is joined by post-breeding migrants from further north in Africa, which stay roughly from November to May or June. Breeds July to December, peaking in October and November, often in recently burnt areas.
size: 25-29 cm: the largest courser, about the size of a Crowned Lapwing, with long legs and a big head.
keys: Bold face: dark brown cheek patch between cream-white stripes over the eye and below it, and very large dark eyes made for night
Grey-brown breast band edged below by a thin black line, white belly
Long dull red legs, upright plover-like stance
In flight: white rump, black flight feathers with violet-bronze tips (the 'bronze wing', only seen in flight). Juvenile duller, with buff feather fringes

confuse.how: Also on roads at night, but bigger, heavily spotted all over, with huge yellow eyes and yellow legs.
Active by day, with a black cap ringed in white, a plain brown chest and a red bill base; no dark cheek patch.

voice: Mostly silent by day; at night gives a haunting, slurred “chee-yaa-oo” and a piping “ji-ku-it”.
behaviour: Nocturnal: it spends the day hidden in the shade of a bush and comes out after dusk to pick insects off the ground, often along gravel roads, where night drives find it in the spotlight. At the nest, parents defend their chicks hard and feign a broken wing to lead predators away.
memo: A night-shift plover with huge dark eyes: the bronze shows only when it flies.

migration: Resident and partly nomadic in South Africa, present all year but only where there is water and sandbanks to nest in. In the Lowveld it is scarce and patchy, mostly along the larger rivers and dams. In the north and east of South Africa it breeds over a long season, with more records in the dry winter and spring.
size: 12 cm: smaller than a Barn Swallow, about the size of a sparrow but slimmer.
keys: Plain mousy brown upperparts, no gloss, no white rump
Brown throat and breast fading to a white belly (a rarer form is brown below all over)
Short, square or barely notched tail, no streamers
Fluttering, jerky flight low over water; juvenile has buff tips to the feathers

confuse.how: Glossy blue-black above, red throat, long tail streamers, and a more dashing flight.
Blackish with a big white rump patch and scythe-shaped wings; never perches on reeds or wires.

voice: A weak, high twittering given almost constantly in flight, becoming a soft murmur at the roost; harsh alarm note.
behaviour: Gregarious: small flocks flutter low over rivers and dams catching midges and other insects, often with other swallows and swifts. They nest in colonies, digging tunnels 30-80 cm long into vertical sandbanks, and roost together in reedbeds at night.
memo: A little brown swallow with a brown throat, fluttering over the river.

migration: A rare, erratic nomad that turns up on muddy, vegetated pans and dam edges when rain creates good wetlands. In southern Africa it is most numerous from December to March, and Kruger is the most reliable place in South Africa to find it, especially in wet years. Breeding mainly September to March.
size: 23-28 cm: about the size of a blackbird, but plumper, with a long, slightly drooping bill.
keys: Bold white 'spectacles' around the eye that run back as a short stripe behind it
Long bill drooping at the tip, and a white strap curving from the breast up over the shoulder
Female brighter than the male: dark rufous neck and head, dark bronze-green back
Male (and juvenile) paler and greyer, with buff-spotted wings and golden 'braces' on the back
voice: Usually silent; in display the female gives a series of soft, owl-like hoots.
behaviour: Sex roles are reversed: the larger, brighter female courts the males and may mate with 2-4 in a season, while each male incubates the eggs and raises the chicks alone. Shy and mostly active at dawn and dusk, it creeps along the edge of reeds and sedges. When flushed it flies off like a rail, legs dangling.
memo: Painted lady, house-husband: she wears the colours, he does the babysitting.

migration: An intra-African migrant that tracks water. Most birds arrive with the summer rains from about November and breed from November to April on flooded pans. In the dry season most move away, some ringed birds reaching beyond the equator over 3,000 km away, while a few gather on permanent dams.
size: 56-76 cm: a big duck, much larger than a White-faced Whistling Duck, and the male is far bigger than the female.
keys: White head and neck speckled black, clean white breast and belly
Glossy blue-black back and wings with green and bronze sheen
Male has a large black fleshy knob on top of the bill, largest in the breeding season; female lacks it
Juvenile brown above and buffy below, with a dark line through the eye

confuse.how: Larger and longer-legged, with a red bill and bare red face and a black, not speckled, head.
Smaller and upright, with a white face, black hind neck, chestnut breast and barred flanks.

voice: Mostly silent. Gives a low croak when flushed, and whistles, hisses and grunts during displays in the breeding season.
behaviour: Often perches in dead trees and nests in tree holes, or even in old Hamerkop nests. Males can hold small harems of females in good years.
memo: The duck with a bump: speckled head, black knob, nests up a tree.

migration: Altitudinal migrant: breeds in summer in the highveld and escarpment grasslands, then drops down to the warmer Lowveld for the cold months. Arrives around April-May and leaves by September, when it returns uphill to breed (laying August to November).
size: 12-13 cm: about the size of a House Sparrow, but rounder and shorter-tailed.
keys: Male: black head, white half-collar on the neck sides and a rich orange-chestnut breast
Black back and wings with a white wing patch, white rump
Female: brown and streaky, with a buff-orange breast and a smaller white wing patch
Almost always perched on the very top of a grass stem or low bush in open grassland

confuse.how: Much bigger (about 21 cm), lives on rocky outcrops, and the male has a chestnut belly and white shoulder, with no white collar or rump.

voice: A hard “tsak-tsak”, often with a whistled “wheet”, like two small stones knocked together; the song is a short, scratchy warble.
behaviour: Sits upright on a high perch, flicking its wings and tail, then drops to the ground to grab an insect and returns to a perch. Pairs are strongly bonded and are rarely far apart, even in winter.
memo: A little black-headed bird with an orange chest on every grass top: winter has come down from the mountains.

migration: Resident and territorial along rivers, dams and seasonal pans. Some birds move to new wetlands during the rains, and in the dry season they gather where water remains. In southern Africa it can breed at almost any time of year.
size: 50-56 cm: about the size of a crow, but with longer legs. A brown heron-like bird with a short neck.
keys: All dull brown, with a faint purple gloss on the back
Thick crest projecting backwards, balancing the bill: the head looks like a hammer
Heavy, flattened black bill, slightly hooked; blackish legs
In flight looks like a small stork with broad rounded wings and the neck slightly bent

confuse.how: Has a long down-curved bill, no crest and a metallic wing sheen. It is loud in flight.
Smaller and greyer, with a black cap, yellow-orange legs and a long pointed bill.

voice: Usually silent alone, apart from a sharp “nyip” or “kek” in flight. Groups get noisy with cackles and a nasal “yip-purr”, and it is said to call loudly before rain.
behaviour: It builds a huge domed nest of sticks and mud, often more than 1.5 m across and able to hold a man's weight, and pairs build several a year even without breeding. Owls, genets and snakes take over these nests. It hunts frogs and fish in the shallows, shuffling a foot or flicking open its wings to flush prey, and sometimes fishes from a hippo's back.
memo: Hammer-head with a mansion: a small brown bird in the biggest nest in the bush.

migration: Resident and very common all year. Mostly sedentary, though some southern African birds make local moves with rainfall. Breeds in every month, with a peak from August to December.
size: About 25-27 cm: smaller and slimmer than a Ring-necked Dove, a little bigger than a blackbird, with a long tail.
keys: Pinkish-brown head and breast with a band of black-and-rufous chequered speckles across the upper breast (no black collar)
Rufous-brown back and a bluish-grey patch on the wing, obvious in flight
Long tail with white outer corners, red legs
Juvenile duller, with no breast speckles

confuse.how: Larger and greyer, with a clear black half-collar on the hindneck and no speckled breast band.
Much larger and darker, with a black half-collar, a red eye-ring and a pinkish-grey head.
Smaller and dumpier, with glossy green wing spots, chestnut wings in flight and a falling 'du-du-du' call.

voice: A soft, bubbling, rising and falling chuckle, 'croo-doo-doo-doo-doo', that gives the bird its name: it sounds like quiet laughter.
behaviour: Feeds on the ground, often tame around camps and lodges, and gathers in numbers to drink at waterholes. In display the male climbs steeply on clapping wings, then glides down with wings and tail spread.
memo: Small pink dove with a speckled necklace that softly laughs.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld and one of its commonest birds. It does not migrate, but in the dry season it gathers at waterholes and roosts, sometimes in flocks of a hundred or more. Breeds all year round.
size: 25-26 cm: a little smaller than a feral pigeon, about the size of a Eurasian Collared Dove.
keys: Plain grey-brown dove, paler pinkish-grey on the breast, with no spots
Black half-collar on the back of the neck, edged pale
Dark eye with no red ring, black bill
In flight, white corners and tips to the tail; juvenile duller and without the collar

confuse.how: Bigger (about 30 cm) and darker, with a red eye-ring around a yellowish-red eye, a deeper pinkish breast and no white in the tail.
Smaller, with no black collar, a pinkish neck and breast spotted with rufous-and-black, and blue-grey panels in the wing.

voice: A loud, harsh, three-note croon repeated 10 to 40 times without pause, usually written as “work harder, work harder”; also a raspy snarl when landing.
behaviour: Walks on the ground bobbing its head as it picks up seeds, then bursts away with loudly clattering wings. In display the male climbs steeply, then spirals down with wings and tail spread, showing the white tail corners.
memo: Plain dove, black collar, dark eye, and “work harder!” all day long.

migration: Resident all year, especially in tall riverine trees along the Lowveld rivers. It only makes small local moves. Can breed in any month, with a peak from September to January.
size: About 30 cm: the largest ring-necked dove in Africa, clearly bigger and heavier than a Laughing Dove, almost the size of a feral pigeon.
keys: Black half-collar on the nape, edged with a thin pale line
Dark red-orange eye surrounded by a bare purplish-red eye-ring
Pale grey forehead and crown, rich wine-pink head and breast, dark grey-brown back
Tail dark above with no white corners: grey tips, shown when it lands

confuse.how: Smaller and paler, with a dark eye and no red eye-ring, a white lower belly and white tail corners in flight; calls “work harder”.
Much smaller, with no black collar but a rusty breast speckled black, and blue-grey wing patches.

voice: A deep, mellow “coo-coo, co-kuk-coo-coo”, usually rendered in South Africa as “I am a red-eyed dove”.
behaviour: Spends more time up in trees than other doves, often in shady riverine woodland near water, and gathers at water in the early morning and evening. The male claps his wings as he climbs, then glides down with tail fanned; in courtship he bows repeatedly, puffing out his neck to show off the collar.
memo: Big dark dove, red eye, black collar: “I am a red-eyed dove”.

migration: Resident all year, in territorial pairs, and sedentary. Often joins mixed-species bird parties in winter. Breeds mainly September to January (laying August to March).
size: 10-12 cm: smaller than a sparrow, and looks tailless.
keys: Almost no tail: a round little body like a ball
Long, slightly curved blackish bill
Grey-brown upperparts, cinnamon-buff underparts and whitish throat
Pale eyebrow and dark line through the eye; sexes alike

confuse.how: Has a normal tail, greenish-yellow tones and a short, fine bill; a summer visitor.
Even smaller, with a tiny conical bill and a visible tail, grey above and buff below, moving in small groups.

voice: A loud, high, repeated 'tree-rrit, tree-rrit' and a dry, rolling 'prrit' contact call.
behaviour: Works methodically up a bush or tree from the bottom to the top, gleaning insects from twigs and bark, then flies with a bouncy flight to the base of the next tree. Its nest is a hanging bag of grass and spider web, camouflaged with leaves and bark, often parasitised by Klaas's Cuckoo.
memo: A tailless ball with a long bill, climbing each bush from bottom to top.

migration: Resident on dams and pans, but quick to move into seasonally flooded pans after rain and to colonise new dams. Can breed in any month in southern Africa, with local peaks depending on water levels.
size: 23-29 cm: a small, round diving bird, smaller than a duck, about the size of a moorhen with a shorter neck.
keys: Small, dumpy, almost tailless with a fluffy rear end, floating like a cork
Breeding: dark brown-black above with chestnut cheeks and neck and a pale yellowish spot at the base of the bill
Non-breeding: dull brown above, buff-grey below, the chestnut and gape spot faded
Chicks are striped black and white on the head

confuse.how: Larger, slate-black with a red shield and yellow-tipped bill, white flank line and flicks a white undertail; swims with jerky head bobs rather than diving.

voice: A loud, high whinnying trill, “wee-wee-wee-wee”, often given in duet by the pair; compared to a horse's whinny.
behaviour: Dives at the slightest alarm and resurfaces far away, or hides among vegetation. Builds a floating nest of water plants and covers the eggs with weed when it leaves. The chicks swim within hours of hatching and often ride on a parent's back.
memo: A floating cork with chestnut cheeks that whinnies like a tiny horse, then vanishes underwater.

migration: The southern African population breeds in mountain cliffs (the nearby Drakensberg escarpment is the closest breeding area). It arrives around August, breeds from August to January and leaves around May, though some stay all winter. Over the Lowveld it is only an occasional visitor, seen foraging high overhead. European birds also winter in southern Africa.
size: 20-22 cm, wingspan 54-60 cm: much bigger than a swallow, the largest swift in the region.
keys: Huge swift, flying fast and high, with long scythe-shaped wings
Brown above and below with a white belly patch
White throat separated from the belly by a brown breast band
Slightly forked tail; slow, powerful wingbeats for a swift

confuse.how: Smaller and all dark below, with only a small pale throat and no white belly.
Much smaller and slender, with a white rump, a deeply forked tail and a dark belly.
Much smaller, with a fluttering flight and an all-pale belly with no breast band.

voice: A loud, shrill trill that speeds up then slows down, given mainly near the colonies.
behaviour: Spends almost its whole life in the air: it feeds, drinks and even sleeps on the wing. Tracked European birds stayed airborne for more than 200 days without landing. It forages very high, often with other swifts and swallows.
memo: A giant swift with a white belly, too high and too fast to stop.

migration: Sedentary all year in pairs that hold the same territory. Breeds September to March, peaking October to December, when males are at their most vocal and do display flights; young stay with the parents for at least five months.
size: 17-20 cm: a bit smaller than a blackbird, slim, with a long, graduated tail.
keys: Brown central crown bordered by two black stripes, with a broad white-buff eyebrow and black line through the eye
Bright rufous-chestnut wings, plain grey-brown back
Long blackish tail with white tips, obvious when fanned
Juvenile duller, with a horn-coloured bill

confuse.how: Larger, with a solid black crown above the white eyebrow (beware: the juvenile Black-crowned has a brown crown, but is bigger and heavier-billed).

voice: In display flight the male rattles its wings (“prrrp-prrrp”) as it rises above the bush, then glides down with fanned tail giving a falling series of about 15 whistled “pa-reeu” notes.
behaviour: Shy and hard to see: pairs skulk low in thickets and hop on the ground, picking insects from the base of grass and shrubs. It is easiest to notice in summer when the male shoots up above the bushes in his rattling, whistling display flight.
memo: Brown cap in black brackets, chestnut wings, and a rattle then a falling whistle over the bush.

migration: Resident and sedentary all year in the Lowveld, in territorial pairs. The breeding season is long, covering most of spring and summer.
size: 19-22 cm: about the size of a blackbird, with a longer tail.
keys: Solid black crown and black stripe through the eye, separated by a broad white eyebrow
Bright chestnut wings contrasting with a pale brown back and pale grey underparts
Black tail with white tips, obvious when the bird flies off low
Stout black bill; juvenile has a brownish crown and a pale bill

confuse.how: Smaller, with a brown (not black) crown and a buff eyebrow edged with black; the Black-crowned's cap is solid black above a white eyebrow.

voice: A loud, rich series of descending whistles, often answered by its mate with a churring rattle.
behaviour: Shy and skulking, it forages mostly on the ground under bushes, then flies low to the next thicket. In display the male rises steeply in a switchback flight over the bush, singing its whistled song as it drops.
memo: Black cap, white eyebrow, chestnut wings: the whistling shrike of the thickets.

migration: Resident all year in dense thickets, especially riverine bush and wooded drainage lines. No seasonal movements are known. Lays mainly October to December, in a flimsy cup nest hidden in a thorny tree or a creeper tangle.
size: 18-19 cm: about the size of a bulbul.
keys: Bright scarlet throat bordered by a broad black breast band (gorget)
Olive-green upperparts and tail, yellow-green to orange-yellow belly
Yellow forehead and eyebrow stripe
Female similar to male; juvenile mostly plain greenish-yellow, without the bold red and black

confuse.how: Grey head, yellow throat and an orange wash on the breast, with no red throat and no black band; often sits more in the open in the canopy.
Much bigger (about 26 cm), with a grey head, a heavy hooked black bill and a pale eye, and no red throat.

voice: A loud, ringing, popping whistle, “kong-kong-koit” or “kon-koit”, which gave it its Afrikaans name “Konkoit”; the mate often answers in duet.
behaviour: Heard far more often than seen: it calls from deep inside tangled thickets and almost never shows itself, even when you are only a few metres away. Gleans insects such as beetles, caterpillars and mantids from leaves in the cover.
memo: “Kong-kong-koit!” from the thicket: four colours you'll hear a hundred times before you see them once.

migration: Resident: adults hold large territories all year and patrol them for hours a day. Young birds disperse widely once independent. It can breed in any month, with a peak from January to April in southern Africa.
size: 55-70 cm long with a wingspan of about 1.7-1.9 m: an eagle much bigger than a Yellow-billed Kite, but with an almost absent tail.
keys: Black eagle with a chestnut back and tail, and a bright red face and red legs
In flight: very long wings and a tiny tail, so the red feet stick out past the tail
Underwing white with black edges: a broad black trailing edge in the male, a narrow one in the female
Juvenile: plain brown with a greenish-blue face and a slightly longer tail; adult plumage takes about 7-8 years

confuse.how: Like the brown juvenile Bateleur, but has a long tail, a big round owl-like head with yellow eyes and pale, unbarred flight feathers from below.
Brown with a normal-length tail and fully feathered legs, and flies on flat wings without the Bateleur's rocking.

voice: Usually silent; the main call is a loud, far-carrying “schaaaa-aw”, with barking “kow-aw” notes.
behaviour: Glides low over the bush for hours with wings held in a strong V, rocking from side to side like a tightrope walker, which gave it its French name meaning “street acrobat”. It often sunbathes with wings spread wide, and it is quick to find carcasses and roadkill.
memo: The tailless tightrope walker: a black-and-red eagle rocking low over the bush.

migration: Most birds are intra-African migrants that breed here in summer: they arrive from September-October and leave in April, wintering further north. A few stay through winter in the Lowveld, where birds from higher, colder areas also come down. Breeds October to December.
size: 17-18 cm without the streamers, about the size of a sparrow; the male's tail streamers can double its total length.
keys: Bright rufous-chestnut back and very long rufous tail (male has streamers 2-3 times the body length)
Glossy blue-black head with a small crest and a bright cobalt-blue eye-ring and bill
Grey underparts; white wing bar in some males
Female and juvenile: same rufous back and dark head but short tail, duller with a thinner eye-ring

confuse.how: The male also has a chestnut back, but a grey crown with a black mask, pale pinkish underparts, a hooked bill and a black-and-white tail.

voice: A loud, rippling “twee-twee-twee-twee” song, repeated almost non-stop by the male, and a harsh scolding “zweet-zwayt” contact call that often gives it away.
behaviour: Restless and conspicuous, flitting through the mid-canopy and fanning its tail, sallying out to snap flying insects. The tiny cup nest, bound with spider web and decorated with lichen, often has a trailing “tail” of web hanging below; the male with his long streamers takes turns incubating.
memo: A flash of chestnut ribbon and a blue eye-ring: summer's long-tailed flycatcher.

migration: Resident all year wherever there are rocky outcrops, cliffs or boulder-strewn hills and riverbeds. Only birds high up (Highveld, Drakensberg) come down lower in winter. Breeds August to December, peaking September to November.
size: 19-21 cm: slightly smaller than a blackbird, a large, upright chat.
keys: Male: glossy black head, breast and back with a bright chestnut-orange belly, vent and rump
White shoulder patch on the male, separated from the chestnut belly by a thin white line
Female: dark grey instead of black, chestnut only on the lower belly and vent, no white shoulder
Slowly raises the tail over its back and fans it out; juvenile like a duller female

confuse.how: All black with no chestnut belly or rump and no white shoulder; perches in trees, not on rocks.
Orange underparts too, but a bold white eyebrow on a black face and an olive-brown back; skulks in thickets, not on rocks.

voice: Both sexes sing loud, rich, melodious phrases, often as a duet, mixed with a faster song that mimics more than 30 other species, which gives it its name.
behaviour: A rock lover that hops from boulder to boulder rather than walking. It often takes over the mud nests of striped swallows, sometimes evicting the swallows while they are still breeding, and nests under overhangs, bridges and culverts. Becomes very tame around farms, camps and picnic sites.
memo: Black on top, chestnut below, on a rock: the cliff chat that copies everyone.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, in territorial pairs. In the dry season it forms small groups that move about locally in search of food. Breeding starts with the first rains (September to March, peaking October to December).
size: 48-60 cm including the bill. Much bigger than a blackbird, about the size of a magpie, with a huge yellow bill.
keys: Big bright yellow, curved bill with a small casque (longer in the male, reaching the tip; shorter in the female)
Black back with the wings spangled white, white belly
Bare pink skin around the eye and on the throat, yellow eye
Juvenile: duller yellow bill blotched brown, grey iris

confuse.how: Smaller, with a red, not yellow, bill. Same black-and-white spotted plumage.
Dull grey-brown plumage, no pure white. Dark bill (creamy white at the base in the male).

voice: A series of deep, clucking “tok-tok-tok” notes that speed up, lower than the other small hornbills. The pair calls in duet, heads bowed and wings half open.
behaviour: Feeds mostly on the ground, turning over debris and hopping heavily after insects. At the nest the female walls herself into a tree hole with droppings and debris, leaving just a slit through which the male feeds her. While sealed in, she moults all her flight feathers.
memo: The “flying banana”: a huge yellow bill on a pied bird.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld. Outside the breeding season it forms small flocks that wander locally. Laying follows good summer rains, from September to March, peaking October to December.
size: About 35-42 cm including the bill: smaller and slimmer than the Southern Yellow-billed Hornbill, about the size of a turtle dove with a long tail and a long bill.
keys: Long, slender, curved red bill with no casque (the male's is longer, with more black at the base of the lower mandible)
Yellow eye set in pale pinkish skin
Pied plumage: grey-brown back with wing coverts spotted white, white face and underparts, dark streak from the ear down the side of the neck

confuse.how: Larger, with a heavy yellow bill and the same pied, white-spotted plumage.
Dull grey-brown with no white-spotted wings and a dark bill (creamy at the base in the male); spends more time in trees than on the ground.

voice: An accelerating series of "kuk-kuk-kuk" notes ending in doubled "kuk-we, kuk-we", given by pairs bowing their heads but, unlike its relatives, without raising the wings.
behaviour: Feeds mostly on the ground, picking beetles, termites and other insects from the soil and dung. When nesting, the female is sealed into a tree hole with her own droppings, leaving a narrow slit through which the male feeds her and the chicks.
memo: Red bill, yellow eye, pecking on the ground: the bush's smallest pied hornbill.

migration: Resident but very wide-ranging: pairs hold huge territories and tracked birds have travelled hundreds of kilometres from the nest, so it is seen at Pidwa irregularly in any month. In southern Africa eggs are laid mainly from May to January, in a big stick nest on top of an acacia.
size: 95-115 cm tall, wingspan 2.5-2.9 m: the largest vulture in Kruger, clearly bigger and heavier-billed than the White-backed Vultures around it.
keys: Bare red to pink head with fleshy folds of skin (the 'lappets') hanging on the sides of the face and neck
Massive, deep yellowish bill, much heavier than other vultures'
Blackish plumage contrasting with white, fluffy thighs and pale streaked underparts; stands very upright
Juvenile all dark brown with a duller head; adult plumage takes about 6 years

confuse.how: Smaller, with a pale, flat-topped white head, a pink-and-blue bill and a white belly, but no red folded skin on the face.
Smaller and browner, with a dark, slim bill and a pale, almost bald dark-grey head and neck; the common vulture in big groups at carcasses.
Much smaller, with a thin, slender bill and a pink face under a downy 'hood'.

voice: Almost always silent; a subordinate bird at a carcass may give a short shriek or yelp.
behaviour: The 'opener' of the carcass: its huge bill tears through tough hide that smaller vultures cannot open, and other vultures usually give way to it. It often arrives late and feeds at the edge of the scrum on skin, tendons and ligaments. Usually alone or in pairs, never in big flocks.
memo: The giant with a red, wrinkled face: when it lands, the other vultures step aside.

migration: Sedentary and territorial all year, flying only short distances; pairs keep the same territory with several roosting holes. Can breed almost all year, but egg-laying peaks from September to December, with up to four broods a season.
size: 22-24 cm: about the size of a Common Starling or a blackbird, but stockier with a heavy bill.
keys: Yellow face speckled with red, and a shaggy black crest
Broad black breast band speckled white, below a yellow-and-red throat area
Yellow belly with red streaks, bright yellow rump
Black back and wings spotted white, stout pale horn-yellow bill; female slightly paler with less red

confuse.how: Bright red face and throat bordered by a black collar, plain greyish-brown back, no crest and no red-speckled yellow face.
Smaller and black-and-white with a red forehead and black throat; no yellow belly or crest.

voice: A long, sustained, even trill that can go on for 30 seconds or more, likened to an alarm clock ringing with the bell removed; the alarm is a loud rattle.
behaviour: Spends much of its time hopping heavily on the ground, picking up termites, beetles and snails, and is a weak flier. It fiercely defends its tree-hole nest and will evict other hole-nesters, and has been recorded killing snakes. Its nest is parasitised by the Lesser Honeyguide.
memo: The 'fruit salad' barbet with a punk crest and an alarm clock that never stops ringing.

migration: Resident, but makes local, sometimes regional, movements to follow fruiting trees, especially wild figs; numbers in one place can change quickly. Breeds mainly August to January in southern Africa.
size: 25-30 cm: about the size of a Laughing Dove, but plumper and shorter-tailed.
keys: Bright yellowish-green to greyish-green plumage that vanishes among leaves
Coral-red bill base and cere with a pale whitish tip, red feet
Mauve-maroon patch on the shoulder, yellow edges to the wing feathers and yellow thighs
Juvenile duller, with an olive (not mauve) shoulder

confuse.how: Also green and clambering in fruiting trees, but has a brown head, a heavy hooked grey bill, yellow underwings in flight and gives shrill screeches.

voice: A strange, far-carrying song of liquid, flowing whistles (“thweeeloo, thweeeoo”) followed by clicks and low, frog-like growls.
behaviour: Clambers through the canopy like a parrot, even hanging upside down and flapping to reach figs at the tips of branches, and rarely comes to the ground. Small groups sit motionless in a fruiting sycamore fig and are only noticed when they burst out in fast, direct flight.
memo: A green parrot-like pigeon hiding in the figs: look for the red bill and feet.

migration: Sedentary: pairs or single birds hold the same territory all year. Lays from August to April, mostly in the spring and summer rains, in a hole it digs in a dead branch.
size: About 17 cm: a little smaller than a Dark-capped Bulbul but much stockier, with a big head and a heavy bill.
keys: Bright red forehead patch on a black-and-white striped head, with a yellow-then-white eyebrow
Narrow black bib on a whitish underside (sometimes faintly spotted)
Blackish back and wings streaked and spotted lemon-yellow; yellow rump
Heavy black bill. Sexes alike; juvenile has no red forehead

confuse.how: Much smaller (about 11 cm), with a yellow, not red, forehead, no black bib and an endless 'tink-tink-tink' call.
Bigger, with the whole face and throat bright red framed by a broad black collar, and a plain brown back.

voice: A drawn-out nasal 'nehh' repeated in series, and a slow series of low hoots; pairs call to keep in contact.
behaviour: Restless but discreet, hopping through acacias and bushes and even hanging upside down to reach fruit, mistletoe berries, insects and aloe nectar. Both partners dig the nest chamber in the underside of a dead branch, and it roosts alone in tree holes or old swallow and weaver nests.
memo: A pied barbet with a red forehead and a black bib, honking through the thorn trees.

migration: Sedentary: adults live in territorial pairs that stay put all year, while immatures wander more widely. Greater Kruger holds South Africa's largest population. In South Africa it lays its single egg in winter (about May to August) on a stick nest on top of a tree, often an acacia or a baobab.
size: 72-85 cm, wingspan about 2.1-2.3 m: a medium-sized vulture, smaller than a White-backed Vulture.
keys: Pale, angular head with a white downy crown and pink face, orange-red bill with a blue base
Dark breast band contrasting with a white belly and white 'trousers'
In flight, the white belly and a white line along the underwing coverts stand out against the black wings
Female has white inner secondaries (a white panel on the wing), the male's are grey; juvenile mostly dark brown

confuse.how: Much larger, with a bare red head and neck folds, a huge bill and streaked white thighs, no clean white belly.
Bigger and plain brown with a dark bill and greyish neck; in flight it shows a white underwing bar on brown body, not a white belly.
Smaller and all dark brown, with a thin, slender bill and a pink face; useful to compare with the dark juvenile White-headed.

voice: Almost always silent; a shrill chattering only when squabbling over food at a carcass.
behaviour: Usually seen alone or in pairs, and often the first vulture to land at a carcass before the big flocks arrive and push it aside. It also kills prey itself, such as mongooses, monitor lizards and hares, and steals food from other birds. It is the only vulture whose sexes differ in plumage, and the female is the larger one.
memo: The punk with a white crest and a pink-orange bill: first to the carcass, and the female wears the white wing patches.

migration: Resident all year in territorial groups that stay in the same patch of thicket; it is a weak flier and hardly disperses. It can breed in almost any month, but mostly in the rainy season.
size: 22-25 cm: about the size of a blackbird, but scruffier and longer-tailed.
keys: Drab grey-brown bird, always in a noisy group low in thickets
Throat and breast streaked with small white arrowhead-shaped tips
Striking eye: yellow-orange iris ringed with red
Sexes alike; juvenile has a brown eye and less arrow-marked breast
voice: A loud, nasal, accelerating 'ra-ra-ra-ra-ra' or 'gra-gra-gra', often given by the whole group at once and sounding like raucous laughter.
behaviour: Lives in groups of 3 to 15 (usually about six) that forage on the ground, flicking leaves for insects, spiders and small lizards. They breed cooperatively: the whole group helps build the nest, incubate and feed the chicks. It is the main host of Levaillant's Cuckoo, whose chick mimics the babblers' begging call to be fed.
memo: A gang of brown laughing birds with fiery eyes in the thicket.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, alone or in pairs that defend a territory all year. It sings most in spring and early summer, and breeds in the warm months (roughly September to January), building a cup nest on a mud base.
size: 21-23 cm: the size of a blackbird.
keys: Bright orange bill and orange eye-ring
White throat with two black streaks (malar stripes) on the sides
Grey head, back and breast, with orange-washed flanks and a whitish belly
Sexes alike; juvenile spotted below with a duller bill

confuse.how: Stands more upright, has a dark bill, a white face with bold black bars, and a heavily black-spotted white breast with no orange.

voice: A loud, ringing whistle “peet-peeoo”, often at dusk, and a mellow song of trills and whistles at dawn.
behaviour: Hops on the ground under bushes and in gardens, stopping upright to watch, and when alarmed it flicks its tail nervously and flies quickly into cover.
memo: The grey thrush with an orange bill and a black-streaked white throat.

migration: Mainly sedentary in the Lowveld, living in pairs in open woodland. Oiseaux.net notes that numbers in Kruger rise from December to February, which suggests some local movement. Breeds in spring and summer, with most nests from September to November.
size: 20-24 cm: about the size of a blackbird, but upright, with a short tail and fairly long legs.
keys: Plain grey-brown upperparts and white underparts covered in bold black spots
White face with strong black vertical bars below and behind the eye, like war paint
Stands very upright on open ground; in flight a big buff-orange wing panel and a black-and-white underwing show
Juvenile browner, spotted above and buffier below

confuse.how: Has a bright orange bill, orange flanks and a white throat with black streaks at the sides, and no spotted breast or black face bars.

voice: A rhythmic “tsi-tsi-tsi-rufa”, echoed by its Setswana-derived species name litsitsirupa. The song is made of short phrases of harsh whistles and clicks, and it often sings at dawn, after dark and before storms.
behaviour: It hops or runs quickly over bare ground, stops bolt upright to scan, then scratches through leaf litter, which gives it its name. It has an odd habit of flicking one wing at a time. Tame around camps and lawns, but pairs fiercely defend their nest, even against people.
memo: A spotted vest, a war-painted face and one wing flicking: the thrush that scrapes the ground.

migration: Locally nomadic in southern Africa: it moves around in response to good rainfall and grass growth, and has been recorded migrating at night in northern South Africa. In the Lowveld it is easiest to find in summer, when it breeds in the rainy season; in dry years and in winter it can be very scarce.
size: 14-16 cm: smaller than a sparrow-sized francolin chick, roughly a plump House Sparrow with almost no tail.
keys: Tiny, round, almost tail-less ground bird, sandy-brown and streaked above
Rufous-orange breast with black spots or crescents on the sides, plain buff face
In flight: low, whirring and short, with pale wing coverts contrasting with darker flight feathers
Female slightly larger and brighter than the male; juvenile more spotted below

confuse.how: Much bigger (about 25 cm) with a proper tail; the male has a plain orange-buff head and the female a striped face, and it walks in pairs rather than whirring up from your feet.

voice: The female gives a deep, far-carrying, ventriloquial “hoom-hoom-hoom”, often compared to a distant foghorn or a lowing cow, mostly at dawn and dusk.
behaviour: Almost impossible to see on the ground: it creeps under grass and freezes, then bursts up almost at your feet, flies a few metres low and drops back into cover, and rarely flushes twice. Roles are reversed: the female courts, calls and defends the territory, and can mate with several males, who incubate the eggs and raise the chicks alone.
memo: A tail-less brown ball that explodes from the grass, where Mum sings and Dad babysits.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, alone or in pairs. Only local movements linked to the rains and water; several may gather at waterholes in the dry season. Builds a flimsy stick nest low in a bush or tree.
size: 20 cm: a small, plump dove, smaller than a Laughing Dove.
keys: Two rows of iridescent emerald-green spots on the folded wing (can look dark in poor light)
Two broad dark bars across the pale lower back and rump, obvious when it flies off
Bright chestnut underwings and flight feathers flashing in flight
Grey-blue crown, pinkish-mauve breast, blackish bill with a dull red base; sexes alike, juvenile duller with buff fringes

confuse.how: Bigger and longer-tailed, pinkish head and a breast band speckled black, blue-grey on the wing but no green spots, back bars or chestnut wings.
Larger and plain grey-brown with a black half-collar on the hind neck; white (not chestnut) in the tail and wings in flight.

voice: A long, mournful cooing: two soft long coos, then a slow series of coos that descend and speed up before fading out in a rapid tumble, one of the classic background sounds of the bushveld. Sometimes heard as “My mother is dead… dead… another… brother is dead, oh boohoohohoho!”
behaviour: Walks quietly on bare ground under bushes, picking up small seeds, and often sits on sandy tracks. When flushed it bursts up with a flash of chestnut wings and dark back bars, flying fast and low to land a short distance away.
memo: Small dove, green jewels on the wing, chestnut flash and a sad falling coo.

migration: Resident in the Greater Kruger, making only local, partly rain-related movements. Breeds from October to February, mainly November to January, in a tree hole or a crevice.
size: 25-29 cm including the long bill: a little bigger than a starling, about the size of a Mistle Thrush.
keys: Rich cinnamon-orange head, breast and back
Long fan-shaped crest with black tips, raised in alarm or excitement and folded flat when feeding
Black-and-white barred wings and tail, which flash in a floppy, butterfly-like flight
Long, thin, slightly down-curved bill; female a little duller, juvenile duller with a shorter crest
voice: A soft, deep “hoop-hoop” or “hoop-hoop-hoop”, repeated in series, from which the bird gets its name.
behaviour: Walks over bare ground and short grass, probing the soil for grubs, beetles and larvae, and beats large prey on the ground before swallowing. During breeding, the female and chicks give off a foul-smelling secretion from the preen gland, and the chicks can squirt droppings at intruders to keep predators away.
memo: A cinnamon punk with a zebra-striped cape that says its own name: “hoop-hoop”.

migration: Sedentary resident in the Lowveld, usually in pairs or family parties, sometimes in small flocks mixed with other seedeaters in the dry season. Breeds year-round, with a laying peak around January, about two months after the heavy rains.
size: 12-13 cm: smaller than a sparrow, slender, with a long pointed tail.
keys: Powder-blue face, breast and flanks, with plain light brown crown and back
Blue rump and long blue tail, obvious when it flies off
Small pinkish-grey conical bill
Female: blue paler and limited to the face and breast, with a buffy or whitish belly; juvenile duller still

confuse.how: Also tiny and in flocks, but brown and finely barred, with a red bill and red eye-stripe, no blue at all.

voice: A thin, high “tsee-tsee” or “seee-seee”, repeated as it moves through low bushes or when flushed.
behaviour: Feeds on grass seeds on or near the ground, flitting up to the nearest bush when disturbed. It often builds its ball-shaped grass nest right next to a paper wasp nest in a thorn tree, possibly using the wasps as a sign that aggressive tree ants are absent.
memo: A little flake of sky hopping in the grass: powder blue below, brown on top.

migration: Resident and sedentary in the Lowveld, where small groups wander locally after fruiting trees. Eggs are laid from about June to February, mostly September to November.
size: 29-37 cm, about half of it tail: a dove-sized body behind a very long, stiff tail.
keys: Bare red mask around the eye and red base to the bill
Crested head and breast pale cinnamon, upperparts and long tail plain blue-grey, belly whitish
Pale grey rump visible in flight; no speckling or barring
Sexes alike; juvenile has no crest and a greenish face mask

confuse.how: Dull mouse-brown all over with no red on the face, a black upper and pinkish lower bill, and a weaker, fluttering flight.

voice: A clear whistled “tree-ree-ree”, often repeated, given in flight and when perched, which keeps the group together.
behaviour: Moves in tight groups of about 3-10 that fly fast, straight and low from bush to bush in single file, calling as they go. Members preen each other and roost huddled together at night. It eats mainly fruit (figs, shepherd's-tree, jackal-berry), plus flowers, nectar and leaves.
memo: Blue-grey with a long tail and a red mask, whistling “tree-ree-ree” as the group dashes past.

migration: Resident all year around the Lowveld's dams, pans and riverbanks, in territorial pairs. It makes only local moves with the rains: in very wet years birds spread out, and they come back to permanent water when it is dry. Eggs can be laid in any month, peaking July to October.
size: 28-31 cm: a little bigger than a blackbird, upright on long black legs.
keys: Bold black, white and grey: white cap and forehead down to the eye, black face, throat and breast
Grey 'cape' on the wings and back, contrasting with a white nape and belly
Dark red eye, black bill and legs. In flight: black flight feathers, white tail with a black tip, and a spur at the wrist
Juvenile: same pattern but duller, with beige-edged feathers above giving a mottled look

confuse.how: Brown, not black-and-grey, with a black cap ringed by a white halo and red legs. Prefers dry, short grass rather than water's edge.
Brownish with yellow facial wattles and yellow legs, no black-and-white pattern.

voice: Its name says it all: a loud, metallic “tink-tink-tink”, like a hammer striking an anvil, speeding up into a frantic alarm when anything comes near.
behaviour: Fearless nest guard: the pair takes turns, one on the eggs while the other keeps watch, and they dive-bomb intruders far bigger than themselves, from harrier-hawks and snakes to monitor lizards, calling loudly. Elephants get wing-spreading and frantic calling until they move away from the nest.
memo: The blacksmith of the dam: grey cape, white cap, and a “tink-tink” hammered on an anvil.

migration: Resident and largely sedentary, though it moves locally when the grass grows too tall in the rains and gathers on short or freshly burnt ground. Breeds all year, with a peak from August to December, before the rains.
size: About 30 cm: roughly the size of a feral pigeon, but with long red legs.
keys: Black cap ringed by a white halo, like a crown
Plain brown head, neck and breast, white belly, with a blackish band at the lower edge of the breast
Red legs and a red bill with a black tip; yellow eye
In flight, a white wing bar and a white tail with a black band. Juvenile duller, with yellowish legs and no red on the bill

confuse.how: Boldly black, white and grey with a white cap, black legs and no brown at all.
Has hanging yellow wattles at the bill base, yellow legs and a white forehead, with no black-and-white crown ring.

voice: Noisy and conspicuous: a series of harsh, scratchy “kreep” or “kirre” notes, sharper and faster when alarmed.
behaviour: Feeds in loose, regularly spaced groups on very short or burnt grass, running, stopping and pecking; termites make up most of its diet. Near the nest the pair dive-bombs intruders with loud calls, and one parent does a distraction display while the chicks hide.
memo: A brown plover wearing a black crown with a white halo on the burnt veld.

migration: Mostly resident in the Lowveld, in pairs near water and damp grassland. Some birds wander locally after the rains, so numbers at a given site vary. Lays from July to December, peaking in September-October, on bare or burnt ground.
size: About 34 cm: a large lapwing, bigger and longer-legged than a Crowned Lapwing.
keys: Bright yellow wattles hanging from the base of the bill, red at the top in front of the eye
Mostly brown-grey with a white forehead patch and a streaked black-and-white head
Long yellow legs and a yellow bill with a black tip
In flight: white bar across the wing between brown coverts and black flight feathers, white tail with a black band

confuse.how: Has a black cap ringed with white, red legs and a red-based bill, and no wattles; prefers dry, short grass.
Boldly black, white and grey, with black legs and no wattles; gives a metallic “tink-tink”.

voice: A loud, sharp, nasal “peep-peep” or “yip-yip”, repeated, given day and night; displaying birds give a fast, laughing series.
behaviour: Walks slowly over damp grass, pausing often on one leg, then dashes onto insects. It also stamps its feet to flush prey. Very noisy and bold around its nest, diving at intruders.
memo: The lapwing with yellow earrings dangling from its bill.

migration: Resident and sedentary, wherever its host the African Firefinch lives (thickets and riverine scrub). Males moult into glossy black breeding plumage for the rainy season, when they sing for hours from a favourite perch; in the dry season they look like brown females and go largely unnoticed.
size: 10-11 cm: smaller than a House Sparrow, about the size of a firefinch.
keys: Breeding male: all glossy blue-black or purplish-black, with browner wings
Short white or pale bill and orange-red legs (the southern race)
Female and non-breeding male: sparrow-like, with bold buff and dark brown head stripes, streaked back and greyish-white underparts
Short tail, no long streamers

confuse.how: Breeding male is black and white with a red bill and very long tail; female and non-breeding birds have a red bill, not a whitish one.
Bigger and longer-tailed, with a thin black bill and dark legs; catches insects from a perch instead of eating seeds on the ground.
Non-breeding birds are also streaky brown, but have a big bright red bill and travel in flocks.

voice: The male mimics its host, the African Firefinch: scratchy notes, trills and tinkling phrases, including the firefinch's fast “pit-pit-pit” alarm, mixed with its own chattering song.
behaviour: A brood parasite that lays only in the nests of the African Firefinch; the chicks even copy the mouth markings of firefinch chicks. Each male defends a song perch, often the top of a bare tree, and returns to it day after day, so if you hear a “firefinch” singing high up in the open, look for a tiny black bird.
memo: A little black bird with a white bill singing firefinch songs from a treetop.

migration: Resident all year in the Lowveld, with only local wandering. Outside the breeding season it joins flocks of seedeaters, often more than a hundred birds. Breeds in the rainy season, from about November to April, when the males wear their long tails.
size: 12 cm without the tail: about the size of a House Sparrow. In summer the breeding male trails a tail of about 20 cm.
keys: Breeding male: black and white, with a black cap, white cheeks and underparts, and a very long, thin black tail
Bright red, waxy bill in all plumages except the juvenile
Female and non-breeding male: streaky brown above, buff face boldly striped black, whitish below
White patches in the dark wings of the breeding male

confuse.how: The female has the same striped head, but a whitish, not red, bill and no long tail in any plumage. The male is all glossy black.
Also streaky brown with a red bill, but the face lacks the bold black stripes. Almost always in big, dense flocks.

voice: From a high perch the male gives a rapid, scratchy series of squeaks and sparrow-like chirps, repeated in a rhythmic pattern.
behaviour: A brood parasite: the female lays her eggs in waxbill nests, above all those of the Common Waxbill, without destroying the host's eggs. The chicks copy the mouth markings of the waxbill chicks. The breeding male guards a small harem from a lookout perch and hovers above the females, bouncing in the air to show off his streaming tail.
memo: A black-and-white sparrow with a red bill, dancing in the air on a ribbon of a tail.

migration: Resident all year wherever water and fringing vegetation remain, such as dams, pans and reedy river pools. It only makes local movements: in a drought birds leave dams that dry out and come back with the rains. Breeds mainly in the rainy season, and a pair can raise up to four broods.
size: 19-23 cm: about the size of a blackbird, but with long red legs and very long toes.
keys: All black or slate-black, with no white anywhere
Bright yellow (greenish-yellow) bill
Red legs and feet, red eye and a thin red eye-ring
Juvenile: browner or greyish, with a dark bill and dull legs

confuse.how: Larger, with a red shield on the forehead, a red-and-yellow bill, a white line along the flanks and white under the tail.
Lives in grassland, not at the water's edge; brown upperparts and flanks boldly barred black and white.

voice: A loud duet: one bird gives a harsh, guttural chatter “krrrok-kraaaa” and its mate answers with soft, dove-like purring coos. Sharp “chip” alarm and soft “pruk” contact calls.
behaviour: Unusually bold for a crake: it walks in the open on floating plants and along the water's edge. It sometimes climbs onto hippos and warthogs to pick off parasites. In the breeding season it is aggressive and chases other rails.
memo: A small black chicken with a banana-yellow bill and red legs, sometimes riding a hippo.

migration: Mostly sedentary, but outside the breeding season it forms flocks that wander locally, possibly moving downslope in winter. Breeds August to April, with a peak from September to December, in a small cup nest bound with spider web in a tree. In the Lowveld it is scarce and local, mainly in riverine bush and gardens.
size: About 12 cm: smaller than a House Sparrow, warbler-like.
keys: Bold ring of white feathers around the eye
Green upperparts, bright yellow throat and undertail
Breast and belly washed greenish-yellow in the local race (virens), grey in the southern race
Small, sharp bill; usually in small, restless groups

confuse.how: No white eye-ring: a pale stripe over the eye instead. Paler, olive-brown above, and alone rather than in chattering groups.

voice: Constant soft, trilled contact calls from the group. The song is a jerky series of reedy phrases that rise and fall, sometimes with imitations of other birds.
behaviour: Moves through the foliage in chattering little groups, gleaning aphids and other small insects from the leaves. It also eats soft fruit such as figs and drinks nectar from aloes and coral-trees. Outside the breeding season the groups merge into larger flocks and join mixed bird parties.
memo: A small green-and-yellow bird with white spectacles, always in a chattering gang.

migration: Adults stay on their home range, while young birds wander after leaving their parents. The atlas reports it so rarely around Pidwa that its months say little, so they are not taken from it.
size: 75-96 cm, wingspan about 1.8-2.3 m: a very large eagle, very similar in size to the Martial Eagle.
keys: Jet-black, with a white V on the back that runs down to the rump, partly hidden when perched
Yellow cere, eye-ring and “eyebrows”, and yellow feet
In flight: paddle-shaped wings, broad in the middle and pinched at the base of the primaries, with a white window on the primaries seen from above and below
Juvenile: brown, with a golden crown, rufous nape, black cheeks and no white V; adult plumage after about 4-6 years

confuse.how: Similar in size, but it has a dark hood, a white spotted belly and dark underwings, without the black body and white V.

voice: Largely silent. In display, a harsh yelping call and a melodious “keee-up”; contact and chase calls such as “whaeee-whaeee” or “keeooo-keeooo”.
behaviour: A bird of cliffs, gorges and rocky hills, usually in pairs. Hyraxes are its main and often only prey, and it rarely comes to carrion. It rides the wind along rock faces, and mates are recorded hunting together, one distracting the prey. Usually lays two eggs, and the older chick nearly always kills the younger one.
memo: The black eagle with a white V on its back: where there are cliffs and hyraxes.
